parts.answer: The guest OS issues the request to its virtual disk; the hypervisor intercepts it and translates it into a request to the host OS / real hardware, which writes the data to a file representing the virtual disk.
parts.working: 1 mark intercepted by hypervisor; 1 mark translated and carried out by host / real hardware.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: The VM emulates hardware, so timing / performance and some devices differ from the real machine.

parts.text: Describe each of these computer architectures: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD.
parts.answer:
SISD: single instruction, single data — one processor carries out one instruction on one data item at a time.
SIMD: single instruction, multiple data — several processors carry out the same instruction on different data items at the same time.
MISD: multiple instruction, single data — several processors carry out different instructions on the same data.
MIMD: multiple instruction, multiple data — several processors each carry out different instructions on different data (e.g. multicore computers).

(i) SIMD — the same instruction (add a brightness value) is applied to many pixels (data items) at once.
(ii) MIMD — each core runs different instructions (different programs) on different data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a massively parallel computer.
parts.answer: A computer with a very large number of processors (hundreds/thousands or more) that work simultaneously on parts of one problem, linked by a network / interconnect so they can communicate.
parts.working: 1 mark very many processors; 1 mark working together on one task / communicating.

stem: The national meteorological department in Pakistan uses a massively parallel computer to produce monsoon forecasts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the characteristics of a massively parallel computer system that make it suitable for weather forecasting.
parts.answer:
1 mark each, max 3:
• thousands of processors work simultaneously
• the forecast area can be split into many grid cells, each handled by a different processor
• processors are linked by a high-speed network to exchange results for neighbouring cells
• each processor has its own memory, so huge amounts of data can be processed at once

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the software must be specially written for this computer.
parts.answer: The program must be split into tasks that can run at the same time (parallel algorithms), and must coordinate / synchronise the processors and the data they share.
parts.working: 1 mark split into parallel tasks; 1 mark coordination / communication.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why some problems do not run much faster on a massively parallel computer.
parts.answer: If each step depends on the result of the previous step, the work cannot be divided, so most processors would be idle / communication overheads outweigh gains.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four differences between RISC and CISC processors.
parts.answer:
1 mark each, max 4:
• RISC has fewer, simpler instructions; CISC has many complex instructions
• RISC instructions are mostly executed in one clock cycle; CISC instructions take several cycles
• RISC instructions have a fixed length; CISC instructions vary in length
• RISC has fewer addressing modes; CISC has many
• RISC uses many general-purpose registers; CISC has fewer
• RISC is hard-wired control; CISC often uses microprogrammed control
• RISC is easier to pipeline
• RISC programs need more instructions / more RAM; CISC programs are shorter (more work for the compiler with RISC)
parts.working: Each difference must compare both.

stem: A processor uses a 5-stage pipeline: instruction fetch (IF), instruction decode (ID), operand fetch (OF), instruction execute (IE) and write back (WB). Each stage takes one clock cycle. Assume there are no branches or interrupts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many clock cycles are needed to complete 8 instructions with pipelining, and how many without pipelining. Show your working.
parts.answer: With pipelining: 12 cycles. Without pipelining: 40 cycles.
parts.working:
M1 first instruction takes 5 cycles, then one more instruction completes every cycle: 5 + (8 − 1) = 12
A1 12
B1 without pipelining 8 × 5 = 40

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which instruction is in each stage during clock cycle 4.
parts.answer: Instruction 1 in IE (execute), instruction 2 in OF (operand fetch), instruction 3 in ID (decode), instruction 4 in IF (fetch); the WB stage is empty.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why RISC processors are well suited to pipelining.
parts.answer: RISC instructions are of fixed length and most take one clock cycle, so each stage takes the same time and the stages stay in step / the pipeline flows smoothly.
parts.working: 1 mark fixed length / one cycle; 1 mark stages balanced.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A RISC processor uses a 5-stage pipeline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the problem caused when an interrupt occurs in a pipelined processor, and describe one way it can be handled.
parts.answer:
Problem: several instructions are partly processed in different stages when the interrupt arrives, so the processor state cannot be saved simply by storing one program counter value.
Handling (any one, 2 marks): the instructions in the early stages are flushed/erased, the instruction(s) already in the execute stage are completed, and the address of the next instruction to restart is saved before the interrupt service routine runs; OR each stage has its own program-counter register so the contents of the pipeline can be saved and restored after the interrupt.
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 2 marks a described method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a conditional branch (jump) instruction reduces the performance of the pipeline.
parts.answer: The next instructions are fetched in sequence before the branch is executed; if the branch is taken, these instructions are wrong and must be discarded (pipeline flushed), so cycles are wasted until the pipeline refills.
parts.working: 1 mark wrong instructions already fetched; 1 mark flush / wasted cycles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one technique used to reduce this loss.
parts.answer: Branch prediction / speculative execution / delayed branch (filling the slot after a branch with a useful instruction).

parts.text: Describe the difference between a logical shift right and a cyclic shift right.
parts.answer: Logical: bits move one place right, the bit leaving the right end is lost and a 0 enters at the left. Cyclic: the bit leaving the right end is moved round into the left-most position, so no bits are lost.
parts.working: B1 logical – 0 enters at left, bit lost. B1 cyclic – bit leaving the right re-enters at the left.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
An 8-bit register holds 11001011. Give its contents after:
(i) a cyclic shift right of one place
(ii) a cyclic shift left of two places
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one use of cyclic shifts.
parts.answer: e.g. in encryption/hashing algorithms, or to examine each bit of a value in turn without losing it.
parts.working: B1 any sensible use.

stem: An 8-bit register holds 11101000, a two's complement integer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the denary value held.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the contents of the register after an arithmetic shift right of two places, and its denary value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the contents after a logical shift right of two places, and explain why this is not suitable for dividing this number by 4.
parts.answer: 00111010 (= 58). Zeros enter at the left, so the sign bit becomes 0 and the number changes from negative to positive.
parts.working: B1: 00111010. B1: sign bit not preserved / result 58 is positive.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The processor has an accumulator (ACC) and an index register (IX). It uses this part of the instruction set:
LDM #n: load the number n into ACC
LDD <address>: load the contents of the address into ACC
LDI <address>: the address holds a second address; load the contents of the second address into ACC
LDX <address>: form the address <address> + contents of IX; load the contents of that address into ACC
LDR #n: load the number n into IX
STO <address>: store the contents of ACC at the address
ADD <address> / ADD #n: add the contents of the address / the number n to ACC
SUB <address> / SUB #n: subtract the contents of the address / the number n from ACC
INC <register> / DEC <register>: add 1 to / subtract 1 from ACC or IX
CMP <address> / CMP #n: compare ACC with the contents of the address / the number n
CMI <address>: the address holds a second address; compare ACC with the contents of the second address
JPE <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was True
JPN <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was False
JMP <address>: jump to the address
IN: read one character from the keyboard and store its ASCII code in ACC
OUT: output the character whose ASCII code is in ACC
END: return control to the operating system
AND / OR / XOR #n, Bn or &n: bitwise operation between ACC and the operand (# denary, B binary, & hexadecimal)
LSL #n / LSR #n: logical shift left / right of ACC by n places; zeros enter the vacated bits

A greenhouse near Multan has a controller. The value at address 70 is a status byte. Each bit shows one device: bit 0 (right-most) is the water pump, bit 3 is the roof vent, bit 5 is the heater. A bit is 1 when the device is ON.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write assembly language code that switches the heater ON without changing any other bit, and stores the result back at address 70.
parts.answer:
LDD 70
OR B00100000
STO 70

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write assembly language code that switches the water pump OFF without changing any other bit, and stores the result back at address 70.
parts.answer:
LDD 70
AND B11111110
STO 70

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write assembly language code that jumps to address 90 if the roof vent is ON.
parts.answer:
LDD 70
AND B00001000
CMP #8
JPE 90
parts.working: B1: load and AND with B00001000. B1: compare with 8 (or compare with 0 and JPN). B1: correct conditional jump to 90.

author: HomiLabs

The processor has an accumulator (ACC) and an index register (IX). It uses this part of the instruction set:
LDM #n: load the number n into ACC
LDD <address>: load the contents of the address into ACC
LDI <address>: the address holds a second address; load the contents of the second address into ACC
LDX <address>: form the address <address> + contents of IX; load the contents of that address into ACC

The register is 8 bits. Address 90 holds 10110010.
10 LDM #0
11 STO 91
12 LDD 90
13 AND #1
14 ADD 91
15 STO 91
16 LDD 90
17 LSR #1
18 STO 90
19 CMP #0
20 JPN 12
21 END

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the contents of addresses 90 and 91 when the program ends.
parts.answer: 90 contains 00000000; 91 contains 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many times the instruction at address 13 is executed.
parts.working: B1: 8 – the value needs 8 shifts before it becomes 0 because its left-most bit is 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the purpose of the program and explain how AND #1 and LSR #1 work together.
parts.answer: It counts the number of 1 bits in the byte at address 90. AND #1 masks out everything except the right-most bit, giving 1 or 0, which is added to the count. LSR #1 then moves the next bit into the right-most position. The loop stops when the remaining value is 0.
parts.working: B1: counts the 1 bits (stores count in 91). B1: AND #1 isolates the least significant bit. B1: LSR #1 brings the next bit to bit 0 / loop ends when value becomes 0.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one disadvantage of the program.
parts.answer: The original value at address 90 is destroyed (overwritten with 0).
parts.working: B1: original data lost / should copy it first.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The processor has an accumulator (ACC) and an index register (IX). It uses this part of the instruction set:
LDM #n: load the number n into ACC
LDD <address>: load the contents of the address into ACC
LDI <address>: the address holds a second address; load the contents of the second address into ACC
LDX <address>: form the address <address> + contents of IX; load the contents of that address into ACC
LDR #n: load the number n into IX
STO <address>: store the contents of ACC at the address
ADD <address> / ADD #n: add the contents of the address / the number n to ACC
SUB <address> / SUB #n: subtract the contents of the address / the number n from ACC
INC <register> / DEC <register>: add 1 to / subtract 1 from ACC or IX
CMP <address> / CMP #n: compare ACC with the contents of the address / the number n
CMI <address>: the address holds a second address; compare ACC with the contents of the second address
JPE <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was True
JPN <address>: jump to the address if the last comparison was False
JMP <address>: jump to the address
IN: read one character from the keyboard and store its ASCII code in ACC
OUT: output the character whose ASCII code is in ACC
END: return control to the operating system
AND / OR / XOR #n, Bn or &n: bitwise operation between ACC and the operand (# denary, B binary, & hexadecimal)
LSL #n / LSR #n: logical shift left / right of ACC by n places; zeros enter the vacated bits

ACC is an 8-bit register. A positive integer is stored at address 600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write assembly language code that multiplies the value at 600 by 10 using shifts and addition only, and stores the result at 602. You may use address 601 for working.
parts.answer:
LDD 600
LSL #3
STO 601
LDD 600
LSL #1
ADD 601
STO 602
parts.working: B1: LSL #3 (× 8). B1: stored temporarily (601). B1: LSL #1 on original (× 2). B1: added and stored at 602. Accept other correct orders, e.g. (×4 + ×1) × 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the largest value at address 600 for which your code gives a correct result, and explain why a larger value fails.
parts.answer: 25. 25 × 10 = 250 fits in 8 bits, but 26 × 10 = 260 is greater than 255, so a 1 is lost from the left and the result is wrong (260 − 256 = 4).
parts.working: B1: 25. B1: result must be ≤ 255 / bits overflow beyond 8 bits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using shifts can be quicker than a loop of repeated additions.
parts.answer: A shift is a single instruction, whereas repeated addition needs many instructions (one pass per addition plus compare and jump).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three factors that affect the performance of a computer system's processor.
parts.answer: Any three of: clock speed, number of cores, size of cache memory, width of the data bus, width of the address bus.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student in Faisalabad replaces a dual-core processor with a quad-core processor of the same clock speed. Explain why her programs may not run twice as fast.
parts.answer: Some programs are not written to run on several cores at once, so tasks cannot be split. Also the cores must communicate/share memory and wait for each other, which takes time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: software not designed for multiple cores / some tasks must be done in sequence; overhead of communication/synchronisation between cores; other bottlenecks (memory, bus).

stem: A school in Lahore is setting up a classroom computer. It will be connected to a projector, a keyboard, a mouse and a printer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the purpose of each port.
(i) USB
(ii) HDMI
(iii) VGA
parts.answer: (i) Universal Serial Bus: a standard serial port used to connect many types of device (keyboard, mouse, printer, flash drive) and can supply power. (ii) High Definition Multimedia Interface: carries high-definition digital video and audio to a monitor, TV or projector. (iii) Video Graphics Array: carries analogue video (no audio) to an older monitor or projector.
parts.working: B1 each: USB – connect many peripheral types/data + power; HDMI – digital video and audio; VGA – analogue video only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The projector has only HDMI and VGA inputs. State which port should be used and give a reason.
parts.answer: HDMI, because it carries digital high-definition video and also the audio, with one cable.
parts.working: B1 HDMI. B1 reason: higher quality digital picture / carries sound too.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A processor has a 24-bit address bus and a 32-bit data bus. Each memory location holds one byte.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of memory locations that can be addressed directly. Give your answer as a power of 2 and in denary.
parts.answer: 2²⁴ = 16 777 216 locations

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the maximum amount of memory, in MiB, that can be addressed.
parts.answer: 16 MiB
parts.working: B1: 2²⁴ bytes ÷ 2²⁰ = 16 MiB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how increasing the width of the data bus can improve performance.
parts.answer: More bits are transferred at the same time, so fewer transfers are needed to move the same amount of data / a whole word can be moved in one transfer.
parts.working: B1 more bits per transfer. B1 fewer fetches needed / faster data transfer.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A processor has a clock speed of 3.2 GHz. Calculate the time for one clock cycle in nanoseconds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how cache memory improves the performance of a processor.
parts.answer: Cache is fast memory on or near the processor. It holds data and instructions that are used often or are likely to be needed next. The processor can read these from cache instead of the slower main memory, so it waits less.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: faster than RAM; stores frequently used / next instructions or data; checked first before RAM; reduces time the processor waits / fewer RAM accesses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why doubling the clock speed does not always double performance.
parts.answer: The processor may still have to wait for data from memory or devices (other bottlenecks), and heat may force it to slow down.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason.

stem:
A video-editing student in Islamabad must choose between two laptops.
Laptop P: 8 cores, 2.6 GHz, 24 MiB cache, 64-bit data bus.
Laptop Q: 4 cores, 3.4 GHz, 8 MiB cache, 32-bit data bus.
Her editing software can use many cores at once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many data bus transfers each laptop needs to move a 4 KiB block of data.
parts.answer: P: 512 transfers; Q: 1024 transfers

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend one laptop for the student. Justify your choice by referring to all the factors given.
parts.answer: Laptop P. The software can use many cores, so 8 cores can process more parts of a video at once than 4, which outweighs Q's higher clock speed. The larger cache holds more of the video data and instructions, so fewer slow RAM accesses. The 64-bit data bus moves twice as much data per transfer (512 rather than 1024 transfers per 4 KiB).
parts.working: B1: P chosen with at least one reason. B1: cores vs clock speed argument (multi-threaded software). B1: larger cache benefit. B1: wider data bus benefit. Q with clock-speed argument only can score max 1.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the Von Neumann model for a computer system.
parts.answer: Programs (instructions) and data are stored together in the same main memory; instructions are fetched one at a time and executed in sequence by a single processor; the processor is connected to memory by buses and uses special registers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: stored program concept; instructions and data in the same memory / same format; single processor / control unit; sequential fetch-execute; uses buses; uses registers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the system clock.
parts.answer: It produces timing signals at a regular rate so that the components of the processor work in step (synchronised).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each description, name the register.
(i) Holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
(ii) Holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed.
(iii) Holds data or an instruction just read from memory, or about to be written to memory.
(iv) Holds the address of the memory location about to be read from or written to.
(v) Holds individual bits (flags) that show the result of an operation, such as a carry or overflow.
parts.answer: (i) Program Counter (PC) (ii) Current Instruction Register (CIR) (iii) Memory Data Register (MDR) (iv) Memory Address Register (MAR) (v) Status Register
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a general-purpose register and a special-purpose register, naming one example of each.
parts.answer: A general-purpose register can hold any data for the program, e.g. the accumulator (ACC). A special-purpose register has one fixed job, e.g. the PC.
parts.working: B1: general purpose – used for any data/temporary values, example ACC. B1: special purpose – dedicated role, example PC/MAR/MDR/CIR/IX/status register.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of each of these buses: address bus, data bus, control bus. Include the direction in which each carries signals.
parts.answer: Address bus: carries memory addresses from the processor to memory/devices; one direction (unidirectional). Data bus: carries data and instructions between the processor, memory and I/O; both directions. Control bus: carries control and timing signals (e.g. memory read, memory write, clock, interrupt) in both directions.
parts.working: B1 each, with direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and the control unit (CU).
parts.answer: ALU: carries out arithmetic (e.g. addition) and logical operations (e.g. AND, comparisons) on data. CU: decodes instructions and sends control signals to coordinate the movement of data and the operation of the other components.
parts.working: B1 ALU. B1 CU.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional.
parts.answer: Only the processor sends addresses (to memory); memory never needs to send an address back.

stem: A processor adds two 8-bit two's complement numbers in the accumulator: 01100100 + 00111100. The status register has a carry flag (C), a negative flag (N) and an overflow flag (V).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the 8-bit result of the addition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of each flag after the addition. Justify each one.
parts.answer: C = 0: there is no carry out of the most significant bit. N = 1: the result's sign bit is 1. V = 1: two positive numbers (100 and 60) have given a negative result, because 160 is too large for 8-bit two's complement (maximum 127).
parts.working: B1 C = 0 with reason. B1 N = 1 with reason. B1 V = 1 with reason (160 > 127 / sign changed).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a program could use the overflow flag.
parts.answer: After an arithmetic instruction it can test the flag and jump to error-handling code, so an incorrect result is not used.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the fetch stage in register transfer notation. [ ] means 'the contents of'.
MAR ← ______
PC ← ______
MDR ← ______
CIR ← ______
parts.answer:
MAR ← [PC]
PC ← [PC] + 1
MDR ← [[MAR]]
CIR ← [MDR]
parts.working: B1 each line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the instruction in the CIR after the fetch stage.
parts.answer: It is decoded by the control unit and then executed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two different sources of an interrupt.
parts.answer: e.g. a printer running out of paper (hardware), a timer signal, a division by zero (software error), a key being pressed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two different sources.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a processor detects and handles an interrupt.
parts.answer: At the end of each fetch-execute cycle the processor checks for interrupts. If there is one of a higher priority than the current task, the contents of the registers (including the PC) are saved on a stack. The address of the matching interrupt service routine (ISR) is loaded into the PC and the ISR is executed. When it finishes, the saved register contents are restored from the stack and the original program continues where it stopped.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: checked at end of each cycle; priority compared; registers/PC saved (on stack); ISR address loaded into PC / ISR executed; registers restored afterwards; original task resumes; lower-priority interrupts may be disabled while ISR runs.

stem: The program counter (PC) contains 310. Memory address 310 holds the instruction LDD 452 and address 452 holds the value 87.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the contents of the PC, MAR, MDR, CIR and ACC after the instruction has been fetched and executed. Give the final values only.
parts.answer: PC 311, MAR 452, MDR 87, CIR LDD 452, ACC 87
parts.working: B1 each. During the fetch MAR = 310 and MDR = LDD 452; during execution the operand 452 is copied to MAR and 87 is read into MDR, then copied to ACC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: While LDD 452 is being executed, a keyboard interrupt arrives. Explain why the processor does not deal with it immediately.
parts.answer: The processor checks for interrupts only at the end of each fetch-execute cycle, so it completes LDD 452 first; this means the instruction is not left half-finished and the register values can be saved in a consistent state.
parts.working: B1: checked at end of cycle / current instruction finished first. B1: so that the state can be saved and resumed correctly.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three differences between a local area network (LAN) and a wide area network (WAN).
parts.answer: LAN covers a small area (one building/site), WAN covers a large geographical area (cities/countries). LAN hardware and cables are usually owned by the organisation; WAN uses leased lines/infrastructure owned by telecom companies. LAN usually has higher data rates and fewer errors than a WAN.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three contrasted differences: area covered; ownership of infrastructure; transmission rate; error rate/reliability; media used (LAN – cable/Wi-Fi, WAN – telephone lines, fibre, satellite).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A textile company has offices in Faisalabad and Dubai connected together. State the type of network that connects the two offices.
parts.answer: WAN
parts.working: B1: WAN.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a star topology.
parts.answer: Each device is connected by its own cable to a central device (a switch or hub); all data between devices passes through this central device.
parts.working: B1: each device has its own link. B1: to a central switch/hub/server.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages of a star topology compared with a bus topology.
parts.answer: A fault in one cable affects only one device; data goes only to the destination device through the switch, so fewer collisions/better security and performance; easy to add devices without disrupting the network.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of a star topology.
parts.answer: If the central switch fails the whole network stops; more cable is needed.
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the topology described in each case.
(i) All devices are attached to one shared cable that has a terminator at each end.
(ii) Every device has a direct link to every other device.
(iii) Two star networks in separate buildings are joined by a single cable between their switches.
parts.answer: (i) bus (ii) (full) mesh (iii) hybrid
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cable in topology (i) needs a terminator at each end.
parts.answer: To absorb the signals at the ends of the cable so they are not reflected back and interfere with other signals.

stem: A research lab connects its six servers in a full mesh topology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of links needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A seventh server is added to the mesh. Calculate how many extra links are needed.
parts.working: B1: 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21; 21 − 15 = 6 (one to each existing server).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a mesh topology for these servers.
parts.answer: Advantage: there are alternative routes, so if one link fails data can still get through (fault tolerant / no single point of failure). Disadvantage: many cables and network ports are needed, so it is expensive and hard to set up.
parts.working: B1 advantage (redundant routes / fast direct links). B1 disadvantage (cost / amount of cabling / complex).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hospital in Peshawar has three buildings. Each building has its own star network with a switch. The three switches are connected to each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of this topology and give one reason it suits the hospital.
parts.answer: Hybrid topology. Each building can be managed and expanded separately, and a fault in one building's star does not stop the others.
parts.working: B1 hybrid. B1 suitable reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a data packet is sent from a computer in the X-ray department to a printer in the same building.
parts.answer: The computer sends the packet along its cable to the building's switch. The switch reads the destination MAC address in the packet. It looks it up in its table and forwards the packet only to the port connected to the printer.
parts.working: B1 packet sent to switch. B1 switch reads destination (MAC) address. B1 forwarded only to the printer's port/link.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A small design studio in Karachi uses a bus network with eight computers. It plans to double the number of computers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the performance of the bus network will become worse as more computers are added.
parts.answer: All devices share one cable, so only one device can transmit at a time. More devices means more traffic and more collisions, so data has to be re-sent more often.
parts.working: B1 single shared cable / one transmission at a time. B1 more collisions / more waiting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to the network if the main cable is cut between the fourth and fifth computers.
parts.answer: The whole network fails / the two halves cannot communicate, and signals reflect from the unterminated broken ends, causing errors even within each half.
parts.working: B1 network (or communication across the break) stops. B1 no terminator at the break – reflections/errors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Recommend a new topology for the studio and justify your choice.
parts.answer: Star topology with a switch: each computer has its own link, the switch sends data only to the destination so there are far fewer collisions, and it is easy to add computers without stopping the network.
parts.working: B1 star. B1 justification linked to the studio (expansion / performance / fault isolation).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bank has its head office in Islamabad and 11 branches in other cities (12 sites in total). The sites must be connected so that every branch can exchange data with every other site.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many links are needed if the 12 sites are connected in a full mesh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many links are needed if every branch is connected only to the head office, in a star arrangement.
parts.working: B1: one link per branch = 11.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss which arrangement the bank should use.
parts.answer: Star: only 11 links so much cheaper; but all traffic passes through head office, which is a single point of failure, and branch-to-branch data must travel two links. Mesh: no single point of failure and direct routes, but 66 links is very expensive. A sensible decision is a star (or partial mesh) with a backup link at head office, because cost matters and most traffic goes to head office anyway.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: star cheaper/fewer links; star single point of failure; mesh redundancy/fault tolerance; mesh cost/complexity; reasoned conclusion (e.g. partial mesh / star with backup).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the role of each device in a LAN.
(i) switch
(ii) router
(iii) network interface card (NIC)
(iv) wireless access point (WAP)
parts.answer: (i) Connects devices in a LAN and forwards each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. (ii) Connects different networks (e.g. the LAN to the internet) and directs packets towards their destination using IP addresses. (iii) Hardware that lets a device connect to the network; it has a unique MAC address. (iv) Lets wireless devices connect to a wired network using radio waves (Wi-Fi).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of a modem when a home connects to the internet over a telephone line.
parts.answer: It converts digital signals from the computer into analogue signals for the line, and analogue back to digital (modulation/demodulation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of fibre-optic cable compared with copper cable.
parts.answer: Higher bandwidth / data rate; signals travel further before needing to be boosted; not affected by electromagnetic interference; harder to tap (more secure); lighter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why copper (twisted-pair) cable is still used inside most office LANs.
parts.answer: It is cheaper; easier to install, bend and join; existing equipment and ports use it; its data rate is enough over short distances.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

stem: A factory in Sialkot has a long production hall. Computers at both ends of the hall are on the same wired network.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a repeater may be needed in the cable along the hall.
parts.answer: Signals become weaker (attenuated) and distorted as they travel along a long cable. A repeater receives the signal and regenerates/boosts it so it can travel further.
parts.working: B1 signal weakens over distance. B1 repeater regenerates/amplifies it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The factory office has its own separate network segment. Describe the role of a bridge in joining the office segment to the factory segment.
parts.answer: A bridge connects two LAN segments that use the same protocol so they act as one network; it only passes on frames that are addressed to a device on the other segment, reducing unnecessary traffic.
parts.working: B1 joins two LANs/segments (same protocol). B1 filters traffic / forwards only frames for the other side.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three differences between a switch and a router.
parts.answer: A switch connects devices within one network; a router connects separate networks. A switch uses MAC addresses; a router uses IP addresses. A router can choose a route for packets and can connect a LAN to the internet / give it a public IP address; a switch cannot.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three contrasted differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a router stores a routing table.
parts.answer: So it can decide which network or next router to send each packet to, to reach its destination.

stem: A village school in Gilgit-Baltistan can connect to the internet either by a geostationary satellite or by a new fibre-optic line. The satellite is 35 786 km above the Earth's surface and radio signals travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum time for a signal to travel from the school up to the satellite and down to the ground station. Give your answer in milliseconds, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 239 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this delay is a problem for video lessons with a live teacher, even when the bandwidth is high.
parts.answer: A request and reply each go up and down (about 0.48 s round trip), so there is a noticeable lag in a two-way conversation; speech overlaps and the lesson feels delayed. Bandwidth affects how much data arrives, not how long it takes to arrive.
parts.working: B1 round trip roughly double / noticeable lag in two-way communication. B1 latency is different from bandwidth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of satellite over fibre for this school.
parts.answer: No cable needs to be laid over mountainous ground; can be set up quickly anywhere with a view of the sky.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A college is setting up a new computer room with 30 desktop computers, a laser printer and a file server. The computers will be used for online practical exams.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hardware devices, other than the computers, printer and cables, needed to build this LAN and connect it to the internet. Give the purpose of each.
parts.answer: Switch – connects all computers, printer and server and forwards data to the correct device. Router – connects the LAN to the internet. NIC in each device – connects it to the network / gives it a MAC address. (Also accept a firewall.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for device + purpose, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The principal suggests using Wi-Fi only. Justify why wired connections are better for the exam computers.
parts.answer: Wired connections give a more reliable, constant data rate, so 30 computers do not compete for the same radio bandwidth; they are not affected by interference or walls; they are more secure because a device must be physically connected, so it is harder for others to intercept or join.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: reliability/stability; speed/bandwidth not shared; less interference; security (cannot eavesdrop/join easily); exams need no dropped connections.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web (WWW).
parts.answer: The internet is the worldwide network of interconnected networks (the hardware and infrastructure). The WWW is a collection of web pages and resources, accessed using HTTP(S), that is carried over the internet.
parts.working: B1 internet = global network of networks / infrastructure. B1 WWW = web pages/resources accessed via browsers/HTTP – a service on the internet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of a uniform resource locator (URL).
parts.answer: It gives the address of a web resource/page so a browser can find it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each of these is a valid IPv4 address. Give a reason for any that are not valid.
(i) 10.0.0.5
(ii) 192.168.1.256
(iii) 203.99.162.4
(iv) 172.16.40
parts.answer: (i) valid (ii) not valid – 256 is greater than 255 (each group is 8 bits) (iii) valid (iv) not valid – only three groups, there must be four
parts.working: B1 each; reason needed for (ii) and (iv).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of different IPv4 addresses.
parts.working: B1: 2³².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the format of an IPv6 address.
parts.answer: 128 bits written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, separated by colons; leading zeros in a group can be left out and one run of all-zero groups can be replaced by ::.
parts.working: B1 128 bits / 8 groups of 16 bits. B1 hexadecimal with colons (shortening rules).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write this IPv6 address in its shortest form: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329
parts.working: B1 leading zeros removed (db8, 42). B1 three zero groups replaced by ::.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why IPv6 was introduced. Include in your answer how many times more addresses IPv6 has than IPv4, as a power of 2.
parts.answer: The number of IPv4 addresses (2³²) is not enough for all the devices now connected to the internet. IPv6 has 2¹²⁸ addresses, which is 2⁹⁶ times as many.
parts.working: B1 IPv4 addresses running out / too many devices. B1 2⁹⁶.

stem: An online clothing shop in Karachi runs its own web server. Its staff use laptops connected to the office network.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a public IP address and a private IP address.
parts.answer: A public IP address is unique on the whole internet and can be reached from anywhere on it. A private IP address is used only inside a LAN, can be reused in other LANs, and cannot be reached directly from the internet.
parts.working: B1 public – globally unique / routable on the internet. B1 private – only within a LAN / not routable / reusable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the web server should have a static public IP address, while the staff laptops can have dynamic private IP addresses.
parts.answer: Customers must always be able to find the server, so its public address must not change (the DNS record points to it). The laptops only need to be reached inside the office; the router can give them any free address each time they connect (by DHCP), which saves addresses and needs no manual set-up.
parts.working: B1 server must be reachable from the internet (public). B1 address must not change so DNS/customers can find it (static). B1 laptops only used internally / addresses assigned automatically and reused (dynamic private).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student types www.example.edu.pk/timetable into a browser.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the domain name and the path in this URL.
parts.answer: Domain name: www.example.edu.pk (example.edu.pk); path: /timetable
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the Domain Name Service (DNS) finds the IP address of the web server.
parts.answer: The browser sends the domain name to a DNS server (set by the ISP). The DNS server looks for the name in its own records/cache. If it does not have it, it passes the request to other DNS servers in the hierarchy (root, .pk, edu.pk …) until one with the record is found. The IP address is returned to the browser (and cached), which then uses it to request the page from the web server.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: request sent to DNS server; lookup in its database/cache; passed to another (higher-level) DNS server if not found; IP address returned to the browser; browser connects to that IP / cached for later; error returned if no record exists.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A laptop in a home network has the private IP address 172.20.15.200. The home router has one public IP address given by the internet service provider.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert 172.20.15.200 to its 32-bit binary form.
parts.working: B1 any two groups correct. B1 all four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the laptop can request a web page from the internet when it has only a private IP address.
parts.answer: The laptop sends the request to the router. The router replaces the private source address with its own public IP address before sending it on to the internet, and records which device made the request. When the reply comes back to the public address, the router sends it on to the laptop's private address.
parts.working: B1 request goes via router. B1 router uses its public IP address for the request. B1 router keeps a record and forwards the reply to the laptop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why many homes can all use the same private address 172.20.15.200 at the same time.
parts.answer: Private addresses are not used on the internet itself; they only need to be unique within each LAN.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the client-server model.
parts.answer: A server is a central computer that provides services or resources (files, web pages, email, printing). Clients are computers that send requests to the server, which processes them and sends back the responses.
parts.working: B1 server provides services/resources centrally. B1 clients make requests and receive responses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two differences between a client-server network and a peer-to-peer network.
parts.answer: Peer-to-peer has no central server – each computer is both client and server and shares its own resources; client-server stores data centrally. Client-server security and backups are managed centrally; in peer-to-peer each user manages their own.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two contrasted differences (central server vs none; central management/security/backup; cost; performance as network grows).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a thin client and a thick client.
parts.answer: A thin client depends heavily on the server: most processing and storage is done by the server. A thick client can do most of its processing and store data itself, using the server only for some resources.
parts.working: B1 thin – server does the processing/stores data. B1 thick – client processes/stores locally.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A call centre in Lahore uses thin clients. Give two advantages and one disadvantage of this.
parts.answer: Advantages: thin client devices are cheap; software is installed/updated only on the server; data is stored centrally, so it is more secure and easier to back up. Disadvantage: if the server or network fails no work can be done; heavy network traffic.
parts.working: B1 each for two advantages; B1 one disadvantage.

stem: A small accountancy firm in Lahore is thinking of moving its client files to cloud storage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a public cloud and a private cloud.
parts.answer: A public cloud is owned by a provider and its resources are shared by many customers over the internet. A private cloud is used by one organisation only, and is run by that organisation or for it.
parts.working: B1 public – third-party, shared by many users. B1 private – one organisation only (on or off site).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of cloud storage for the firm.
parts.answer: Benefits: files can be accessed from anywhere with internet; the provider handles backups and maintenance; storage can be increased easily; no need to buy servers. Drawbacks: needs a reliable internet connection; confidential client data is held by a third party (security/privacy and legal concerns); ongoing subscription cost; the firm depends on the provider staying in business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits and two drawbacks.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a file is shared on a peer-to-peer network that is used to distribute a large open-source software package.
parts.answer: The file is split into small pieces that are held on many peer computers. A downloading peer gets different pieces from several peers at the same time, and then shares its own pieces with others.
parts.working: B1 file split and pieces stored on many peers. B1 downloaded from several peers at once / each peer also uploads.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two situations where a peer-to-peer network is more suitable than a client-server network.
parts.answer: A small home network with a few devices; a group of friends sharing files temporarily; where there is no money for a server; distributing very large files to many users.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two suitable situations.

stem: A university in Quetta has 1200 students. Each student is to be given 2.5 GiB of storage for coursework.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total storage needed in TiB, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.93 TiB

parts.label: b
parts.text: The university can either buy its own servers (client-server, on site) or use a public cloud. Evaluate the two options and make a recommendation.
parts.answer: Own servers: high initial cost and staff needed for maintenance, but data is under the university's control and access on campus does not depend on the internet link. Public cloud: no hardware to buy and storage scales easily if student numbers grow, the provider does backups; but needs reliable, fast internet, there are subscription costs every year and student data is held by an outside company. Recommendation, e.g. public cloud because 3 TiB is modest and it removes maintenance, provided the internet link is reliable (or the reverse with reason).
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: initial cost; maintenance/staff; control/security of data; dependence on internet; scalability; ongoing cost; backups; justified recommendation (needed for full marks).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by Ethernet.
parts.answer: A family of standards (protocols) for wired LANs that defines how data is put into frames and transmitted over the cable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Every Ethernet network interface has a 48-bit MAC address. State how many hexadecimal digits are used to write a MAC address and calculate how many different MAC addresses are possible.
parts.answer: 12 hexadecimal digits; 2⁴⁸ = 281 474 976 710 656 addresses

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what CSMA/CD stands for.
parts.answer: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how CSMA/CD is used when a device on a shared Ethernet cable wants to send data.
parts.answer: The device listens to the cable to check whether it is idle (carrier sense). If it is idle it starts to transmit; if not, it waits. While transmitting it keeps checking for a collision (a change in voltage). If a collision is detected it stops sending and transmits a jam signal so all devices know. Each device then waits a random time before trying again; after repeated collisions the waiting time increases / it gives up after a set number.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: listens for traffic; transmits only if idle; monitors for collision during transmission; jam signal sent; random wait before retransmitting; repeated failures – longer wait / give up after limit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why collisions can happen on a bus network even when every device uses carrier sense.
parts.answer: Two devices can both find the cable idle at the same moment and start transmitting together; because signals take time to travel along the cable, each device does not detect the other's transmission straight away.
parts.working: B1 two devices start at (nearly) the same time. B1 propagation delay – signal not yet reached the other device.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why collisions are rare on a modern Ethernet LAN where every computer is connected to its own port on a switch.
parts.answer: Each link between a computer and the switch is used only by that computer and the switch, and the switch can send and receive at the same time (full duplex). The switch sends each frame only to the destination port, so frames from different computers do not share a cable.
parts.working: B1 each device has a dedicated link / own collision domain. B1 full duplex or switch forwards to the destination port only.

stem: An Ethernet LAN uses this rule after a collision: after the nth collision of the same frame, a device waits k slot times, where k is chosen at random from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 (inclusive). One slot time is 51.2 µs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the longest possible wait after the third collision of a frame.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two devices collide for the first time. Calculate the probability that they choose the same k and so collide again.
parts.working: M1: k is 0 or 1 for each device. A1: P(same) = 2 × (1/2 × 1/2) = 1/2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the range of random waiting times grows after each collision.
parts.answer: Repeated collisions mean the network is busy. A wider range makes it less likely that the devices choose the same waiting time again, so the chance of another collision falls, at the cost of a longer average wait.
parts.working: B1 network is busy/many devices competing. B1 larger range reduces chance of choosing the same slot / repeated collision.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Wireless networks may use radio waves, microwaves or satellites. Give one benefit and one drawback of each.
parts.answer: Radio waves: travel through walls and over long distances / cheap; but low bandwidth and suffer interference. Microwaves: higher bandwidth than radio; but need line of sight and are absorbed by walls/rain. Satellites: cover very large or remote areas; but long delay (latency) and expensive.
parts.working: B1 each correct benefit + drawback pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of a wireless LAN compared with a wired LAN in a busy café in Islamabad.
parts.answer: Advantages: customers can connect their own devices without cables; easy to add many users / move around; no cabling to install. Disadvantages: less secure – signals can be intercepted, so encryption and passwords are needed; bandwidth is shared, so it slows with many users; interference and walls reduce range and reliability.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages.

stem: A commuter makes a video call on her smartphone while riding the Lahore Metro bus from one end of the route to the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a cellular network is organised.
parts.answer: The area is divided into small regions called cells, each with a base station (mast) that transmits and receives radio signals. Neighbouring cells use different frequencies so they do not interfere, and frequencies are reused in cells that are far apart. Base stations are connected by cable/fibre to the operator's core network and the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: cells; base station/mast per cell; different frequencies for adjacent cells / frequency reuse; base stations linked to the wider network.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the call continues without interruption as she moves from one cell to the next.
parts.answer: The network monitors signal strength from nearby base stations. When the signal from the next cell's base station becomes stronger, the call is handed over to that base station (handover/handoff) without dropping the connection.
parts.working: B1 signal strength monitored. B1 handover/handoff to next base station.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the call quality may fall in a crowded station.
parts.answer: Many phones share the same cell's limited bandwidth/channels, so each gets a smaller share.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a non-composite data type and a composite data type.
parts.answer: A non-composite data type is defined without reference to any other data type (it holds a single value, e.g. an enumerated or pointer type). A composite data type is made up of / refers to one or more other data types (e.g. a record, set, array or class).
parts.working: B1 non-composite – not defined in terms of other types / single value. B1 composite – built from other data types.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State whether each user-defined type is composite or non-composite.
(i) enumerated
(ii) record
(iii) pointer
(iv) set
(v) class
parts.answer: (i) non-composite (ii) composite (iii) non-composite (iv) composite (v) composite
parts.working: 3 marks all five correct; 2 marks four correct; 1 mark three correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why programming languages allow programmers to define their own data types.
parts.answer: The built-in types may not match the data in the problem; user-defined types make the program easier to read and maintain and let the translator check that only suitable values are used.
parts.working: B1 any one valid reason.

stem: A weather app records the type of day: Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy, Windy, Stormy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode to declare an enumerated data type TDayType for these values.
parts.answer: TYPE TDayType = (Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy, Windy, Stormy)
parts.working: B1 TYPE TDayType = ( … ). B1 all five values as identifiers, not strings (no quotation marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write pseudocode to declare a variable Today of this type and assign it the value Rainy.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Today : TDayType
Today ← Rainy
parts.working: B1 declaration. B1 assignment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the result of the expression Today < Windy when Today has the value Rainy. Give a reason.
parts.answer: TRUE, because the values of an enumerated type are ordered as they are listed, and Rainy comes before Windy.
parts.working: B1 TRUE. B1 values are ordinal / ordered by position in the declaration.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school library in Hyderabad stores data about each book: ISBN (13 characters), title, author, price in rupees, and whether it is on loan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode to declare a record type TBook for this data.
parts.answer:
TYPE TBook
   DECLARE ISBN : STRING
   DECLARE Title : STRING
   DECLARE Author : STRING
   DECLARE Price : REAL
   DECLARE OnLoan : BOOLEAN
ENDTYPE
parts.working: B1 TYPE TBook … ENDTYPE. B1 ISBN, Title, Author as STRING. B1 Price as REAL (or CURRENCY/INTEGER if justified). B1 OnLoan as BOOLEAN. (ISBN must not be INTEGER – it may start with 0 and is not used in calculations.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write pseudocode to declare a 1D array, Library, to store 500 books, and to set the price of the first book to 1250.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Library : ARRAY[1:500] OF TBook
Library[1].Price ← 1250
parts.working: B1 array declaration of TBook. B1 dot notation assignment.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a pointer data type.
parts.answer: A data type whose variables store a memory address, which is the location of (references) a value of another given type.
parts.working: B1 stores a memory address. B1 of a variable/data of a stated type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write pseudocode to declare a pointer type TRealPtr that points to a REAL, and a variable PriceRef of this type.
parts.answer:
TYPE TRealPtr = ^REAL
DECLARE PriceRef : TRealPtr
parts.working: B1 TYPE TRealPtr = ^REAL. B1 DECLARE PriceRef : TRealPtr.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the meaning of PriceRef^ and of @Price, where Price is a REAL variable.
parts.answer: PriceRef^ is the value stored at the address held in PriceRef (dereferencing). @Price is the memory address of the variable Price.
parts.working: B1 each.

stem:
TYPE TIntPointer = ^INTEGER
DECLARE Num1, Num2 : INTEGER
DECLARE P : TIntPointer
Num1 ← 20
Num2 ← 35
P ← @Num1
P^ ← P^ + 5
P ← @Num2
Num1 ← Num1 + P^
OUTPUT Num1, " ", Num2, " ", P^

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the output of the pseudocode.
parts.working: B1 Num1 = 60 (20 + 5 = 25 via the pointer, then 25 + 35). B1 Num2 = 35 (unchanged). B1 P^ = 35.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the statement P^ ← P^ + 5 changes the value of Num1.
parts.answer: P holds the address of Num1, so P^ refers to the same memory location as Num1; storing a value in P^ stores it in Num1.
parts.working: B1 P contains the address of Num1. B1 dereferencing accesses/changes that location.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A set data type is declared in pseudocode like this:
TYPE TLetterSet = SET OF CHAR
DEFINE Vowels ('A', 'E', 'I', 'O', 'U') : TLetterSet

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a DEFINE statement for a set Initials of type TLetterSet containing the characters 'A', 'B', 'P', 'T', 'E'.
parts.answer: DEFINE Initials ('A', 'B', 'P', 'T', 'E') : TLetterSet

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Give the result of each set operation.
(i) Vowels UNION Initials
(ii) Vowels INTERSECTION Initials
(iii) Initials DIFFERENCE Vowels
parts.working: B1 each (any order).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two properties of a set that make it different from an array.
parts.answer: A set has no order (elements cannot be accessed by index), and each value can appear only once (no duplicates).
parts.working: 1 mark each: unordered / no index; no duplicate values; size can change; supports set operations such as membership test.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
TYPE TSeason = (Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter)
A farmer in Punjab uses a program that plans crops by season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a function NextSeason(S : TSeason) RETURNS TSeason that returns the season after S. The season after Winter is Spring.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION NextSeason(S : TSeason) RETURNS TSeason
   DECLARE Result : TSeason
   CASE OF S
      Spring : Result ← Summer
      Summer : Result ← Autumn
      Autumn : Result ← Winter
      Winter : Result ← Spring
   ENDCASE
   RETURN Result
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: B1 function header and ENDFUNCTION. B1 CASE (or IF) structure on S. B1 Spring→Summer, Summer→Autumn, Autumn→Winter. B1 Winter→Spring and value returned. Accept IF S = Winter THEN RETURN Spring ELSE RETURN S + 1 if the language allows arithmetic on ordinal values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using TSeason is better than storing the season as an integer 1 to 4.
parts.answer: The code is easier to read and understand (Summer rather than 2), and the variable can only take one of the four valid values, so invalid values such as 7 are rejected.
parts.working: B1 readability / self-documenting. B1 restricts to valid values / fewer errors.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A cricket league stores data about each player as a record.
TYPE TPlayer
   DECLARE Name : STRING
   DECLARE Team : STRING
   DECLARE Innings : INTEGER
   DECLARE Runs : INTEGER
ENDTYPE
DECLARE Squad : ARRAY[1:25] OF TPlayer

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a pseudocode procedure ShowAverages() that outputs the name and batting average (Runs ÷ Innings) of every player in Squad. Players who have not batted (Innings = 0) must be output with the message "no innings" instead of an average.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE ShowAverages()
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 25
      IF Squad[Index].Innings = 0 THEN
         OUTPUT Squad[Index].Name, " no innings"
      ELSE
         OUTPUT Squad[Index].Name, " ", Squad[Index].Runs / Squad[Index].Innings
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: procedure header/end; loop 1 to 25; test for Innings = 0 with message; average calculated as Runs / Innings; correct dot notation used to access fields with output of name.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A player has 412 runs from 9 innings. Calculate the average to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text: The state of a traffic light: Red, Amber, Green.
parts.answer: Enumerated – a small fixed list of named values.
parts.working: B1 data type. B1 reason.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text: The next node in a linked list stored in dynamic memory.
parts.answer: Pointer – it holds the memory address of the next node.
parts.working: B1 data type. B1 reason.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.text: A customer's ID, name, phone number and loyalty points.
parts.answer: Record – it groups related data items of different types under one identifier.
parts.working: B1 data type. B1 reason.

parts.answer: Set – an unordered collection of unique values that can be tested for membership.
parts.working: B1 data type. B1 reason.

stem: For each item of data, choose the most suitable user-defined data type from: enumerated, pointer, set, record. Give a reason for each.

A linked list is held in dynamic memory.
TYPE TNodePtr = ^TNode
TYPE TNode
   DECLARE Data : INTEGER
   DECLARE Next : TNodePtr
ENDTYPE
DECLARE StartPtr : TNodePtr
StartPtr holds the address 3040. The nodes are:
address 3040: Data 12, Next 3016
address 3016: Data 30, Next 3088
address 3088: Data 7, Next NULL

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value of StartPtr^.Next^.Data.
parts.working: B1: StartPtr^ is the node at 3040; its Next is 3016; the Data there is 30.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a function ListTotal() RETURNS INTEGER that follows the pointers from StartPtr and returns the total of all the Data values.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION ListTotal() RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Current : TNodePtr
   DECLARE Total : INTEGER
   Total ← 0
   Current ← StartPtr
   WHILE Current <> NULL
      Total ← Total + Current^.Data
      Current ← Current^.Next
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN Total
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: local pointer declared and set to StartPtr; total initialised to 0; loop until NULL; Data added using Current^.Data; pointer moved using Current^.Next and total returned.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value returned by the function for this list.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
TYPE TIntPtr = ^INTEGER
DECLARE Score, Bonus : INTEGER
DECLARE Ptr : TIntPtr
The variables are stored at these memory addresses: Score 5120, Bonus 5121, Ptr 5122.
Score ← 48
Bonus ← 7
Ptr ← @Score
Ptr^ ← Ptr^ + Bonus
Ptr ← @Bonus
Bonus ← Ptr^ * 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the final values: Score, Bonus, Ptr, Ptr^ and @Ptr.
parts.answer: Score 55, Bonus 14, Ptr 5121, Ptr^ 14, @Ptr 5122

        Cost = 180 + (Kilos - 1) * 90
        if self.__Express:

stem:
Student ID numbers are stored in a hash table so they can be found quickly. Write your answers in Python. (Java or VB.NET are also accepted.)
The global list HashTable has 11 elements, numbered 0 to 10. An element with the value −1 is empty. The hash value of a key is Key MOD 11. Collisions are dealt with by linear probing (wrapping round from 10 to 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a function Insert(Key) that stores Key in HashTable and returns True, or returns False if the table is full.
parts.answer:
TableSize = 11
HashTable = [-1] * TableSize

def Hash(Key):
    return Key % TableSize

def Insert(Key):
    Index = Hash(Key)
    Count = 0
    while HashTable[Index] != -1 and Count < TableSize:
        Index = (Index + 1) % TableSize
        Count = Count + 1
    if Count == TableSize:
        return False
    HashTable[Index] = Key
    return True
parts.working: 1 mark each: hash calculated with MOD 11; loop while location not empty; index incremented with wrap-around (MOD 11); full table detected and False returned; key stored and True returned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a function Search(Key) that returns the index where Key is stored, or −1 if it is not in the table. The search must stop at an empty element.
parts.working: 1 mark each: starts at hash position; loops until key found; returns −1 at an empty element or after checking every element; returns index when found.

stem: A hospital in Peshawar sends large files of patient scan results to a laboratory in Islamabad over the internet. Both have asymmetric key pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method that uses both symmetric and asymmetric encryption so that the files are sent securely and efficiently.
parts.answer: The hospital generates a random symmetric session key. It encrypts the scan files with this symmetric key. It encrypts the session key with the laboratory's public key and sends both. The laboratory decrypts the session key with its own private key, then uses the session key to decrypt the files. Symmetric encryption is used for the files because it is fast for large data; asymmetric encryption safely delivers the session key.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: random session/symmetric key generated; files encrypted with symmetric key; session key encrypted with lab's public key; lab decrypts session key with its private key; lab decrypts files with session key; reason – speed for large files / key distribution solved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one further measure that would let the laboratory check that the files really came from the hospital.
parts.answer: The hospital adds a digital signature (hash encrypted with the hospital's private key) which the lab checks with the hospital's public key.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zara downloads what she believes is her bank's public key from an email link. In fact an attacker has sent her the attacker's own public key.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the attacker can read the messages Zara sends to the bank, without the bank or Zara noticing.
parts.answer: Zara encrypts messages with the attacker's public key thinking it is the bank's. The attacker intercepts them and decrypts them with the attacker's private key. The attacker can then re-encrypt them with the bank's real public key and forward them, so the bank receives them normally (a man-in-the-middle attack).
parts.working: B1 Zara uses attacker's public key. B1 attacker decrypts with own private key. B1 re-encrypts with the bank's key and forwards / man-in-the-middle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a digital certificate would have prevented this.
parts.answer: A certificate binds the bank's identity to its public key and is signed by a trusted certificate authority. Zara's software can check the CA's signature; the attacker cannot produce a valid certificate for the bank's name with their own key.
parts.working: B1 certificate links public key to verified owner. B1 signed by trusted CA / signature can be checked, so a fake key would be detected.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student writes: "If I encrypt a message with my private key, nobody else can read it." Explain why this statement is wrong and state what encrypting with your private key does provide.
parts.answer: Your public key is available to everyone, and anything encrypted with your private key can be decrypted with your public key, so anyone can read it. What it does provide is authentication: only you could have produced it, because only you have the private key (this is the basis of a digital signature / non-repudiation).
parts.working: B1 public key decrypts it. B1 public key is available to anyone so not confidential. B1 provides proof of origin/authenticity/non-repudiation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could send a message that is both confidential and provably from them.
parts.answer: Sign the message (encrypt its hash with their own private key), then encrypt the message and signature with the receiver's public key. The receiver decrypts with their private key and checks the signature with the sender's public key.
parts.working: B1 sign with sender's private key. B1 encrypt with receiver's public key (and correct decryption order described).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a digital certificate.
parts.answer: An electronic document issued by a trusted certificate authority that links (binds) a public key to the identity of its owner, so that others can trust the key belongs to that person or organisation.
parts.working: B1 issued/signed by a certificate authority. B1 confirms that a public key belongs to a named owner.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give four items of data that are found in a digital certificate.
parts.answer: Any four of: owner's (subject's) name/organisation or domain; owner's public key; serial number; validity period (start and expiry dates); name of the issuing CA; the CA's digital signature; the algorithm used for the signature; certificate version.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of a digital signature.
parts.answer: To prove that a message really came from the stated sender (authentication / non-repudiation) and that it has not been altered since it was signed (integrity).
parts.working: B1 authenticity of sender / non-repudiation. B1 integrity – message not altered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which key is used to create a digital signature, and which key is used to check it.
parts.answer: Created with the sender's private key; checked with the sender's public key.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether a digital signature keeps the content of the message secret. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No – the message itself is not encrypted by signing (and the signature can be checked by anyone with the public key).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of a certificate authority (CA).
parts.answer: A CA is a trusted organisation that checks the identity of people or organisations applying for certificates, issues digital certificates that link their identity to their public key, signs the certificates with its own private key, and revokes certificates that are no longer valid.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: trusted third party; verifies applicant's identity; issues certificates; signs them with the CA's private key; maintains revocation list / revokes certificates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a web browser can check a certificate signed by a CA without contacting that CA first.
parts.answer: The browser/operating system already stores the trusted root CAs' certificates, including their public keys, so it can check the CA's signature directly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a digital signature and a digital certificate.
parts.answer: A digital signature is created by the sender for a particular message (an encrypted hash of that message) to prove who sent it and that it is unchanged. A digital certificate is issued by a CA to an owner and is used to prove that a public key belongs to that owner. The certificate itself contains the CA's digital signature, and it supplies the public key used to check the sender's signature.
parts.working: B1 signature – made by sender, unique to each message, proves origin/integrity. B1 certificate – issued by CA, proves ownership of public key. B1 link: certificate provides the trusted public key used to verify signatures / certificate is signed by the CA.

stem: Mr Khan, a contractor in Multan, sends a signed quotation by email to a client.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Mr Khan's software creates the digital signature for the quotation.
parts.answer: The quotation is put through a hashing algorithm to produce a message digest (hash). The digest is encrypted using Mr Khan's private key; this encrypted digest is the digital signature. The signature is attached to the quotation and both are sent.
parts.working: B1 hash/digest of the message produced. B1 digest encrypted with Mr Khan's private key. B1 signature sent with the message.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the signature is different for every quotation he sends.
parts.answer: The digest depends on the content of the message, so different quotations give different digests and therefore different signatures.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A client receives a message and a digital signature. Describe how the client's software checks the signature.
parts.answer: It obtains the sender's public key (from the sender's digital certificate). It decrypts the signature with that public key to get the original message digest. It applies the same hashing algorithm to the received message to make a new digest. It compares the two digests: if they match, the message is authentic and unchanged; if not, it has been altered or did not come from the sender.
parts.working: 1 mark each: public key of sender obtained (certificate); signature decrypted with sender's public key; received message hashed with the same algorithm; digests compared – match means authentic and unaltered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two possible reasons why the two digests might not match.
parts.answer: The message was altered (tampered with or corrupted) in transmission; it was signed with a different private key (not from the claimed sender / wrong public key used).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: An online tutoring company in Lahore wants a digital certificate for its website.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps the company follows to obtain a digital certificate.
parts.answer: The company generates a public/private key pair. It sends a certificate request to a CA containing its public key and details of its identity (organisation name, domain). The CA checks the company's identity and that it controls the domain. The CA creates the certificate containing the company's details and public key, signs it with the CA's private key, and sends it to the company, which installs it on its web server.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: key pair generated; request with public key and identity details sent to CA; CA verifies identity/domain; CA creates certificate and signs with its private key; certificate issued/installed on server.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the company must never send to the CA.
parts.answer: Its private key.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: When a user visits a website using HTTPS, the browser checks the website's digital certificate. Describe three checks the browser makes.
parts.answer: It checks that the certificate was signed by a trusted CA (by verifying the CA's signature with the CA's public key); that the certificate is within its validity dates (not expired); that the domain name in the certificate matches the website address; and that the certificate has not been revoked.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the browser does if one of the checks fails.
parts.answer: It displays a security warning / blocks the connection and tells the user the site may not be secure.

stem:
A simplified example of signing uses tiny keys. The sender's private key is (d = 27, n = 55) and public key is (e = 3, n = 55).
The 'digest' of a message is the sum of the ASCII codes of its characters MOD 55. The signature is digest^d MOD n; it is checked by calculating signature^e MOD n.
ASCII codes: P 80, A 65, Y 89, space 32, 0 48, 5 53, 9 57.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the digest of the message PAY 500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: You are told that 30²⁷ MOD 55 = 35, so the signature is 35. Show how the receiver checks this signature.
parts.answer: 35³ = 42 875; 42 875 MOD 55 = 30, which equals the digest of the received message, so the signature is valid.
parts.working: M1 35³ MOD 55 calculated = 30. A1 compared with digest of received message – match.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An attacker changes the message to PAY 900 but keeps the signature 35. Show how the receiver detects this.
parts.answer: Digest of PAY 900 = 419 MOD 55 = 34. Checking the signature still gives 30. 34 ≠ 30, so the message has been altered.
parts.working: M1 new digest 34. A1 does not match 30 → tampering detected.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the attacker cannot create a new valid signature for PAY 900.
parts.answer: A valid signature needs the sender's private key, which the attacker does not have.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A software company in Lahore distributes updates for its accounting app. Each update is code-signed: it carries a digital signature and the company's digital certificate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how code signing protects users who install an update.
parts.answer: The user's computer checks the certificate (signed by a trusted CA) to get the company's genuine public key, then verifies the update's signature with it. If the update has been changed (e.g. malware inserted) or was not produced by the company, the digests will not match and the installation is blocked/warned.
parts.working: B1 certificate verified to obtain trusted public key. B1 signature verified / digest comparison. B1 tampered or fake updates detected and not installed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company discovers that its private key has been stolen. Describe what should happen and why.
parts.answer: The company tells the CA, which revokes the certificate (adds it to its revocation list), so software will no longer trust signatures made with that key.
