The company generates a new key pair, obtains a new certificate and re-signs its updates. Otherwise the thief could sign malware that users' computers would accept as genuine.
parts.working: B1 certificate revoked by CA. B1 new key pair/certificate obtained. B1 reason – thief could sign malicious software as the company.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a digital signature encrypts a hash of the message rather than the whole message.
parts.answer: A hash is short and of fixed length, so encrypting it with the slow asymmetric algorithm is much quicker than encrypting a long message; the hash still represents the whole message because any change to the message changes the hash.
parts.working: B1 hash is small/fixed length – faster to encrypt/decrypt. B1 still detects any change to the message.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three properties a hashing algorithm needs for use in digital signatures.
parts.answer: It always gives the same digest for the same message; a tiny change in the message gives a completely different digest; it is not possible to work back from the digest to the message (one-way); it is very unlikely that two different messages give the same digest (collision resistant); it produces a fixed-length output.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

stem: A company in Islamabad sends a confidential signed contract to a partner in Dubai. Each has a key pair and a digital certificate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the four keys, state who uses it and for what purpose.
(i) Islamabad company's private key
(ii) Islamabad company's public key
(iii) Dubai partner's private key
(iv) Dubai partner's public key
parts.answer: (i) used by Islamabad to sign the contract (encrypt its hash). (ii) used by Dubai to verify the signature (decrypt the hash). (iii) used by Dubai to decrypt the contract. (iv) used by Islamabad to encrypt the contract (or the session key that encrypts it).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each security aim, state whether it is achieved by the signature, by the encryption, or by both: confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation.
parts.answer: Confidentiality – encryption. Integrity – signature (hash comparison). Non-repudiation – signature.
parts.working: B1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.
parts.answer: To provide secure communication between a client and a server over a network: data is encrypted so it stays private, the server (and optionally the client) is authenticated, and data integrity is checked.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2: encryption/privacy; authentication of server/client; integrity (data not altered).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two situations where TLS is used.
parts.answer: Online banking / shopping websites (HTTPS); email between client and mail server; instant messaging; VoIP calls; logging in to accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the relationship between SSL and TLS.
parts.answer: TLS is the newer, more secure protocol that replaced SSL (it was developed from SSL).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps of a TLS handshake when a browser connects to a secure website.
parts.answer: The browser (client) sends a 'hello' message with the TLS versions and cipher suites (encryption methods) it supports and a random number. The server replies choosing the version and cipher suite and sends its digital certificate (containing its public key). The browser checks the certificate with the CA's public key. The client and server then agree a shared session key (e.g. the client sends secret data encrypted with the server's public key, or a key-exchange method is used). Both confirm the handshake is finished, and the rest of the session is encrypted with the symmetric session key.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: client hello with supported versions/ciphers; server hello chooses cipher; server sends certificate/public key; client verifies certificate; session key agreed/exchanged using asymmetric encryption; encrypted communication begins with symmetric key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the session key is discarded when the session ends.
parts.answer: A new key for each session means that if one session key is discovered, only that session's data is exposed, not past or future sessions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: TLS is made up of two layers: the handshake protocol and the record protocol. Describe the role of each.
parts.answer: Handshake protocol: lets the client and server authenticate each other, agree on the encryption algorithms to use and set up the shared session keys. Record protocol: carries the application data once the handshake is done; it divides the data into blocks (records), adds a message authentication code to check integrity, and encrypts them with the session key.
parts.working: B1 handshake – authentication. B1 handshake – agree cipher/keys. B1 record – encrypts and transmits data. B1 record – integrity checking / splitting into records.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which layer of the TCP/IP model TLS works between, and give the protocol formed when HTTP is used over TLS.
parts.answer: Between the application layer and the transport layer; HTTPS.
parts.working: B1 between application and transport (TCP). B1 HTTPS.

stem: A user in Karachi connects to an online shop. The browser shows https:// and a padlock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why TLS uses asymmetric encryption during the handshake but symmetric encryption for the rest of the session.
parts.answer: Asymmetric encryption lets the two sides agree a secret key safely over an insecure network without having shared a key before, and the certificate authenticates the server. But it is slow, so once the shared session key is set up, the much faster symmetric encryption is used for the bulk of the data.
parts.working: B1 asymmetric solves key exchange/authentication. B1 asymmetric is slow / processor-intensive. B1 symmetric faster for large amounts of data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The user assumes that the padlock means the shop is honest. Explain why this is not necessarily true.
parts.answer: The padlock only shows that the connection is encrypted and that the certificate matches the domain; a criminal can obtain a valid certificate for their own fake domain, so the site itself may still be fraudulent.
parts.working: B1 padlock = encrypted connection / certificate valid for the domain. B1 does not prove the owner is trustworthy – fake sites can have certificates.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by quantum cryptography.
parts.answer: It uses the properties of quantum physics – usually the polarisation of single photons of light sent through fibre-optic cable – to exchange an encryption key between two parties securely (quantum key distribution).
parts.working: B1 uses quantum properties of photons (polarisation). B1 used to distribute/exchange a secret key securely.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of quantum cryptography.
parts.answer: Benefits: any attempt to eavesdrop on the key changes the photons and can be detected; the key exchange is considered virtually unbreakable / not threatened by faster computers; long keys can be generated. Drawbacks: requires expensive dedicated hardware and fibre links; works only over limited distances before the signal is lost; data rate is low; photon polarisation can be altered as they travel long distances, causing errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits and two drawbacks.

stem:
In a simplified quantum key distribution, the sender transmits photons. Each photon carries a bit using one of two bases: rectilinear (+) or diagonal (×). The receiver chooses a basis at random for each photon. Afterwards they compare bases (not bits) publicly and keep only the bits where the bases matched.
Photon:          1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
Sender's bit:    1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0
Sender's basis:  + × × + + × + ×
Receiver's basis: + + × × + × × ×

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the shared key that both keep, assuming no eavesdropper.
parts.answer: 11000 (from photons 1, 3, 5, 6, 8)
parts.working: M1 bases match for photons 1, 3, 5, 6 and 8. A1 key 11000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the sender and receiver could detect that an eavesdropper had intercepted the photons.
parts.answer: An eavesdropper must measure each photon, and measuring in the wrong basis changes its polarisation, so the photon passed on may carry the wrong value. The two parties publicly compare a sample of their kept bits; if more of them disagree than expected, an eavesdropper is present and the key is thrown away.
parts.working: B1 measuring a photon disturbs/changes its state (cannot be copied). B1 compare a sample of the key bits. B1 errors above expected level reveal eavesdropping – key discarded.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school in Peshawar has a network of 120 computers. Describe the difference between a virus and a worm.
parts.answer: A virus attaches itself to (is hidden inside) another program or file and needs that file to be run/opened to spread; a worm is a standalone program that replicates itself and spreads across the network on its own, without a host file or user action.
parts.working: 1 mark: virus needs a host file / user action to run and spread. 1 mark: worm is standalone and self-replicates across the network by itself.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what spyware does and give one way it could harm the school.
parts.answer: Spyware secretly monitors/records activity on a computer (e.g. key presses with a key-logger) and sends the data to a third party. Harm: teachers' passwords or students' personal data could be stolen.
parts.working: 1 mark: secretly records/monitors user activity and sends it to a third party. 1 mark: a relevant harm in context, e.g. stolen login details giving access to the results system.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one software measure that protects the network against both viruses and spyware.
parts.answer: Anti-malware software (anti-virus / anti-spyware) that is kept up to date.
parts.working: B1 anti-virus or anti-spyware/anti-malware software (accept up-to-date scanning software).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Customers of an online bank receive an email that looks as if it is from the bank. It asks them to click a link and 'confirm' their card details. Identify this threat and describe how it works.
parts.answer: Phishing. A legitimate-looking email is sent to many people; the link leads to a fake website; details the user types in are captured by the criminal.
parts.working: B1 phishing. Then 1 mark each for any two of: email/message pretends to be from a trusted organisation; contains a link to a fake website; user is tricked into entering personal/financial details; details are sent to the criminal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another customer types the bank's correct web address but is taken to a fake site. Identify this threat and explain how it differs from the threat in (a).
parts.answer: Pharming. Malicious code on the user's computer or a compromised (poisoned) DNS server redirects the correct URL to a fake website. Unlike phishing, the user does not have to click a link in a message – typing the genuine address is enough.
parts.working: B1 pharming. 1 mark: malicious code installed on the computer / DNS cache or server altered. 1 mark: redirection happens even when the correct URL is typed / no email link needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one action a customer can take to avoid being caught by the threat in (a).
parts.answer: Do not click links in unexpected emails; type the bank's address directly / check the sender and the URL carefully.
parts.working: B1 any sensible action.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small accountancy firm in Dubai connects its LAN to the internet. Describe how a firewall helps to protect the LAN.
parts.answer: The firewall sits between the LAN and the internet and examines every packet entering or leaving. It compares packets with a set of rules/criteria (e.g. allowed IP addresses, ports, protocols). Packets that do not meet the rules are blocked; it can also log traffic and stop unauthorised access from outside.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: positioned between LAN and internet (or on a computer); monitors incoming and outgoing traffic/packets; checks against rules/criteria set by the administrator; blocks/rejects packets that fail; can block certain IP addresses/ports/websites; keeps a log of attempted access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other security measures the firm could use to protect client data on its server, other than a firewall.
parts.answer: Any two of: strong passwords / user accounts; access rights; encryption of stored data; anti-malware software; biometrics; two-step verification.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two distinct measures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital in Karachi gives doctors access to patient records. At present each doctor logs in with a user ID and password. Explain why adding two-step (two-factor) verification would make the system more secure.
parts.answer: A second, different factor is required (e.g. a one-time code sent to the doctor's phone, or a fingerprint). A criminal who has stolen or guessed the password still cannot log in without that second factor.
parts.working: 1 mark: a second, independent form of authentication is needed (something you have/are). 1 mark: a stolen/guessed password alone is no longer enough.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The hospital considers fingerprint scanners instead of passwords. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using biometrics in this situation.
parts.answer: Advantage: fingerprints are unique and cannot be forgotten, shared or guessed. Disadvantage: e.g. scanners may fail with dirty or gloved hands (doctors wear gloves) / cost of equipment / biometric data cannot be changed if stolen.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid advantage; 1 mark for a valid disadvantage (credit context such as surgical gloves).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how access rights should be used so that reception staff cannot view patients' medical history.
parts.answer: Each user account is placed in a group with set permissions. Reception staff are given access only to contact/appointment data (read/write) and no access (or read-only to limited fields) for medical history, which only doctors can read/edit.
parts.working: 1 mark: different users/groups given different permissions. 1 mark: reception have no access to medical-history data while doctors do.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photographer in Lahore stores all her client images on one external hard disk. Identify two ways her data could be lost other than by malware or hacking.
parts.answer: Any two of: hardware failure of the disk; accidental deletion/overwriting; physical damage (fire, flood, dropping it); theft/loss of the disk; power cut while writing corrupts data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two distinct causes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two measures she could take to reduce the risk of losing her data, and explain how each helps.
parts.answer: Regular backups to a second device or cloud storage, kept in a different place – a copy can be restored if the original is lost or damaged. Disk mirroring (RAID 1) – data is written to two disks at the same time so if one fails the other still has the data. (Also accept: UPS to allow safe shutdown in a power cut; keeping disk in a fireproof safe; making files read-only.)
parts.working: For each of two measures: 1 mark naming/describing it, 1 mark explaining how it prevents loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how anti-virus software detects and deals with a virus.
parts.answer: It scans files (on access or on a schedule) and compares their code with a database of known virus signatures; heuristic checking looks for virus-like behaviour in unknown files; a suspicious file is quarantined (isolated) or deleted, and the user is alerted; the signature database must be updated regularly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: scans files/memory; compares with known signatures; heuristic/behaviour analysis; quarantines infected files; deletes/repairs files; alerts the user; needs regular updates of the database.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a computer with up-to-date anti-virus software can still be infected.
parts.answer: A brand-new virus may not yet have a signature in the database (zero-day), and heuristics may not spot it, so it is not detected until an update is released.
parts.working: 1 mark: new/unknown virus not in the signature database. 1 mark: so it is not recognised until the database is updated / heuristics miss it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An online shoe shop based in Islamabad reports these problems:
1. Staff passwords were captured by a program that recorded every key pressed.
2. An attachment opened by one employee copied itself into many other files on the server.
3. Someone outside the company gained access to the customer database by guessing a weak administrator password.
For each problem, identify the threat and recommend one specific measure that would have prevented it. Justify each recommendation.
parts.answer:
1. Spyware (key-logger) – anti-spyware software / use of on-screen or drop-down entry of password characters / two-step verification so a captured password alone is useless.
2. Virus – anti-virus software scanning email attachments; staff training not to open unknown attachments.
3. Hacking (unauthorised access) – strong password policy (length, mixed characters, changed regularly) plus lock-out after several failed attempts / firewall / two-step verification.
parts.working: For each of the three problems: 1 mark for the correct threat; 1 mark for a suitable measure with a justification linked to the problem (a measure without a reason scores 0 for that mark).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms plaintext, ciphertext and encryption key.
parts.answer: Plaintext: the original, readable data before encryption. Ciphertext: the scrambled data produced by encryption, unreadable without the key. Key: a value used by the encryption algorithm to encrypt/decrypt the data.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
parts.answer: Symmetric encryption uses the same (secret) key to encrypt and decrypt. Asymmetric encryption uses a pair of mathematically related keys: a public key and a private key – data encrypted with one key can only be decrypted with the other.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric – one shared secret key. 1 mark: asymmetric – public/private key pair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha wants to send a confidential file to Bilal using asymmetric encryption so that only Bilal can read it. State which key Ayesha uses to encrypt the file and which key Bilal uses to decrypt it.
parts.answer: Ayesha encrypts with Bilal's public key; Bilal decrypts with his own private key.
parts.working: B1 Bilal's public key. B1 Bilal's private key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person who intercepts the file cannot read it, even though Bilal's public key is freely available.
parts.answer: The file can only be decrypted with the matching private key, which only Bilal holds and never shares; the public key cannot be used to decrypt it (and the private key cannot practically be worked out from the public key).
parts.working: 1 mark: only the private key can decrypt. 1 mark: only Bilal has the private key / it is never transmitted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Bilal replies with a message that Ayesha must be sure came from him. Describe how keys are used so that Ayesha can be sure of this.
parts.answer: Bilal encrypts (a digest of) the message with his own private key; Ayesha decrypts it with Bilal's public key – if it decrypts correctly it must have come from Bilal, because only he has the private key.
parts.working: 1 mark: Bilal uses his private key. 1 mark: Ayesha uses Bilal's public key, proving the sender.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software company in Bengaluru signs every update it releases with a digital signature. Describe how the digital signature is produced.
parts.answer: A hashing algorithm is applied to the update file to produce a message digest. The digest is encrypted with the company's private key. The encrypted digest (the digital signature) is attached to/sent with the file.
parts.working: 1 mark each: hash/digest of the file; digest encrypted with the sender's private key; signature sent with the file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a user's computer checks the signature before installing the update.
parts.answer: It decrypts the signature using the company's public key to recover the original digest. It applies the same hashing algorithm to the received file to make a new digest. If the two digests match, the file is genuine and unaltered; if not, it is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark each: decrypt signature with company's public key; re-hash the received file with the same algorithm; compare digests – match means authentic and unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online university portal uses a digital certificate. Describe how the university obtains its digital certificate.
parts.answer: The university generates a public/private key pair and sends a request containing its public key and identity details to a Certificate Authority (CA). The CA checks the university's identity. The CA issues the certificate containing the public key and details, signed with the CA's own private key.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: applies to a Certificate Authority; supplies public key and identification details; CA verifies identity; CA creates certificate and signs it with the CA's private key; certificate issued with expiry date.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three items of information that a digital certificate contains.
parts.answer: Any three of: the owner's (subject's) name/domain; the owner's public key; the name of the issuing CA; the CA's digital signature; serial number; validity (start and expiry) dates; algorithm used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a student's browser uses the certificate to decide whether to trust the portal.
parts.answer: The browser checks the CA's signature on the certificate using the CA's public key (which it already trusts); it also checks the certificate has not expired/been revoked and that the domain name matches the site. If all checks pass, it trusts the public key in the certificate.
parts.working: 1 mark: verifies CA signature with CA's public key. 1 mark: checks validity dates/domain/revocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the TLS protocol.
parts.answer: To provide a secure (encrypted) connection between a client and a server across the internet, giving confidentiality, integrity of the data and authentication of the server.
parts.working: 1 mark: encrypts data in transit/secure connection. 1 mark: authenticates server / ensures data not altered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two situations where TLS is used.
parts.answer: Any two of: HTTPS web browsing (e.g. online banking/shopping); secure email transfer (SMTP/IMAP over TLS); VoIP/video calls; online payment systems; VPN connections.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a session key in TLS.
parts.answer: A symmetric key that is agreed/created during the handshake and used only for the current session to encrypt the data exchanged; it is discarded at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric key created in the handshake. 1 mark: used only for that session.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main steps of a TLS handshake between a browser and a web server.
parts.answer: The client sends a 'hello' listing the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports. The server replies, choosing the version/cipher suite, and sends its digital certificate. The client checks the certificate with the CA's public key. The client and server then agree a session key – e.g. the client creates a secret and encrypts it with the server's public key, and only the server can decrypt it with its private key. Both sides derive the same symmetric session key and confirm the handshake is finished; data is then encrypted with that key.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: client hello with supported versions/ciphers; server hello choosing cipher; server sends certificate/public key; client verifies certificate (via CA); key exchange using server's public key (or key-agreement method); server uses private key; both generate same session key; 'finished' messages / encrypted data transfer begins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why TLS uses asymmetric encryption only during the handshake and symmetric encryption for the data that follows.
parts.answer: Asymmetric encryption solves the problem of sharing a key securely but is slow/processor-intensive; symmetric encryption is much faster, so it is used for the bulk of the data once the session key has been shared safely.
parts.working: 1 mark: asymmetric allows secure key exchange (no shared secret needed in advance). 1 mark: symmetric is faster/less processing for large amounts of data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how quantum cryptography is used to share an encryption key.
parts.answer: The key is sent as a stream of photons (light particles) whose polarisation represents the bits, using a quantum key distribution protocol. The receiver measures the photons with randomly chosen filters and the two sides compare which filters they used to build a shared key. Any attempt to observe the photons changes their state, so eavesdropping can be detected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: uses the properties of photons/quantum mechanics; bits represented by polarisation; quantum key distribution (QKD); measuring a photon changes its state; eavesdropper is detected; key is then used for encryption.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one benefit and one drawback of quantum cryptography.
parts.answer: Benefit: eavesdropping on the key exchange can always be detected, so the key is (in theory) completely secure / longer keys can be shared. Drawback: needs expensive specialist hardware/dedicated fibre links, limited distance, and the technology is still developing.
parts.working: 1 mark for a benefit; 1 mark for a drawback.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'A digital signature is made by encrypting the whole document with the sender's private key.' Explain why a hash (message digest) is signed instead of the whole document.
parts.answer: The digest is short and of fixed length, so encrypting it with the private key is much quicker than encrypting a large document; it still identifies the document uniquely because any change to the document gives a different digest.
parts.working: 1 mark: digest is small/fixed length – faster to encrypt and send. 1 mark: digest still detects any change to the document.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A contract file signed by a lawyer in Faisalabad has one figure changed in transit. Explain how the receiver detects this.
parts.answer: The receiver hashes the received (altered) file and gets a new digest; this does not match the digest recovered by decrypting the signature with the lawyer's public key, so the file is shown to have been altered.
parts.working: 1 mark: new hash computed from received file differs. 1 mark: compared with digest from decrypted signature – mismatch shows tampering.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a digital signature on its own does not prove that the public key used really belongs to the lawyer, and state what solves this problem.
parts.answer: Anyone could create a key pair and claim the public key is the lawyer's; a digital certificate issued and signed by a trusted Certificate Authority links the public key to the lawyer's identity.
parts.working: 1 mark: public key could belong to an impostor. 1 mark: digital certificate from a CA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college in Multan stores student marks in a database. Explain what is meant by access rights.
parts.answer: Permissions given to each user (or group of users) that control which data/files they can see and what they can do with them, e.g. no access, read-only, or read/write.
parts.working: 1 mark: permissions set per user/group. 1 mark: levels such as read-only / read-write / no access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest suitable access rights for students, teachers and the examinations officer, and give a reason for each.
parts.answer: Students: read-only access to their own marks – they need to see results but must not change them. Teachers: read and write access to marks for their own classes – they enter and correct marks. Examinations officer: full access (read/write/delete) to all records – manages all results.
parts.working: 1 mark for each user type with suitable rights and a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A research group of 12 scientists in different countries each wants to exchange private messages with every other member. Calculate how many different secret keys are needed if symmetric encryption is used with a separate key for each pair of members.
parts.answer: 66 keys
parts.working: M1 number of pairs = n(n − 1) ÷ 2. A1 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many keys in total are needed if asymmetric encryption is used instead.
parts.answer: 24 keys (one public and one private key for each of the 12 members)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from the number of keys, explain one other problem with symmetric encryption that asymmetric encryption solves.
parts.answer: The key distribution problem: the shared secret key must first be sent to the other person, and if it is intercepted in transit the messages can be read. With asymmetric encryption the public key can be sent openly and the private key never leaves its owner.
parts.working: 1 mark: secret key has to be shared/transmitted and could be intercepted. 1 mark: asymmetric public key can be shared openly; private key never sent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between validation and verification.
parts.answer: Validation is an automatic check by the computer that data is reasonable/sensible and follows set rules (it cannot tell if the data is actually correct). Verification checks that data has been copied or entered accurately, i.e. it matches the original.
parts.working: 1 mark: validation – checks data is sensible/meets rules. 1 mark: verification – checks data matches the source/is copied correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods of verification that could be used when a clerk types customers' names into a utility company's system.
parts.answer: Double entry: the name is typed twice (possibly by two people) and the computer compares the two versions; if they differ the clerk is asked to re-enter. Visual check (proof-reading): the clerk compares the data on screen with the original paper form before confirming.
parts.working: For each method: 1 mark for the name, 1 mark for a description.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An online form for a cricket academy in Rawalpindi collects the data below. For each item, identify the most suitable validation check.
(i) The player's age, which must be between 8 and 18.
(ii) The player's email address, which must contain one '@'.
(iii) The player's surname, which must not be left blank.
(iv) The batting style, which must be one of 'Left', 'Right'.
parts.answer: (i) Range check. (ii) Format check. (iii) Presence check. (iv) Lookup (existence/list) check.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'character check' for (ii); accept 'list check' for (iv).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why validation cannot ensure that a player's date of birth is correct.
parts.answer: Validation only checks the date is reasonable/possible (e.g. a valid date in a sensible range); a wrong but valid date, such as 12/03/2012 typed instead of 21/03/2012, would still be accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark: validation only checks data is sensible/follows rules. 1 mark: a plausible but wrong value passes (example).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A warehouse in Sialkot gives each product a five-digit code followed by a modulo-11 check digit. The weights 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 are applied to the five digits from left to right. The check digit is 11 minus the remainder when the weighted sum is divided by 11 (a result of 11 becomes 0 and a result of 10 becomes X). Calculate the check digit for the code 70386. Show your working.
parts.answer: Check digit = 9 (full code 703869)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a check digit detects an error when the code is typed in.
parts.answer: The computer recalculates the check digit from the first five digits entered and compares it with the check digit typed; if they differ, an error (e.g. a wrong or transposed digit) has occurred and the code is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: check digit recalculated from the entered digits. 1 mark: compared with entered check digit – mismatch means error.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A system uses even parity, with the parity bit as the most significant bit of each byte. Write the 8-bit byte that is sent for each of these 7-bit data values.
(i) 1011001
(ii) 0110100
(iii) 1111111
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) four 1s → parity bit 0. (ii) three 1s → parity bit 1. (iii) seven 1s → parity bit 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The byte 10110110 is received using even parity. State whether an error has been detected and explain your answer.
parts.answer: An error has been detected: the byte contains five 1s, an odd number, but even parity requires an even number of 1s.
parts.working: 1 mark: error detected. 1 mark: five 1s / odd count.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a parity check might not detect an error in a byte.
parts.answer: If an even number of bits (e.g. two) are changed, the number of 1s stays even, so the parity is still correct.
parts.working: B1 two (an even number of) bits flipped – parity unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four bytes and a parity byte are sent using even parity (parity bit is the most significant bit of each byte; the parity byte gives even parity for each bit column). The block received is:
Byte 1: 01011010
Byte 2: 00110011
Byte 3: 01100001
Byte 4: 10001110
Parity byte: 10000010
Identify the byte and the bit position (1 = leftmost, 8 = rightmost) that contains the error. Explain how you found it.
parts.answer: Byte 3, bit position 6.
parts.working: M1 byte 3 has three 1s – odd, so the error is in byte 3 (all other bytes have an even number of 1s). M1 column 6 (bytes 1–4 plus parity byte) has an odd number of 1s – all other columns even. A1 byte 3, bit 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the corrected value of the byte containing the error.
parts.working: B1 bit 6 of byte 3 changed from 0 to 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the advantage of a parity block over a parity check on each byte alone.
parts.answer: A parity check on bytes only shows which byte is wrong; the parity block (column check) also identifies which bit, so a single-bit error can be located and corrected automatically without re-transmission.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies exact bit position (row and column). 1 mark: error can be corrected without resending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A block of five bytes is sent with a checksum. The checksum is calculated by adding the denary values of the bytes and taking the remainder when the total is divided by 256. The bytes have the denary values 58, 127, 196, 21 and 155. Calculate the checksum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the receiving computer uses the checksum.
parts.answer: The receiver recalculates the checksum from the bytes it has received using the same algorithm. It compares its value with the checksum sent with the block. If they are the same the data is accepted; if they differ an error has occurred and the block is requested again.
parts.working: 1 mark each: recalculates using same algorithm; compares with transmitted checksum; mismatch → error, request re-transmission.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A delivery company in Karachi uses parcel codes in the format LLDDDD-D: two upper-case letters, four digits, a hyphen, and one more digit (for example KH4021-7). The code is stored as a STRING.
Write a pseudocode function ValidCode(Code : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN that returns TRUE only if Code matches this format. You may use LENGTH() and MID().
parts.answer:
FUNCTION ValidCode(Code : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   IF LENGTH(Code) <> 8 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 8
      Ch ← MID(Code, Index, 1)
      IF Index <= 2 THEN
         IF Ch < 'A' OR Ch > 'Z' THEN
            RETURN FALSE
         ENDIF
      ELSE
         IF Index = 7 THEN
            IF Ch <> '-' THEN
               RETURN FALSE
            ENDIF
         ELSE
            IF Ch < '0' OR Ch > '9' THEN
               RETURN FALSE
            ENDIF
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each for: function header and RETURNS BOOLEAN with correct ENDFUNCTION; length check (= 8); loop through characters using MID(Code, Index, 1); checks positions 1–2 are 'A' to 'Z'; checks position 7 is '-'; checks positions 3–6 and 8 are '0' to '9' and returns FALSE on any failure / TRUE only at the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an echo check verifies data sent from a computer to a remote device.
parts.answer: The receiving device sends a copy of the data it received back to the sender. The sender compares the returned data with the original. If they are different, an error occurred and the data is sent again.
parts.working: 1 mark each: data sent back to sender; compared with original; resent if different.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of an echo check.
parts.answer: It doubles the amount of data transmitted / if they differ you cannot tell whether the error was on the outward or the return journey.
parts.working: B1 either point.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Six-digit library card numbers at a university in Quetta are given a modulo-11 check digit using weights 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 (left to right). Check digit = (11 − (weighted sum MOD 11)), with 11 written as 0 and 10 written as 'X'.
Calculate the check digit for the card number 481305.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a pseudocode function CheckDigit(CardNo : STRING) RETURNS STRING that takes a six-digit card number as a string and returns its check digit as a one-character string ('0'–'9' or 'X'). You may use MID(), STR_TO_NUM() and NUM_TO_STR().
parts.answer:
FUNCTION CheckDigit(CardNo : STRING) RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE Index, Total, Digit, Result : INTEGER
   Total ← 0
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 6
      Digit ← STR_TO_NUM(MID(CardNo, Index, 1))
      Total ← Total + Digit * (8 - Index)
   NEXT Index
   Result ← 11 - (Total MOD 11)
   IF Result = 11 THEN
      Result ← 0
   ENDIF
   IF Result = 10 THEN
      RETURN "X"
   ELSE
      RETURN NUM_TO_STR(Result)
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each for: initialise Total to 0 (outside loop); loop for 6 digits extracting each with MID; convert to number; multiply by the correct weight (8 − Index, or a weight array 7..2) and add to Total; Result ← 11 − Total MOD 11 with 11 → 0; return 'X' for 10, otherwise digit as character.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinic in Hyderabad uses double entry to verify patients' phone numbers. Describe how double entry works and explain one limitation of it.
parts.answer: The number is entered twice (by the same or a different person) and the computer compares the two entries; if they do not match, the user is asked to re-enter. Limitation: if the same mistake is made both times (e.g. reading the number wrongly from a badly written form), the wrong number is accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark: entered twice. 1 mark: computer compares and rejects/asks again on mismatch. 1 mark: limitation – same error in both entries / original source wrong / slow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The clinic also applies a length check that only accepts phone numbers of exactly 11 digits. Explain why using both validation and verification is better than using only one of them.
parts.answer: Validation rejects impossible/unreasonable data (e.g. 10 digits) but cannot detect a valid-looking wrong number; verification catches copying/typing errors against the source. Together they reduce both kinds of error.
parts.working: 1 mark: validation catches unreasonable data but not wrong-but-sensible data. 1 mark: verification catches transcription errors that validation would miss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between data privacy and data integrity.
parts.answer: Data privacy means keeping personal data confidential so only authorised people can see it and it is used only for the agreed purpose. Data integrity means the data is accurate, complete and consistent, and has not been changed in an unauthorised or accidental way.
parts.working: 1 mark: privacy – restricting who can access/see personal data. 1 mark: integrity – accuracy/consistency of the data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many countries have data protection laws. State three requirements that such laws usually place on organisations that hold personal data.
parts.answer: Any three of: data must be collected and processed fairly and lawfully; used only for the stated purpose; adequate, relevant and not excessive; kept accurate and up to date; not kept longer than necessary; kept secure; not transferred abroad without adequate protection; individuals can see/correct their data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital in Islamabad stores patients' blood groups and allergies in a database. Describe two ways in which the integrity of this data could be lost.
parts.answer: Any two of: typing errors when data is entered; errors during transmission between systems; data corrupted by hardware/software failure; malicious alteration by a hacker or virus; two users updating the same record at once.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the integrity of this data is especially important, and suggest two measures that would help to maintain it.
parts.answer: Importance: doctors make treatment decisions based on the data – a wrong blood group or missing allergy could cause serious harm. Measures (any two): validation (e.g. lookup check that blood group is one of A+, A−, …); verification (double entry / visual check); access rights so only authorised staff can change records; parity/checksums when transferring data; regular backups; record locking.
parts.working: 1 mark for importance linked to patient safety; 1 mark for consequence; 1 mark each for two suitable measures (max 4).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A national examination board will publish students' results through a website. Students log in with their roll number and date of birth. Discuss the privacy and integrity issues involved and recommend measures the board should take.
parts.answer: Privacy: roll numbers and dates of birth are easy to obtain or guess, so other people could view a student's results; results must only be visible to the student/school; data must be transmitted securely; data must not be shared or sold. Integrity: results must not be changed after publication by hackers or staff; errors when importing marks could publish wrong grades; transmission errors. Measures: stronger authentication (password or one-time code sent to registered phone); HTTPS/TLS encryption; access rights so only exam officers can edit marks and website accounts are read-only; audit log of changes; validation and verification when marks are entered; checksums/hashes when files are transferred; backups; firewall.
parts.working: Level of response. 5–6: clear separation of privacy and integrity issues, each linked to the scenario, with at least three justified measures. 3–4: several relevant issues and measures, some justification or context. 1–2: a few general points, little linking to the website. Indicative points listed in the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of a structure chart.
parts.answer: To show the modular structure of a program: how the problem is broken down into modules, how modules relate (which module calls which) and what data/parameters pass between them.
parts.working: B1 shows decomposition into modules and the relationships/parameters between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Describe what each of the following shows on a structure chart.
(i) An arrow with an empty (hollow) circle at its tail.
(ii) An arrow with a filled (solid) circle at its tail.
(iii) A small diamond where a module joins the lines to two lower modules.
(iv) A curved arrow passing across the lines to some lower modules.
parts.answer: (i) A data couple – a data item (parameter) passed between modules. (ii) A flag – a Boolean/control value passed between modules. (iii) Selection – only one of the lower modules is called, depending on a condition. (iv) Iteration – the lower modules are called repeatedly.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A ticket barrier at a metro station in Lahore has two states: Closed (the start state) and Open. Its behaviour is:
• In Closed, tapping a valid card opens the barrier and the green light comes on.
• In Closed, tapping an invalid card keeps the barrier closed and the red light comes on.
• In Open, when the passenger walks through, the barrier closes.
• In Open, if no one walks through within 10 seconds, the barrier closes.
Complete a state-transition table with the columns: Current state | Event | Output | Next state.
parts.answer:
Closed | valid card tapped | green light | Open
Closed | invalid card tapped | red light | Closed
Open | passenger walks through | (none) | Closed
Open | 10 s time-out | (none) | Closed
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct row (current state, event, output and next state all correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the start state is shown on a state-transition diagram.
parts.answer: By an arrow pointing to that state that does not come from any other state (often with a solid dot at its tail).
parts.working: B1 arrow into the state from no other state.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A structure chart for an online grocery order in Karachi is described as follows.
• ProcessOrder is the top module.
• ProcessOrder calls GetOrder, which passes OrderID (STRING) and Quantity (INTEGER) up to ProcessOrder.
• ProcessOrder calls CheckStock, passing it OrderID and Quantity; CheckStock returns the flag InStock (BOOLEAN).
• A diamond on ProcessOrder joins two modules: ConfirmOrder and RejectOrder. Each receives OrderID.
Write the pseudocode module headers for GetOrder, CheckStock and ConfirmOrder.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE GetOrder(BYREF OrderID : STRING, BYREF Quantity : INTEGER)
FUNCTION CheckStock(OrderID : STRING, Quantity : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
PROCEDURE ConfirmOrder(OrderID : STRING)
parts.working: 1 mark: GetOrder as a PROCEDURE. 1 mark: both its parameters BYREF with correct types. 1 mark: CheckStock as FUNCTION with two parameters (by value). 1 mark: RETURNS BOOLEAN and ConfirmOrder as PROCEDURE with OrderID. (Accept CheckStock as a procedure with a BYREF BOOLEAN parameter for the third mark.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why GetOrder's parameters must be passed by reference.
parts.answer: GetOrder must send two values back to ProcessOrder. Passing BYREF passes the address of the caller's variables, so the values assigned inside GetOrder change the caller's variables (a function can return only one value).
parts.working: 1 mark: values must be returned to the calling module. 1 mark: by reference means the original variable is updated / address passed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A phone-charging locker in a shopping mall in Doha is described by this state-transition table.
Current state | Event | Next state
Available | door closed and PIN set | Locked
Locked | correct PIN entered | Open
Locked | wrong PIN (1st or 2nd attempt) | Locked
Locked | wrong PIN (3rd attempt) | Blocked
Blocked | staff key used | Open
Open | door closed | Available
The locker starts in Available. State the final state after each sequence of events.
(i) door closed and PIN set; wrong PIN; correct PIN; door closed
(ii) door closed and PIN set; wrong PIN; wrong PIN; wrong PIN; correct PIN
parts.answer: (i) Available (ii) Blocked
parts.working: 1 mark each. In (ii) the correct PIN has no transition from Blocked, so the locker stays Blocked.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the locker leaves the Blocked state and why this design improves security.
parts.answer: Only a member of staff using the staff key can move it to Open. This stops someone guessing the PIN by trying many values (brute force), because after three wrong attempts entering PINs has no effect.
parts.working: 1 mark: staff key → Open. 1 mark: prevents repeated guessing of the PIN.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one extra transition that would be useful, giving the current state, event and next state.
parts.answer: e.g. Open | time-out with door left open | Open with alarm/ 'Alarm' state; or Available | staff key used | Open (for cleaning).
parts.working: B1 any sensible, complete transition.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A structure chart for a weather-station program is described as follows.
• Main is the top module.
• Main first calls InitialiseTotals, which returns Total (REAL) and Count (INTEGER).
• A curved arrow then shows that Main repeatedly calls ReadReading and UpdateTotals.
• ReadReading returns Reading (REAL) and the flag EndOfData (BOOLEAN).
• UpdateTotals receives Reading and also receives and returns Total and Count.
• Finally Main calls OutputAverage, passing Total and Count.
The repetition stops when EndOfData is TRUE; the reading returned with EndOfData = TRUE is not a real reading and must not be added.
Write pseudocode for module Main, including the declarations of its variables.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Total, Reading : REAL
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
DECLARE EndOfData : BOOLEAN
CALL InitialiseTotals(Total, Count)
CALL ReadReading(Reading, EndOfData)
WHILE EndOfData = FALSE
   CALL UpdateTotals(Reading, Total, Count)
   CALL ReadReading(Reading, EndOfData)
ENDWHILE
CALL OutputAverage(Total, Count)
parts.working: 1 mark each for: declarations with suitable types for all four variables; CALL InitialiseTotals with Total and Count; a pre-condition loop (or equivalent) controlled by EndOfData; ReadReading called before the loop and at the end of each iteration (so the end marker is not processed); UpdateTotals called inside the loop with Reading, Total, Count; OutputAverage called after the loop with Total and Count.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An alarm system for a shop in Nairobi has states Disarmed (start), Arming, Armed and Alarm. The rules are:
• Disarmed: entering the correct code starts a 30-second countdown (Arming).
• Arming: when the countdown ends the system becomes Armed; entering the correct code during the countdown returns it to Disarmed.
• Armed: if a sensor is triggered, the siren sounds (Alarm); entering the correct code disarms the system.
• Alarm: entering the correct code stops the siren and disarms the system.
State the number of transitions in the state-transition diagram and list them as 'state –(event)→ state'.
parts.answer:
6 transitions:
Disarmed –(correct code)→ Arming
Arming –(countdown ends)→ Armed
Arming –(correct code)→ Disarmed
Armed –(sensor triggered / siren on)→ Alarm
Armed –(correct code)→ Disarmed
Alarm –(correct code / siren off)→ Disarmed
parts.working: 1 mark for 6. Then 4 marks for the six transitions: 6 correct = 4, 5 = 3, 4 = 2, 2–3 = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why entering the correct code has a different effect depending on the current state.
parts.answer: The next state depends on both the event and the current state – the same input causes different transitions from different states.
parts.working: B1 output/next state depends on current state as well as the event.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A front-loading washing machine has these states: Idle (start), Filling, Washing, Draining, Spinning and Paused. The machine behaves as follows.
• Pressing Start in Idle begins filling with water.
• When the water level is reached, washing begins.
• When the wash timer ends, the water drains.
• When the drum is empty, spinning begins; when the spin timer ends, the machine returns to Idle and beeps.
• Pressing Pause during Washing moves to Paused; pressing Start in Paused returns to Washing.
Write the state-transition table (Current state | Event | Output | Next state) for this machine.
parts.answer:
Idle | Start pressed | water valve opens | Filling
Filling | water level reached | motor on | Washing
Washing | wash timer ends | pump on | Draining
Draining | drum empty | fast spin | Spinning
Spinning | spin timer ends | beep | Idle
Washing | Pause pressed | motor stops | Paused
Paused | Start pressed | motor on | Washing
parts.working: 7 transitions required. 1 mark for each correct transition, max 6 (outputs other than the beep may be any sensible action or left blank).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The door must stay locked in every state except Idle. Explain how a state-transition diagram helps the programmer check this requirement.
parts.answer: Every state and every possible transition is shown, so the programmer can check each state/transition to make sure no event leads to the door being unlocked except on entering Idle; missing or unsafe transitions are easy to spot.
parts.working: 1 mark: all states/transitions listed explicitly. 1 mark: can check each one for the door-lock condition / spot missing or unsafe transitions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The pseudocode below is the main program of a quiz app.
CALL ShowRules()
FOR Round ← 1 TO 5
   CALL AskQuestion(Round, Answer)
   Correct ← CheckAnswer(Round, Answer)
   IF Correct = TRUE THEN
      CALL AddPoint(Score)
   ENDIF
NEXT Round
CALL ShowScore(Score)
Describe the structure chart that represents this program. Your description should name the modules, the parameters passed (and their direction) and any symbols for iteration or selection.
parts.answer: Top module: Main. Lower modules (left to right): ShowRules (no parameters); AskQuestion – Round passed down, Answer returned up (data couples); CheckAnswer – Round and Answer passed down, Correct returned up as a flag; AddPoint – Score passed down and returned up; ShowScore – Score passed down. A curved iteration arrow covers AskQuestion, CheckAnswer and AddPoint (the loop). A diamond (selection) on the line to AddPoint, because it is only called if Correct is TRUE.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: Main at the top with the five modules beneath; ShowRules with no parameters; AskQuestion with Round down and Answer up; CheckAnswer with Round/Answer down; Correct shown as a flag (solid circle) returned up; AddPoint with Score down and up; ShowScore with Score down; iteration arrow over the three loop modules; selection diamond for AddPoint.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A pedestrian crossing in Abu Dhabi has states CarsGo (start), CarsAmber, WalkGo and WalkFlash.
Current state | Event | Output | Next state
CarsGo | button pressed | 'WAIT' lamp on | CarsAmber
CarsGo | timer ends | (none) | CarsGo
CarsAmber | timer ends | car red, walk green | WalkGo
WalkGo | timer ends | walk green flashes | WalkFlash
WalkFlash | timer ends | car green, walk red | CarsGo
WalkFlash | button pressed | (none) | WalkFlash
Give the outputs produced, in order, and the final state, for the event sequence: timer ends, button pressed, button pressed, timer ends, timer ends, button pressed, timer ends.
parts.answer: Outputs in order: 'WAIT' lamp on; car red, walk green; walk green flashes; car green, walk red. Final state: CarsGo.
parts.working: Trace: CarsGo –timer→ CarsGo (no output); –button→ CarsAmber ('WAIT' on); –button→ no transition from CarsAmber, stays CarsAmber; –timer→ WalkGo (car red, walk green); –timer→ WalkFlash (walk flashes); –button→ WalkFlash (no output); –timer→ CarsGo (car green, walk red). 1 mark for each of the first three outputs in the correct order, 1 mark for final output and final state CarsGo.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The table has no entry for 'button pressed' in CarsAmber or WalkGo. Explain what this means for the system.
parts.answer: There is no transition, so pressing the button in those states is ignored: the state does not change and no output is produced (the crossing is already on its way to letting pedestrians cross).
parts.working: 1 mark: event ignored / state unchanged. 1 mark: reason – a crossing request is already in progress.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each situation, identify the type of maintenance: corrective, adaptive or perfective.
(i) A tax app crashes when an income of exactly zero is entered, so the code is fixed.
(ii) The government changes the sales-tax rate from 17% to 18%, so the program is updated.
(iii) The app works correctly but the report is redesigned to load twice as fast.
(iv) The app is changed so that it runs on a new version of the phone's operating system.
parts.answer: (i) Corrective (ii) Adaptive (iii) Perfective (iv) Adaptive
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why maintenance is part of the program development life cycle.
parts.answer: Programs need to keep working after release – errors are found, requirements and environments change – so maintenance continues for the life of the program.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between black-box testing and white-box testing.
parts.answer: Black-box testing: the tester does not look at the code; test data is chosen from the specification and the actual outputs are compared with the expected outputs. White-box testing: the tester knows the code/structure; test data is chosen to test every path/branch through the code, checking that each path works.
parts.working: Black box: 1 mark – code not seen / based on specification; 1 mark – compare expected and actual outputs. White box: 1 mark – code structure is known; 1 mark – tests every path/branch/statement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why both methods are used.
parts.answer: Black-box testing checks the program meets the requirements, while white-box testing finds faults in paths that black-box data might never reach.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A function ValidMark(Mark : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN returns TRUE if Mark is from 0 to 100 inclusive. Complete a test plan with one test for each type of data below, giving the test value and the expected result.
(i) normal (ii) extreme (iii) abnormal (erroneous) (iv) boundary data that should be rejected
parts.answer: (i) e.g. 57 → TRUE (ii) 0 or 100 → TRUE (iii) e.g. −20 or 250 → FALSE (iv) −1 or 101 → FALSE
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct value with its expected result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a programmer produces a test plan before testing starts.
parts.answer: So testing is systematic: every requirement and type of data is covered and nothing is forgotten; the expected results are decided in advance so actual results can be compared objectively.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software house in Islamabad is writing a stock-control program for a chain of pharmacies. Describe alpha testing, beta testing and acceptance testing in this context.
parts.answer: Alpha testing: done in-house by the software house's own testers/programmers before release, with the program still being developed, using realistic test data. Beta testing: an almost finished version is given to a small number of pharmacy staff/selected users, who use it in real conditions and report faults back. Acceptance testing: carried out with the pharmacy chain (client) at the end to show that the program meets every requirement in the agreed specification, so the client agrees to accept it.
parts.working: For each type: 1 mark for who carries it out, 1 mark for when/purpose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A programmer is writing the module CalculateDiscount, which calls a function GetLoyaltyPoints(CustomerID : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER. GetLoyaltyPoints has not been written yet. Explain what stub testing is and why it is useful here.
parts.answer: A stub is a simple dummy version of a module that has not been written yet. It has the correct header and returns a fixed (or simple) value, perhaps outputting a message to show it was called. This lets CalculateDiscount be tested now, before GetLoyaltyPoints is finished.
parts.working: 1 mark: stub = dummy/placeholder module. 1 mark: correct interface, returns a fixed value/outputs message. 1 mark: allows the calling module to be tested early.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a stub of GetLoyaltyPoints.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION GetLoyaltyPoints(CustomerID : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   OUTPUT "GetLoyaltyPoints called with ", CustomerID
   RETURN 250
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark: correct header and ENDFUNCTION. 1 mark: returns a fixed integer value (message optional).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of testing carried out when the real GetLoyaltyPoints has been written and is combined with CalculateDiscount.
parts.answer: Integration testing

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bus company uses this function.
FUNCTION Fare(Distance : REAL, IsStudent : BOOLEAN) RETURNS REAL
   DECLARE Cost : REAL
   IF Distance <= 5 THEN
      Cost ← 40
   ELSE
      Cost ← 40 + (Distance - 5) * 6
   ENDIF
   IF IsStudent = TRUE THEN
      Cost ← Cost * 0.5
   ENDIF
   RETURN Cost
ENDFUNCTION
Give the value returned for each call.
(i) Fare(3, FALSE) (ii) Fare(5, TRUE) (iii) Fare(12, FALSE) (iv) Fare(12, TRUE)

parts.label: b
parts.text: White-box testing is used. State the minimum number of tests needed so that every IF condition is tested both TRUE and FALSE, and the number needed to test every possible path through the function. Give test data for the minimum set.
parts.answer: Minimum 2 tests, e.g. Fare(3, TRUE) and Fare(12, FALSE). Number of paths = 4.
parts.working: 1 mark: 2 tests. 1 mark: suitable pair where each condition is TRUE in one test and FALSE in the other. 1 mark: 4 paths (2 × 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what integration testing is.
parts.answer: Testing modules together after they have been tested individually, to check they work correctly when combined, e.g. that parameters are passed correctly between them.
parts.working: 1 mark: modules combined after unit testing. 1 mark: checks interfaces/data passed between them work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three items that a test plan for a program usually contains.
parts.answer: Any three of: test number; description/purpose of the test; test data; type of test data (normal/abnormal/extreme/boundary); expected result; actual result; comments/action needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The function below should return the grade for an exam score (A: 80 or more, B: 65–79, C: 50–64, U: below 50).
FUNCTION Grade(Score : INTEGER) RETURNS CHAR
   IF Score > 80 THEN
      RETURN 'A'
   ENDIF
   IF Score >= 65 THEN
      RETURN 'B'
   ENDIF
   IF Score > 50 THEN
      RETURN 'C'
   ENDIF
   RETURN 'U'
ENDFUNCTION
Identify the two errors by giving test data that would reveal each one, the expected result and the actual result.
parts.answer: Score 80: expected 'A', actual 'B'. Score 50: expected 'C', actual 'U'.
parts.working: For each error: 1 mark for the boundary test value (80, 50), 1 mark for expected vs actual result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the corrected lines of code.
parts.answer:
IF Score >= 80 THEN
IF Score >= 50 THEN
parts.working: 1 mark for each corrected line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of testing data that found these errors and the type of maintenance used to fix them.
parts.answer: Boundary (extreme) data; corrective maintenance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school-fees program used in several schools in Lahore must be changed because the schools now also accept payment by a mobile-wallet app. Identify the type of maintenance and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Adaptive maintenance – the program works correctly but must be changed because the requirements/environment have changed (a new payment method).
parts.working: 1 mark: adaptive. 1 mark: justification – change in requirements, not fixing an error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two activities the developers should carry out after making the change and before releasing the new version.
parts.answer: Test the new code (and regression-test the existing features to make sure they still work); update the documentation (user guide and technical documentation); train/inform users about the new option; acceptance testing with the schools.
parts.working: For each of two activities: 1 mark for the activity, 1 mark for the reason/description.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe each type of error and give an example of each.
(i) syntax error (ii) logic error (iii) run-time error
parts.answer: (i) Breaking the grammar rules of the language, so the program cannot be translated – e.g. ENDIF missing, misspelt keyword. (ii) The program runs but gives the wrong result because the algorithm is wrong – e.g. using < instead of <=, wrong formula. (iii) An error that occurs while the program is running and makes it crash or stop – e.g. dividing by zero, array index out of range, opening a file that does not exist.
parts.working: For each type: 1 mark for the description, 1 mark for a suitable example.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student's program in an IDE gives a wrong answer. Describe how each of these IDE features could help her find the error.
(i) breakpoint (ii) single stepping (iii) variable watch window (report window)
parts.answer: (i) A breakpoint pauses execution at a chosen line, so she can check the state of the program at that point. (ii) Single stepping runs the program one statement at a time, so she can see exactly which path is taken and where it goes wrong. (iii) The watch window shows the current values of chosen variables as the program runs, so she can see when a value becomes incorrect.
parts.working: For each feature: 1 mark for what it does, 1 mark for how it helps find the error.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
This pseudocode should output the average of the 10 marks in the array Marks[1:10].
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 9
   Total ← Total + Marks[Index]
NEXT Index
Average ← Total / 10
OUTPUT Average
The array holds 56, 72, 48, 90, 65, 81, 39, 77, 60, 84 in that order. State the value that is output, and the value that should be output.
parts.answer: Output: 58.8. Should be: 67.2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the type of error and write the corrected line.
parts.answer: Logic error; corrected line: FOR Index ← 1 TO 10
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A program calculates fuel economy for taxi drivers in Lahore using:
INPUT Distance
INPUT Litres
Economy ← Distance / Litres
OUTPUT Economy
State the type of error that occurs when a driver enters 0 for Litres, and explain why it cannot be found by the translator.
parts.answer: Run-time error (division by zero). The code is syntactically correct; the error only happens with certain input values while the program is running.
parts.working: 1 mark: run-time error. 1 mark: syntax is valid / depends on data at run time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite the pseudocode so this error cannot happen.
parts.answer:
INPUT Distance
REPEAT
   INPUT Litres
   IF Litres <= 0 THEN
      OUTPUT "Litres must be greater than 0"
   ENDIF
UNTIL Litres > 0
Economy ← Distance / Litres
OUTPUT Economy
parts.working: 1 mark: validation of Litres before the division. 1 mark: loop to re-input (or IF to avoid the calculation). 1 mark: message to the user and correct condition (> 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
This function should return the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in a lower-case word, but it contains three errors.
01 FUNCTION CountVowels(Word : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
02    DECLARE Count, Index : INTEGER
03    DECLARE Ch : CHAR
04    FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Word)
05       Count ← 0
06       Ch ← MID(Word, Index, 1)
07       IF Ch = 'a' OR 'e' OR 'i' OR 'o' OR 'u' THEN
08          Count ← Count + 1
09       ENDIF
10    NEXT Index
11    OUTPUT Count
12 ENDFUNCTION
Give the line number of each error and write the corrected code.
parts.answer:
Line 05: Count ← 0 must be before the loop (move it to between lines 03 and 04), otherwise Count is reset every time.
Line 07: IF Ch = 'a' OR Ch = 'e' OR Ch = 'i' OR Ch = 'o' OR Ch = 'u' THEN
Line 11: RETURN Count
parts.working: For each error: 1 mark for identifying the line, 1 mark for the correct correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
This pseudocode should calculate N! (N factorial = 1 × 2 × … × N).
01 Result ← 1
02 Count ← 1
03 WHILE Count < N
04    Result ← Result * Count
05    Count ← Count + 1
06 ENDWHILE
07 OUTPUT Result
With N = 5 the output is wrong. The programmer sets a breakpoint on line 04 and watches Count and Result. Give the values of Count and Result each time the program pauses at the breakpoint (before line 04 runs), and the final output.
parts.answer: Pause 1: Count 1, Result 1. Pause 2: Count 2, Result 1. Pause 3: Count 3, Result 2. Pause 4: Count 4, Result 6. Output: 24.
parts.working: 1 mark: four pauses only. 1 mark: Count values 1, 2, 3, 4. 1 mark: Result values 1, 1, 2, 6. 1 mark: output 24.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the watched values show and correct the error.
parts.answer: The loop stops before multiplying by 5 (Count never reaches N inside the loop), so the result is 4! = 24 instead of 120. Correct line 03 to WHILE Count <= N.
parts.working: 1 mark: loop ends one iteration early / last multiplication by N missing. 1 mark: WHILE Count <= N.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the five stages of the program development life cycle in order.
parts.answer: Analysis, design, coding, testing, maintenance.
parts.working: 2 marks for all five in the correct order; 1 mark for all five in the wrong order or four in the correct order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens in the analysis stage.
parts.answer: The problem is investigated and defined: the current system is studied (e.g. interviews, observation, questionnaires) and a requirements specification is produced that states what the new program must do.
parts.working: 1 mark: investigate/understand the problem. 1 mark: produce requirements specification.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two items produced in the design stage.
parts.answer: Any two of: structure chart; pseudocode/flowcharts; state-transition diagram; identifier table/data structures; interface (screen) designs; test plan.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the waterfall model of program development.
parts.answer: The stages are carried out one after another in a fixed order; each stage must be completed (and signed off) before the next begins; the output of one stage is the input to the next; there is little or no going back to an earlier stage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of the points listed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one benefit and one drawback of the waterfall model.
parts.answer: Benefit: simple to understand and manage, with clear milestones and documentation. Drawback: the client sees a working program only at the end, so changes to requirements are difficult and expensive to make.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the rapid application development (RAD) model.
parts.answer: Development is done quickly using prototypes; the client gives continual feedback on each prototype, which is improved until it meets their needs; modules may be developed in parallel by small teams, often re-using existing code/tools; little time is spent on detailed planning up front.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of the points listed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A start-up in Karachi wants a food-delivery app quickly, but it is not yet sure exactly which features customers want. Explain why RAD is suitable, and give one drawback of using it.
parts.answer: Suitable: prototypes can be shown to the client/customers early and changed as the requirements become clear; a working product is produced quickly. Drawback: needs the client to be available for frequent feedback / less focus on non-functional requirements and documentation / not good for very large projects.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons linked to the scenario; 1 mark for a drawback.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the iterative model of program development.
parts.answer: A simple version meeting part of the requirements is developed first; the life-cycle stages are then repeated in cycles (iterations), each adding or improving features; each version is tested and reviewed by the client before the next iteration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: initial simple version; stages repeated in cycles; features added each time; feedback/review after each iteration; working version available early.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between the iterative model and the waterfall model.
parts.answer: In the iterative model the stages are repeated many times and a working version is available early, whereas in the waterfall model each stage is done once in sequence and the full program is only delivered at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark for each side of the comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Recommend a development model for each project and justify your choice.
(i) Software that controls the dosage of an infusion pump in a hospital; the requirements are fixed by safety regulations.
(ii) A university in Istanbul wants a student timetable app, and expects students to suggest new features after using early versions.
(iii) A small charity in Peshawar needs a donation website within six weeks and the director will meet the developers every week.
parts.answer: (i) Waterfall – requirements are clear and fixed; each stage must be completed and fully documented and signed off, which suits safety-critical software. (ii) Iterative – a basic version can be released and improved in repeated cycles using student feedback. (iii) RAD – the deadline is short and the client is available for regular feedback on prototypes.
parts.working: For each project: 1 mark for a suitable model, 1 mark for a justification linked to the scenario (accept other models only with a strong scenario-based justification).

parts.label: a
parts.text: During the design stage of a library loans system, the team produces an identifier table, a structure chart, pseudocode and a state-transition diagram for the loan status of a book. Explain the purpose of each of these four design outputs.
parts.answer: Identifier table: lists each variable/constant/array with its data type and purpose, so programmers use them consistently. Structure chart: shows the modules, their hierarchy and the parameters passed between them. Pseudocode: describes the algorithm for each module in a language-independent way, ready to be coded. State-transition diagram: shows the states a book can be in (e.g. Available, OnLoan, Reserved, Overdue) and the events that move it between them.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why time spent on the design stage can reduce the total cost of the project.
parts.answer: Errors and misunderstandings found at design are much cheaper to correct than after coding or release; a clear design also lets several programmers work on separate modules in parallel and makes testing and maintenance easier.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Define each of these object-oriented terms.
(i) class (ii) object (iii) attribute (iv) method
parts.answer: (i) A template/blueprint that defines the attributes and methods shared by objects of one type. (ii) An instance of a class, with its own values for the attributes. (iii) A data item (property) belonging to a class/object. (iv) A procedure or function defined in a class that acts on an object's data.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by encapsulation.
parts.answer: Combining the data (attributes) and the methods that act on it in one class, and hiding the data (PRIVATE) so it can only be accessed or changed through the class's own public methods.
parts.working: 1 mark: data and methods bundled together in a class/object. 1 mark: attributes hidden – accessed only via methods (getters/setters).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A transport app has a class Vehicle with attributes RegNumber and MaxPassengers and a method Describe(). The classes Rickshaw and Bus are derived from Vehicle. Explain what is meant by inheritance, using these classes.
parts.answer: Inheritance means a subclass (derived class) automatically gets the attributes and methods of its parent (base) class. Rickshaw and Bus inherit RegNumber, MaxPassengers and Describe() from Vehicle and can add their own, e.g. Bus could add RouteNumber.
parts.working: 1 mark: subclass receives attributes and methods of the superclass. 1 mark: applied to Vehicle/Rickshaw/Bus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by polymorphism, using the method Describe().
parts.answer: Polymorphism allows a method inherited from the base class to be redefined (overridden) in a subclass so that it behaves differently: calling Describe() on a Rickshaw object gives a different output from calling it on a Bus object, even though both use the same method name.
parts.working: 1 mark: same method name, different behaviour in different classes (overriding). 1 mark: example with Describe() for Rickshaw/Bus.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bookshop in Lahore uses a class Book with these private attributes: ISBN (STRING), Title (STRING), Price (REAL). It has a constructor that takes values for all three attributes, a getter for Price and a method ApplyDiscount(Percent : INTEGER) that reduces Price by that percentage.
Write pseudocode for the class Book.
parts.answer:
CLASS Book
   PRIVATE ISBN : STRING
   PRIVATE Title : STRING
   PRIVATE Price : REAL
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenISBN : STRING, GivenTitle : STRING, GivenPrice : REAL)
      ISBN ← GivenISBN
      Title ← GivenTitle
      Price ← GivenPrice
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION GetPrice() RETURNS REAL
      RETURN Price
   ENDFUNCTION
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE ApplyDiscount(Percent : INTEGER)
      Price ← Price * (100 - Percent) / 100
   ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS
parts.working: 1 mark each for: CLASS Book … ENDCLASS; three PRIVATE attribute declarations with types; constructor PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW with three parameters; assignments to the attributes in the constructor; GetPrice function returning Price; ApplyDiscount procedure with correct calculation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a pseudocode statement to create a Book object called NewBook with ISBN "978-1-7290-4471-0", title "Mountain Roads" and price 1450.
parts.answer: NewBook ← NEW Book("978-1-7290-4471-0", "Mountain Roads", 1450)

parts.label: c
