parts.text: NewBook.ApplyDiscount(20) is called. State the value then returned by NewBook.GetPrice().

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between inheritance and containment (aggregation) in object-oriented programming. Give an example of each from a school system with classes Person, Teacher and Department.
parts.answer: Inheritance is an 'is a' relationship: a subclass gets the attributes and methods of a superclass – e.g. Teacher inherits from Person (a teacher is a person). Containment/aggregation is a 'has a' relationship: one class contains objects of another class as attributes – e.g. a Department has (contains) several Teacher objects.
parts.working: 1 mark: inheritance = 'is a'/subclass gets parent's members. 1 mark: suitable inheritance example. 1 mark: aggregation = 'has a'/object contains other objects. 1 mark: suitable aggregation example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by method overriding.
parts.answer: A subclass defines its own version of a method that it has inherited, with the same name/identifier (and parameters); when the method is called on a subclass object, the subclass's version is used instead of the parent's.
parts.working: 1 mark: subclass redefines an inherited method with the same name. 1 mark: subclass version runs for subclass objects.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bank uses this class.
CLASS Account
   PRIVATE AccountNo : STRING
   PRIVATE Balance : REAL
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenNo : STRING)
      AccountNo ← GivenNo
      Balance ← 0
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION GetBalance() RETURNS REAL
      RETURN Balance
   ENDFUNCTION
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE Deposit(Amount : REAL)
      Balance ← Balance + Amount
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION Withdraw(Amount : REAL) RETURNS BOOLEAN
      IF Amount <= Balance THEN
         Balance ← Balance - Amount
         RETURN TRUE
      ENDIF
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
A class SavingsAccount inherits from Account. It has an extra private attribute WithdrawalsLeft (INTEGER), set to 3 by its constructor. Its Withdraw method overrides the parent's: it allows a withdrawal only if WithdrawalsLeft is greater than 0 and the parent's Withdraw succeeds, and it then reduces WithdrawalsLeft by 1.
Write pseudocode for the class SavingsAccount.
parts.answer:
CLASS SavingsAccount INHERITS Account
   PRIVATE WithdrawalsLeft : INTEGER
   PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenNo : STRING)
      SUPER.NEW(GivenNo)
      WithdrawalsLeft ← 3
   ENDPROCEDURE
   PUBLIC FUNCTION Withdraw(Amount : REAL) RETURNS BOOLEAN
      IF WithdrawalsLeft > 0 THEN
         IF SUPER.Withdraw(Amount) = TRUE THEN
            WithdrawalsLeft ← WithdrawalsLeft - 1
            RETURN TRUE
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDFUNCTION
ENDCLASS
parts.working: 1 mark each for: CLASS SavingsAccount INHERITS Account … ENDCLASS; PRIVATE WithdrawalsLeft : INTEGER; constructor NEW with GivenNo parameter; SUPER.NEW(GivenNo) called; WithdrawalsLeft ← 3; Withdraw header matching the parent (overriding) and check WithdrawalsLeft > 0; calls SUPER.Withdraw(Amount), decrements WithdrawalsLeft only on success and returns the correct Boolean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why SavingsAccount must call the parent's Withdraw method rather than changing Balance directly.
parts.answer: Balance is PRIVATE to Account, so it cannot be accessed directly from the subclass; it can only be changed through Account's public methods.

parts.text:

parts.text:

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a class Student, the attribute DateOfBirth is declared PRIVATE and is accessed with the methods GetDateOfBirth() and SetDateOfBirth(). Explain why the attribute is private and accessed through these methods.
parts.answer: Making it PRIVATE means code outside the class cannot read or change it directly (encapsulation/data hiding). Access is only through the getter and setter, so the class controls how the data is used. The setter can validate the new value (e.g. reject a future date) before storing it, keeping the object's data valid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between method overloading and method overriding.
parts.answer: Overloading: several methods in the same class have the same name but different parameter lists (number or types), and the one called depends on the arguments given. Overriding: a subclass redefines a method inherited from its superclass with the same name and parameters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A class Shape has a method Area(). Classes Circle and Rectangle inherit from Shape. A program stores a mixture of Circle and Rectangle objects in one array of type Shape and calls Area() on each element in a loop. Explain how polymorphism makes this possible, and why it is useful.
parts.answer: Each subclass overrides Area() with its own formula. At run time, the version of Area() that runs depends on the actual class of each object, so the same call Area() gives the correct result for every shape. This means the loop does not need IF statements to test the type, and new shapes (e.g. Triangle) can be added without changing the loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

parts.answer: (i) Records are stored one after another in the order in which they were added (chronological), not sorted. (ii) Records are stored one after another in order of a key field. (iii) Records are stored at an address calculated from the key field by a hashing algorithm, so they can be accessed directly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between sequential access and direct access.
parts.answer: Sequential access reads records one after another from the start of the file until the required record is reached; direct access goes straight to the required record (using its address/index/hash) without reading the earlier records.
parts.working: 1 mark for each.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: 1611 MOD 97 = 59, the same address as customer 4521 – a collision. One method: linear probing (open addressing / closed hashing) – look at the next position(s) (60, 61 …) until an empty one is found and store the record there (when searching, start at the hashed address and keep checking the following positions). Alternatively use an overflow area where colliding records are stored and searched serially.
parts.working: 1 mark: address 59 / same as 4521 – collision. 1 mark: method named (linear probing / overflow area / chaining). 1 mark: method described, including how the record is found later.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop stores products in the random file "Stock.dat". Each record has the type:
TYPE TProduct
   DECLARE ProductCode : INTEGER
   DECLARE Description : STRING
   DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
ENDTYPE
The record for a product is stored at the address given by the function Hash(ProductCode) (assume there are no collisions).
Write a pseudocode procedure UpdateStock(Code : INTEGER, Sold : INTEGER) that finds the record for the product, reduces its Quantity by Sold, and writes the record back to the file.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE UpdateStock(Code : INTEGER, Sold : INTEGER)
   DECLARE ThisProduct : TProduct
   DECLARE Address : INTEGER
   Address ← Hash(Code)
   OPENFILE "Stock.dat" FOR RANDOM
   SEEK "Stock.dat", Address
   GETRECORD "Stock.dat", ThisProduct
   ThisProduct.Quantity ← ThisProduct.Quantity - Sold
   SEEK "Stock.dat", Address
   PUTRECORD "Stock.dat", ThisProduct
   CLOSEFILE "Stock.dat"
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each for: declare a variable of type TProduct; Address calculated with Hash(Code); OPENFILE … FOR RANDOM; SEEK to the address then GETRECORD into the variable; update the Quantity field using dot notation; SEEK again, PUTRECORD and CLOSEFILE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sequential file "Members.txt" holds club member records in ascending order of MemberID. Describe, without writing pseudocode, the steps needed to add one new member record so that the file stays in order.

While the MemberID read is less than the new MemberID, write the record to the new file. When the first record with a larger ID is reached (and the new record has not yet been written), write the new record and then that record. Copy all remaining records. If the end of the old file is reached without writing the new record, write it at the end. Close both files, then delete/rename so the new file replaces the old one.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: open old file for read and new file for write; read records one at a time until end of file; copy records with smaller key; insert new record at the correct position (before first larger key); copy remaining records; handle new record belonging at the end; close both files; replace old file with new file.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: In a random file the address is calculated from the key, so the record is written straight to that position; a sequential file must be copied record by record to a new file to keep it in order.
parts.working: 1 mark: random – direct write to hashed address. 1 mark: sequential – whole file has to be read/copied.

parts.text:

A canteen uses this Prolog knowledge base:
contains(biryani, rice).
contains(biryani, chicken).
contains(halwa, semolina).
contains(halwa, nuts).
contains(kheer, rice).
contains(kheer, milk).
contains(kheer, nuts).
allergic(sara, nuts).
allergic(usman, milk).
cannot_eat(P, D) :- allergic(P, I), contains(D, I).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the results of the goal cannot_eat(sara, D).

parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using this goal, what is meant by instantiation and backtracking.
parts.answer: Instantiation: a variable is given (bound to) a value when a match is found – e.g. I is instantiated to nuts from allergic(sara, nuts), then D to halwa. Backtracking: after a solution is found (or a sub-goal fails), Prolog goes back to the most recent choice point and tries the next possible match – e.g. it returns to contains(D, nuts) and finds contains(kheer, nuts), giving D = kheer.
parts.working: 1 mark: instantiation definition. 1 mark: instantiation example from the goal. 1 mark: backtracking definition. 1 mark: backtracking example.

stem:
A family tree is stored in Prolog:
parent(rashid, sana).
parent(rashid, imran).
parent(sana, ali).
parent(ali, zoya).
parent(imran, hira).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), ancestor(Z, Y).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State all the results of the goal ancestor(rashid, Y), in the order Prolog finds them.
parts.answer: Y = sana; Y = imran; Y = ali; Y = zoya; Y = hira
parts.working: 1 mark: sana, imran first (from the first clause). 1 mark: ali, zoya, hira all present. 1 mark: correct order. (Second clause: Z = sana gives ali then, recursively, zoya; Z = imran gives hira.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the base case and the general (recursive) case in the definition of ancestor, and explain why the base case is needed.
parts.answer: Base case: ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y). General case: ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), ancestor(Z, Y). The base case stops the recursion: without it, the rule would keep calling itself and never succeed (infinite recursion).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two features of declarative programming that make it different from imperative programming.
parts.answer: In declarative programming the programmer states facts and rules describing the problem (what is true), not the step-by-step method; the language's inference engine searches the knowledge base (with backtracking) to find solutions to goals. In imperative programming the programmer writes a sequence of instructions that change the program's state (variables) step by step.
parts.working: For each of two features: 1 mark for the feature, 1 mark for the contrast with imperative programming (e.g. facts/rules vs sequence of commands; goal-directed search/backtracking vs explicit control flow; no assignment/state change vs variables updated).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one type of application for which declarative programming is well suited.
parts.answer: Expert systems / knowledge-based systems / natural language processing / AI problems such as route-finding or puzzles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the main characteristic of each programming paradigm.
(i) low-level (ii) imperative (procedural) (iii) object-oriented (iv) declarative
parts.answer: (i) Instructions closely match the processor's instruction set (assembly/machine code), working directly with registers and memory addresses. (ii) The program is a sequence of statements that change the program's state, organised into procedures and functions. (iii) The program is built from objects (instances of classes) that combine data and methods, using encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. (iv) The program states facts and rules; the system works out how to reach a goal.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The program below uses the instruction set: LDR #n (load n into the index register IX), LDM #n (load n into ACC), LDD <address> (load contents of address into ACC), LDX <address> (load contents of (address + IX) into ACC), ADD <address> (add contents of address to ACC), STO <address> (store ACC at address), INC IX / DEC ACC (add/subtract 1), CMP #n (compare ACC with n), JPN <address> (jump if the comparison was not equal), END.
100 LDR #0
101 LDM #0
102 STO 210
103 LDX 200
104 ADD 210
105 STO 210
106 INC IX
107 LDD 211
108 DEC ACC
109 STO 211
110 CMP #0
111 JPN 103
112 END
Memory before running: address 200 = 12, 201 = 7, 202 = 25, 203 = 9, 211 = 4.
State the contents of address 210, address 211 and IX when the program ends, and the number of times the instruction at address 103 is executed.
parts.answer: Address 210 = 53; address 211 = 0; IX = 4; instruction 103 executed 4 times.
parts.working: 1 mark each. 210 holds 12 + 7 + 25 + 9 = 53.

parts.label: b

A linked list is stored in the array List[0:9] of records of type TNode:

Write a pseudocode function DeleteNode(Item : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN that removes the first node whose Data is Item, adds that node to the front of the free list, and returns TRUE. It returns FALSE if Item is not in the list.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION DeleteNode(Item : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Current, Previous : INTEGER
   Current ← StartPointer
   Previous ← NullPointer
   WHILE Current <> NullPointer AND List[Current].Data <> Item
      Previous ← Current
      Current ← List[Current].Pointer
   ENDWHILE
   IF Current = NullPointer THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   IF Previous = NullPointer THEN
      StartPointer ← List[Current].Pointer
   ELSE
      List[Previous].Pointer ← List[Current].Pointer
   ENDIF
   List[Current].Pointer ← FreeListPointer
   FreeListPointer ← Current
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION Push(Value : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   IF TopPointer = 10 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   TopPointer ← TopPointer + 1
   Stack[TopPointer] ← Value
   RETURN TRUE

FUNCTION Pop() RETURNS INTEGER

      RETURN -1
   ENDIF
   Value ← Stack[TopPointer]
   TopPointer ← TopPointer - 1

Write program code for:

• a procedure OutputList() that outputs the items in list order. (Python shown; Java or VB.NET solutions are equally acceptable.)
parts.answer:
NULL = -1
SIZE = 8
data = [""] * SIZE
pointer = [i + 1 for i in range(SIZE)]   # every node starts in the free list
pointer[SIZE - 1] = NULL
start_pointer = NULL
free_pointer = 0

def insert(item):
    global start_pointer, free_pointer
    if free_pointer == NULL:
        return False                       # list is full
    new_node = free_pointer
    free_pointer = pointer[free_pointer]   # take the first free node
    data[new_node] = item
    previous = NULL
    current = start_pointer
    while current != NULL and data[current] < item:   # find position
        previous = current
        current = pointer[current]
    pointer[new_node] = current
    if previous == NULL:                   # new first node
        start_pointer = new_node
    else:
        pointer[previous] = new_node
    return True

def output_list():
    current = start_pointer
    while current != NULL:
        print(data[current])
        current = pointer[current]

parts.text:
A bank branch in Hyderabad issues numbered tokens to customers. Waiting tokens are stored in a circular queue of size 5 using a global array Queue, and global variables Front (0), Rear (−1) and NumItems (0).
Write program code for:
• a function Enqueue(Token) that adds a token and returns True, or returns False if the queue is full
• a function Dequeue() that removes and returns the token at the front, or returns −1 if the queue is empty. (Python shown; Java or VB.NET solutions are equally acceptable.)
parts.answer:
SIZE = 5
queue = [0] * SIZE
front = 0
rear = -1
num_items = 0

def enqueue(token):
    global rear, num_items
    if num_items == SIZE:
        return False                     # queue full
    rear = (rear + 1) % SIZE             # wrap round to 0 after the last index
    queue[rear] = token
    num_items = num_items + 1
    return True

def dequeue():
    global front, num_items
    if num_items == 0:
        return -1                        # queue empty
    token = queue[front]
    front = (front + 1) % SIZE
    num_items = num_items - 1
    return token
parts.working: 1 mark each for: globals initialised; Enqueue checks full (NumItems = size); Rear moved on with wrap-round (MOD or IF); token stored and NumItems incremented, returning True; Dequeue checks empty and returns −1; reads token at Front; moves Front with wrap-round and decrements NumItems.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a pseudocode function BinarySearch(SearchItem : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER that searches the global sorted array Names[1:500] and returns the index of SearchItem, or −1 if it is not found. Use an iterative (not recursive) method.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION BinarySearch(SearchItem : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Low, High, Mid : INTEGER
   Low ← 1
   High ← 500
   WHILE Low <= High
      Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2
      IF Names[Mid] = SearchItem THEN
         RETURN Mid
      ELSE
         IF Names[Mid] < SearchItem THEN
            Low ← Mid + 1
         ELSE
            High ← Mid - 1
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN -1
ENDFUNCTION

parts.label: a
parts.text: An algorithm with time complexity O(n²) takes 2 seconds to process 1000 records on a server in Islamabad. Estimate the time to process 5000 records on the same server.
parts.answer: 50 seconds
parts.working: M1 records × 5, so time × 5² = 25. A1 2 × 25 = 50 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A linear search of 2000 records takes 0.4 ms in the worst case. Estimate the worst-case time for 10 000 records.
parts.answer: 2 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: A binary search needs at most 10 comparisons for an array of 1000 items. State the maximum number of comparisons for 1 000 000 items and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 20 comparisons. Binary search is O(log n): multiplying n by 1000 ≈ 2¹⁰ adds about 10 more halvings (log₂ 1 000 000 ≈ 19.9, so ⌊19.9⌋ + 1 = 20).
parts.working: 1 mark: 20. 1 mark: explanation based on log₂ n / each doubling adds one comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sorted array contains 64 items. State the maximum number of comparisons needed to find an item using (i) a linear search (ii) a binary search.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Binary search: ⌊log₂ 64⌋ + 1 = 7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The array grows to 128 items. State how the maximum number of comparisons changes for each search.
parts.answer: Linear search doubles to 128; binary search increases by only one, to 8.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write program code for:
• a function InsertionSort(Items) that sorts a list/array of integers into ascending order in place and returns the number of comparisons made between Items[j] and the value being inserted
• a function BinarySearch(Items, Target) that returns the index of Target in the sorted list (indices start at 0), or −1 if not present. (Python shown; Java or VB.NET solutions are equally acceptable.)
parts.working: InsertionSort (5): outer loop from the second element; store key; inner loop moving left while previous element is larger; shift elements right and insert key in the gap; count each comparison and return the count. BinarySearch (4): low/high initialised; loop while low <= high with mid calculated by integer division; return mid when found; move low or high correctly and return −1 after loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The main program sorts the list 8611, 4692, 7027, 3500, 8126, 6050, 5100, 7788 and then searches for 7027 and for 6000. State the sorted list, the number of comparisons returned by InsertionSort, and the two values returned by BinarySearch.
parts.answer: 3500, 4692, 5100, 6050, 7027, 7788, 8126, 8611; 20 comparisons; BinarySearch(…, 7027) returns 4; BinarySearch(…, 6000) returns −1.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bubble sort can be improved by using a Boolean flag. Describe how the flag improves the algorithm.
parts.answer: The flag is set to FALSE at the start of each pass and set to TRUE whenever a swap is made. At the end of a pass, if no swap was made (flag still FALSE), the array is already sorted, so the algorithm stops early instead of doing the remaining passes.
parts.working: 1 mark each: flag reset each pass; set when a swap happens; algorithm stops when a pass has no swaps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the best-case and worst-case time complexity of the improved bubble sort, describing the data that gives each.
parts.answer: Best case O(n) – the data is already sorted (one pass, no swaps). Worst case O(n²) – the data is in reverse order.
parts.working: 1 mark each (complexity with matching data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a recursive subroutine and state the two types of case it must have.
parts.answer: A subroutine that is defined in terms of itself / calls itself. It must have a base case (a stopping condition that returns without a further call) and a general (recursive) case that calls itself with a value that moves towards the base case.
parts.working: 1 mark: calls itself. 1 mark: base case. 1 mark: general case.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
FUNCTION Mystery(N : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   IF N = 0 THEN
      RETURN 0
   ELSE
      RETURN (N MOD 10) + Mystery(N DIV 10)
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION
State the value returned by Mystery(4073), the number of times Mystery is called in total, and what the function calculates.
parts.answer: Returns 14; 5 calls (4073, 407, 40, 4, 0); it calculates the sum of the digits of N.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
PROCEDURE Show(N : INTEGER)
   IF N > 0 THEN
      CALL Show(N DIV 2)
      OUTPUT N MOD 2
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE
The procedure outputs each value on the same line with no spaces. State the output of CALL Show(13) and explain why the digits appear in this order.
parts.answer: 1101. Each call makes its recursive call before outputting, so the deepest call (N = 1) outputs first as the calls unwind: 1 (N = 1), 1 (N = 3), 0 (N = 6), 1 (N = 13).
parts.working: 1 mark: 1101. 1 mark: output happens after the recursive call / on unwinding. 1 mark: correct link of digits to calls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the procedure does, and the output of CALL Show(0).
parts.answer: It outputs the binary equivalent of N. Show(0) outputs nothing (the base case is reached immediately).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
FUNCTION Power(B : INTEGER, E : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Half : INTEGER
   IF E = 0 THEN
      RETURN 1
   ENDIF
   IF E MOD 2 = 0 THEN
      Half ← Power(B, E DIV 2)
      RETURN Half * Half
   ELSE
      RETURN B * Power(B, E - 1)
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION
List the calls made when Power(3, 10) is evaluated, and state the value returned.
parts.answer: Power(3, 10) → Power(3, 5) → Power(3, 4) → Power(3, 2) → Power(3, 1) → Power(3, 0). Value returned: 59049.
parts.working: 2 marks: all six calls in order (1 mark for five correct). 1 mark: unwinding values 1, 3, 9, 81, 243, 59049 (or equivalent working). 1 mark: 59049.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the stack is used when Power(3, 10) runs, and state the maximum number of stack frames for Power at any one time.
parts.answer: Each call pushes a stack frame holding the return address, parameters (B, E) and local variable Half. Frames are popped in reverse order as each call returns its value to the caller. Maximum 6 frames (calls with E = 10, 5, 4, 2, 1, 0).
parts.working: 1 mark: frame with return address/parameters/local variables pushed for each call. 1 mark: popped in reverse order on return (LIFO). 1 mark: 6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why an iterative solution might be preferred to a recursive one.
parts.answer: Recursion uses more memory (a stack frame per call) and could cause stack overflow for deep recursion; it can also be slower because of the call overheads.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A child can climb a staircase by taking either 1 step or 2 steps at a time. The number of different ways to climb N steps is: Ways(1) = 1, Ways(2) = 2, and Ways(N) = Ways(N − 1) + Ways(N − 2) for N > 2.
Write program code for a recursive function Ways(N) and an iterative function WaysIterative(N) that give the same results. (Python shown; Java or VB.NET solutions are equally acceptable.)
parts.working: Recursive (3): base case N = 1 returns 1; base case N = 2 returns 2; general case returns Ways(N − 1) + Ways(N − 2). Iterative (3): handles N ≤ 2; keeps the last two values; loop updates them N − 2 times and returns the result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the values returned for N = 5 and N = 10.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The recursive function makes 109 calls in total to calculate Ways(10). Explain why it is very slow for large N and how the iterative version avoids this.
parts.answer: Each call makes two further calls, so the same values (e.g. Ways(3)) are recalculated many times and the number of calls grows roughly exponentially; the iterative version calculates each value once (O(n)) by keeping the previous two results.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeated recalculation / exponential growth. 1 mark: iterative computes each value once / linear time.

A clinic in Faisalabad stores patient data in the table PATIENT. Some of the data is shown.
PATIENT
PatientID | FirstName | LastName | City | BloodGroup | Age
P101 | Ayesha | Khan | Lahore | O+ | 34

stem:
A school in Quetta has these two tables:

FROM STUDENT
INNER JOIN CLASS ON STUDENT.ClassID = CLASS.ClassID

stem:
A sports club in Singapore uses three tables:
MEMBER(MemberID, MemberName, JoinDate)
COURT(CourtID, Surface, Indoor)
BOOKING(BookingID, MemberID, CourtID, BookingDate, StartTime)
Indoor is a Boolean field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the name of each member and the number of bookings that member has made, for bookings of courts that are indoor. Output the members with the most bookings first.
parts.answer:
SELECT MEMBER.MemberName, COUNT(BOOKING.BookingID)
FROM MEMBER
INNER JOIN BOOKING ON MEMBER.MemberID = BOOKING.MemberID
INNER JOIN COURT ON BOOKING.CourtID = COURT.CourtID
WHERE COURT.Indoor = TRUE
GROUP BY MEMBER.MemberName
ORDER BY COUNT(BOOKING.BookingID) DESC;
parts.working: 1 mark each: SELECT MemberName, COUNT(BookingID); join MEMBER to BOOKING on MemberID; join BOOKING to COURT on CourtID; WHERE Indoor = TRUE; GROUP BY MemberName (or MemberID); ORDER BY COUNT(…) DESC. Accept joins written as conditions in WHERE.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why GROUP BY is needed in your query.
parts.answer: Without GROUP BY, COUNT would give one total for all rows; GROUP BY makes a separate count for each member.
parts.working: 1 mark: aggregate function COUNT combines rows; 1 mark: GROUP BY makes one result row (count) per member instead of a single overall count.

stem:
An airline at Islamabad airport wants a list of flight numbers, destinations and departure times for flights to Dubai that still have seats, earliest first. A trainee wrote:
SELECT FlightNo Destination, DepartTime
FROM FLIGHT
ORDER BY DepartTime ASCENDING
WHERE Destination = Dubai AND Seats > 0;
The table is FLIGHT(FlightNo, Destination, DepartTime, Seats).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The script contains four errors. Identify three of the errors and write the fully corrected script.
parts.answer:
Any three of the four errors: (1) SELECT list items must be separated by commas (FlightNo, Destination); (2) the condition is written 'Destination = Dubai' without quotes – a string must be in quotes 'Dubai'; (3) ORDER BY is written before WHERE – WHERE must come before ORDER BY. (4) ASCENDING is not valid – use ASC or omit it.
Corrected:
SELECT FlightNo, Destination, DepartTime
FROM FLIGHT
WHERE Destination = 'Dubai' AND Seats > 0
ORDER BY DepartTime;
parts.working: 1 mark for each error identified (max 3): comma missing between FlightNo and Destination; 'Dubai' not in quotes; clause order (WHERE must come before ORDER BY); 'ASCENDING' should be ASC or omitted. 3 marks for the corrected script: 1 mark SELECT list with commas; 1 mark WHERE Destination = 'Dubai' AND Seats > 0 placed before ORDER BY; 1 mark ORDER BY DepartTime (or DepartTime ASC).

stem: A secondary school in Hyderabad stores its data in separate files.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The school's fee office and exam office each keep their own file containing students' names and addresses. Describe two problems this file-based approach can cause.
parts.answer: Data redundancy: the same student data is stored twice, wasting storage. Data inconsistency: if a family moves and only one office updates the address, the two files disagree.
parts.working: Max 2 problems, 2 marks each (identify + describe in context): data redundancy – same data stored in several files; data inconsistency – copies updated in one file but not another; data dependence – programs tied to file structure so changing a file means rewriting programs; difficult to share / search across files.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how a relational database would reduce one of these problems.
parts.answer: Student details are stored once in one table and linked to other tables using keys, so there is only one copy to update.
parts.working: B1: data stored once / in one table, linked by primary–foreign keys.

stem: A hospital in Peshawar uses a relational DBMS.

parts.label: b

parts.working: 1 mark: overall view/model of the structure (tables, fields, relationships); 1 mark: independent of the physical storage / DBMS software.

stem: A private medical centre in Islamabad stores patient records, appointments and diagnoses in a database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three ways the DBMS can be used to keep the patient data secure.
parts.answer: Access rights: each user group (e.g. receptionists) is given permission to read/edit only some tables, so receptionists cannot see diagnoses. Usernames and passwords: only authorised staff can log in to the database. Backups: regular copies of the database are made (e.g. nightly) so data can be restored after loss.

stem: A developer is building a stock database for an electronics shop in Dubai.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the purpose of the developer interface of a DBMS.
parts.answer: It lets a developer create and manipulate the database structure and objects (tables, queries, forms, reports) without writing all the code, e.g. using design views and drag-and-drop tools.
parts.working: 1 mark: allows developers to create/design tables, queries, forms, reports; 1 mark: by a visual interface / without writing low-level code / with wizards.

parts.text: Describe the purpose of the query processor of a DBMS.
parts.answer: It takes a query (e.g. in SQL), checks and optimises it and then executes it on the database, returning the results.
parts.working: 1 mark: receives/interprets queries (SQL); 1 mark: optimises and executes them, searching the data and returning results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why the developer would use SQL directly instead of the developer interface.

stem: A car-rental firm in Lahore has the tables CUSTOMER(CustomerID, Name, Phone) and RENTAL(RentalID, CustomerID, CarReg, StartDate).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by referential integrity.
parts.answer: Every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the linked table (or be null), so no record refers to a record that does not exist.
parts.working: 1 mark: foreign key value must exist as a primary key in the related table; 1 mark: prevents records referring to non-existent records / orphan records.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The DBMS enforces referential integrity. Describe two actions that would be refused.
parts.answer: Adding a RENTAL record with a CustomerID that is not in CUSTOMER would be refused. Deleting a CUSTOMER record while RENTAL records still contain that CustomerID would be refused.
parts.working: 2 marks each: inserting a child (RENTAL) record whose foreign key does not exist in the parent table; deleting/changing a parent (CUSTOMER) primary key that is still used by child records.

stem: A regional cricket league in Sialkot keeps player details, team lists, match scores and player medical notes in several spreadsheets, one per team. Many players appear in more than one spreadsheet. Results are also shown on a public website.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using a relational database managed by a DBMS will improve data integrity, data privacy and data independence for the league, compared with the spreadsheets. Refer to the scenario.
parts.answer: Integrity: each player is stored once in a PLAYER table and linked by PlayerID, so there are no conflicting copies; validation rules and referential integrity stop scores being recorded for non-existent players. Privacy: access rights mean coaches can view only their own team's medical data, and the public website account can only read results. Independence: the data dictionary/schema separates the data from the programs, so a new field (e.g. strike rate) can be added without rewriting the scoring and website programs.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each of the three areas (1 for the DBMS feature, 1 for linking it to the cricket scenario): integrity – single copy, validation, referential integrity; privacy – access rights, passwords, views, encryption; independence – structure held separately in schema/data dictionary so applications unaffected by changes.

stem: A vehicle-licensing office stores data about vehicles and their owners in two tables, VEHICLE and OWNER(OwnerID, Name, Address).

stem:

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the condition for a table to be in first normal form (1NF).
parts.answer: It has no repeating groups of attributes (each field holds a single atomic value).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the extra condition for a table in 1NF to be in second normal form (2NF).

stem: A city air-quality project in Lahore records PM2.5 readings. Each sensor has a 4-character ID, a location (up to 30 characters) and the date it was installed. parts.text: Write the SQL DDL to create both tables, including all primary and foreign keys and suitable data types.

 SensorID CHARACTER(4),
 Location VARCHAR(30),
 Installed DATE,
 PRIMARY KEY (SensorID)
);
CREATE TABLE AIRREADING(
 SensorID CHARACTER(4),
 ReadDate DATE,

);
parts.working: 1 mark SENSOR table structure; 1 mark SENSOR primary key; 1 mark AIRREADING fields with DATE/TIME/REAL/BOOLEAN; 1 mark composite primary key (SensorID, ReadDate, ReadTime); 1 mark FOREIGN KEY (SensorID); 1 mark REFERENCES SENSOR(SensorID). SENSOR must be created first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the location and PM2.5 value of every reading on 14/11/2026 where an alert was sent, highest PM2.5 first.

FROM SENSOR
INNER JOIN AIRREADING ON SENSOR.SensorID = AIRREADING.SensorID

stem: A language-learning app for children in Malaysia counts vowels in words.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function CountVowels(Word : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER. The function returns the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in Word. Vowels may be upper or lower case.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION CountVowels(Word : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Count, Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Count ← 0
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Word)
      Ch ← LCASE(MID(Word, Index, 1))
      IF Ch = 'a' OR Ch = 'e' OR Ch = 'i' OR Ch = 'o' OR Ch = 'u' THEN
         Count ← Count + 1
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: function header and ENDFUNCTION with Count initialised to 0; loop from 1 to LENGTH(Word); extract each character with MID; correct test for all five vowels in both cases (e.g. using LCASE); increment count and RETURN Count (not OUTPUT).

stem: A weather station in Murree stores the rainfall, in mm, for each day of a 30-day month in the global array Rainfall[1:30] OF REAL.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a procedure WettestDay() that finds the largest value in Rainfall and outputs the day number and the rainfall on that day. If two days have the same largest value, output the first one.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE WettestDay()
   DECLARE Day, MaxDay : INTEGER
   MaxDay ← 1
   FOR Day ← 2 TO 30
      IF Rainfall[Day] > Rainfall[MaxDay] THEN
         MaxDay ← Day
      ENDIF
   NEXT Day
   OUTPUT "Day ", MaxDay, " had ", Rainfall[MaxDay], " mm"
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark procedure header/end; 1 mark initialise max (to first element, or index 1); 1 mark loop through all 30 elements; 1 mark compare with strict > so that the first is kept, updating index; 1 mark output day number and rainfall after the loop.

stem: A science club in Kampala records temperatures from a classroom thermometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode that inputs temperatures until the value −999 is entered. −999 is not a temperature. The program then outputs the average temperature, or the message "No data" if no temperatures were entered.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Temp, Total : REAL
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
INPUT Temp
WHILE Temp <> -999
   Total ← Total + Temp
   Count ← Count + 1
   INPUT Temp
ENDWHILE
IF Count = 0 THEN
   OUTPUT "No data"
ELSE
   OUTPUT Total / Count
ENDIF
parts.working: 1 mark initialise Total and Count before the loop; 1 mark first INPUT before a WHILE loop (or equivalent so −999 is not added); 1 mark correct loop condition and second INPUT inside the loop; 1 mark add to total and count inside the loop; 1 mark IF Count = 0 then 'No data' else output Total / Count.

stem: A courier company in Lahore gives each parcel a tracking code.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function IsValidCode(Code : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN. A valid code has exactly 8 characters: three upper-case letters, a hyphen, then four digits, for example "LHR-2041". The function returns TRUE if Code is valid and FALSE otherwise.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION IsValidCode(Code : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   IF LENGTH(Code) <> 8 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
      Ch ← MID(Code, Index, 1)
      IF Ch < 'A' OR Ch > 'Z' THEN
         RETURN FALSE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   IF MID(Code, 4, 1) <> '-' THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   FOR Index ← 5 TO 8
      Ch ← MID(Code, Index, 1)
      IF Ch < '0' OR Ch > '9' THEN
         RETURN FALSE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: header/ENDFUNCTION returning BOOLEAN; length check of 8; loop over characters 1 to 3; test each is 'A'–'Z' (or UCASE/ASC range); check character 4 is '-'; loop over characters 5 to 8 testing '0'–'9' (or IS_NUM); RETURN TRUE only after all tests pass and FALSE otherwise. Accept a flag variable instead of early returns.

stem: A water-quality sensor at a treatment plant in Johannesburg logs pH readings to a text file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function CopyHigh(Limit : REAL) RETURNS INTEGER. The function reads every line of the text file "Readings.txt". Each line holds one reading as a string. Every reading greater than Limit is written to a new text file "High.txt". The function returns the number of readings written.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION CopyHigh(Limit : REAL) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   DECLARE Count : INTEGER
   Count ← 0
   OPENFILE "Readings.txt" FOR READ
   OPENFILE "High.txt" FOR WRITE
   WHILE NOT EOF("Readings.txt")
      READFILE "Readings.txt", Line
      IF STR_TO_NUM(Line) > Limit THEN
         WRITEFILE "High.txt", Line
         Count ← Count + 1
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Readings.txt"
   CLOSEFILE "High.txt"
   RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: open Readings.txt FOR READ; open High.txt FOR WRITE; loop WHILE NOT EOF("Readings.txt"); READFILE each line into a variable; convert with STR_TO_NUM and compare with the parameter Limit; WRITEFILE and increment counter (initialised to 0); close both files and RETURN Count. Do not credit INPUT of Limit.

stem: An electricity company charges for each month: the first 100 units at Rs 10 per unit, the next 200 units (units 101 to 300) at Rs 15 per unit, and every unit above 300 at Rs 22 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function BillAmount(Units : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER that returns the bill in rupees.

FUNCTION BillAmount(Units : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Cost : INTEGER
   IF Units <= 100 THEN
      Cost ← Units * 10
   ELSE
      IF Units <= 300 THEN
         Cost ← 1000 + (Units - 100) * 15
      ELSE
         Cost ← 1000 + 3000 + (Units - 300) * 22
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
   RETURN Cost
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark header/end with RETURN; 1 mark first band Units × 10; 1 mark correct boundary tests (≤ 100, ≤ 300); 1 mark second band 1000 + (Units − 100) × 15; 1 mark third band 4000 + (Units − 300) × 22; 1 mark nested IF / CASE structure correct.

stem: An auditorium in Kuala Lumpur has 10 rows of 20 seats. The global 2D array Booked[1:10, 1:20] OF BOOLEAN stores TRUE if a seat is booked and FALSE if it is free.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for a procedure BestRow() that outputs the number of the row with the most free seats and how many free seats it has. If several rows have the same number, output the lowest row number.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE BestRow()
   DECLARE Row, Seat, Free, BestRowNo, BestFree : INTEGER
   BestFree ← -1
   BestRowNo ← 0
   FOR Row ← 1 TO 10
      Free ← 0
      FOR Seat ← 1 TO 20
         IF Booked[Row, Seat] = FALSE THEN
            Free ← Free + 1
         ENDIF
      NEXT Seat
      IF Free > BestFree THEN
         BestFree ← Free
         BestRowNo ← Row
      ENDIF
   NEXT Row
   OUTPUT "Row ", BestRowNo, " has ", BestFree, " free seats"
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: outer loop 1 to 10 for rows; reset count of free seats for each row; inner loop 1 to 20 for seats; test Booked[Row, Seat] = FALSE and increment; compare with best so far using > (lowest row kept); store best row and count; output after both loops.

stem: A text-analysis tool for a newspaper in Dhaka counts words typed by reporters.

parts.label: a

parts.answer:
FUNCTION CountWords(Sentence : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Index, Count : INTEGER
   DECLARE InWord : BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Count ← 0
   InWord ← FALSE
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Sentence)
      Ch ← MID(Sentence, Index, 1)
      IF Ch = ' ' THEN
         InWord ← FALSE
      ELSE
         IF InWord = FALSE THEN
            Count ← Count + 1
            InWord ← TRUE
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: initialise count and flag; loop through every character; extract with MID; space sets 'not in word'; non-space after space (start of a word) increments count; RETURN Count. Accept counting positions where a non-space follows a space or is at position 1.

stem: A security club at a school in Rawalpindi is learning about simple ciphers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function Encrypt(Message : STRING, Shift : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING. Each upper-case letter is replaced by the letter Shift places later in the alphabet, wrapping from Z back to A. Shift is from 1 to 25. All other characters are copied unchanged.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Encrypt(Message : STRING, Shift : INTEGER) RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE Result : STRING
   DECLARE Index, Code : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Result ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Message)
      Ch ← MID(Message, Index, 1)
      IF Ch >= 'A' AND Ch <= 'Z' THEN
         Code ← ASC(Ch) - ASC('A')
         Code ← MOD(Code + Shift, 26)
         Ch ← CHR(Code + ASC('A'))
      ENDIF
      Result ← Result & Ch
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Result
ENDFUNCTION

For example, if Size is 7 and the elements are 3, 3, 5, 8, 8, 8, 9, then afterwards the first four elements are 3, 5, 8, 9 and 4 is returned.

FUNCTION RemoveDuplicates(Size : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE ReadPos, WritePos : INTEGER
   IF Size = 0 THEN
      RETURN 0
   ENDIF
   WritePos ← 1
   FOR ReadPos ← 2 TO Size
      IF Codes[ReadPos] <> Codes[WritePos] THEN
         WritePos ← WritePos + 1
         Codes[WritePos] ← Codes[ReadPos]
      ENDIF
   NEXT ReadPos
   RETURN WritePos
ENDFUNCTION

stem: A teacher in Mombasa keeps test scores in a text file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure AboveAverage(). The text file "Scores.txt" has one line per student in the form StudentID,Score, for example "S0412,67". Score is an integer from 0 to 100 and StudentID is always 5 characters. The procedure must calculate the average score, then write the StudentID of every student whose score is above the average to the file "Above.txt", and finally output the average. Assume the file contains at least one line.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE AboveAverage()
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   DECLARE Total, Count, Score : INTEGER
   DECLARE Average : REAL
   Total ← 0
   Count ← 0
   OPENFILE "Scores.txt" FOR READ
   WHILE NOT EOF("Scores.txt")
      READFILE "Scores.txt", Line
      Score ← STR_TO_NUM(MID(Line, 7, LENGTH(Line) - 6))
      Total ← Total + Score
      Count ← Count + 1
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Scores.txt"
   Average ← Total / Count
   OPENFILE "Scores.txt" FOR READ
   OPENFILE "Above.txt" FOR WRITE
   WHILE NOT EOF("Scores.txt")
      READFILE "Scores.txt", Line
      Score ← STR_TO_NUM(MID(Line, 7, LENGTH(Line) - 6))
      IF Score > Average THEN
         WRITEFILE "Above.txt", LEFT(Line, 5)
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Scores.txt"
   CLOSEFILE "Above.txt"
   OUTPUT "Average score: ", Average
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: Level-style marking, 1 mark each to max 8: open Scores.txt for READ; loop until EOF; READFILE each line; extract the score after the comma (MID/RIGHT and STR_TO_NUM); total and count, then average calculated after the first pass; close and reopen the file (second pass) or store the data in arrays; open Above.txt for WRITE and write LEFT(Line, 5) when Score > Average; close all files and output the average.

parts.answer:
FUNCTION IsPalindrome(Phrase : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Clean : STRING
   DECLARE Index, LeftPos, RightPos : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Clean ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Phrase)
      Ch ← MID(Phrase, Index, 1)
      IF Ch <> ' ' THEN
         Clean ← Clean & LCASE(Ch)
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   LeftPos ← 1
   RightPos ← LENGTH(Clean)
   WHILE LeftPos < RightPos
      IF MID(Clean, LeftPos, 1) <> MID(Clean, RightPos, 1) THEN
         RETURN FALSE
      ENDIF
      LeftPos ← LeftPos + 1
      RightPos ← RightPos - 1
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: build a string without spaces; convert to one case; set pointers to both ends (or build reversed string); compare matching characters; move pointers inwards / loop to the middle; RETURN FALSE on a mismatch and TRUE otherwise.

Do not use a built-in conversion function. Then write a main program that calls the function with 45, 0, 255 and 130 and outputs each result. Give the outputs of your test run. (Python shown; Java or VB.NET solutions are equally acceptable.)

def DenaryToBinary(Number):
    # Number is a non-negative integer
    if Number == 0:
        return "0"
    Result = ""
    while Number > 0:
        Remainder = Number % 2
        Result = str(Remainder) + Result
        Number = Number // 2
    return Result

parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure SortScores() which uses an efficient bubble sort to put the global array Scores[1:100] OF INTEGER into descending order (highest first). The sort must stop as soon as a complete pass makes no swaps.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE SortScores()
   DECLARE Index, Temp, Last : INTEGER
   DECLARE Swapped : BOOLEAN
   Last ← 99
   REPEAT
      Swapped ← FALSE
      FOR Index ← 1 TO Last
         IF Scores[Index] < Scores[Index + 1] THEN
            Temp ← Scores[Index]
            Scores[Index] ← Scores[Index + 1]
            Scores[Index + 1] ← Temp
            Swapped ← TRUE
         ENDIF
      NEXT Index
      Last ← Last - 1
   UNTIL Swapped = FALSE OR Last = 0
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: outer conditional loop; flag reset to FALSE at the start of each pass; inner loop 1 to 99 (or reducing upper bound); compare adjacent elements with < for descending order; swap using a temporary variable; set flag TRUE when a swap happens; outer loop ends when no swaps (reducing the bound is credit-worthy but not required).

parts.text: A field researcher works in remote areas of Gilgit-Baltistan with an internet connection only once a week, using a single laptop. Suggest which protocol is more suitable and justify your choice.
parts.answer: POP3 – all messages are downloaded when connected and can then be read offline for the rest of the week on the single laptop; synchronisation across devices is not needed.
parts.working: 1 mark POP3; 1 mark justification linked to offline reading / one device.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the transport layer when a large file is sent across the internet using TCP.
parts.answer: Splits the data into segments (packets); adds a header with source/destination port numbers so data reaches the correct application; adds sequence numbers so the receiver can reassemble segments in order; receiver sends acknowledgements and missing segments are retransmitted, giving reliable delivery; also controls flow (rate of sending).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: segmentation; port numbers; sequence numbers / reassembly; acknowledgements; retransmission of lost segments; flow control; establishes the connection (handshake).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of the internet layer.
parts.answer: Adds the IP header containing source and destination IP addresses, and routes each packet across networks (via routers) towards the destination.
parts.working: 1 mark IP addressing (source and destination IP in header); 1 mark routing packets between networks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the link layer.
parts.answer: Places the data on the physical medium: puts packets into frames with MAC (hardware) addresses for the next device on the local network, and transmits them as signals over the cable or wireless link.
parts.working: 1 mark framing / MAC addresses of next hop on the local network; 1 mark physical transmission of bits over the medium; accept error detection on the link.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of using a layered protocol suite such as TCP/IP.
parts.answer: Each layer has a separate job, so a layer's protocol can be changed or improved (e.g. replacing wired Ethernet with Wi-Fi at the link layer) without changing the other layers. Different manufacturers can develop hardware/software for one layer independently, and products still work together because the interfaces between layers are standard. Complex communication is broken into simpler parts that are easier to design and debug.
parts.working: 2 marks per benefit (identify + explain), any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A user in Islamabad types the address of a news website into a browser. Describe how the TCP/IP layers on the user's computer prepare the request for transmission.
parts.answer: Application layer: the browser creates an HTTP GET request for the page. Transport layer: TCP opens a connection, splits the request into segments and adds a header with port numbers (e.g. destination port for HTTP) and sequence numbers. Internet layer: each segment is put in an IP packet with source and destination IP addresses. Link layer: each packet is put in a frame with MAC addresses and transmitted over the Wi-Fi/Ethernet link to the router.
parts.working: 1 mark HTTP request at application layer; 1 mark TCP segments with sequence numbers; 1 mark port numbers; 1 mark IP header with addresses; 1 mark link layer framing and transmission. Max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to these headers at the web server.
parts.answer: Each layer removes (strips) its own header and passes the data up to the layer above until the HTTP request reaches the web-server application.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the process of encapsulation in the TCP/IP suite, and explain why it means a router does not need to process the application data.
parts.answer: Data from the application layer is passed down; each layer treats what it receives as its payload and adds its own header (TCP header, then IP header, then link-layer header and trailer). At the receiver, each layer removes its header and passes the payload up. A router works only up to the internet layer: it removes the link-layer frame, reads the IP header to choose the next hop, and re-frames the packet; it never opens the TCP segment or the application data inside, so it does not need to understand HTTP, SMTP etc.
parts.working: 1 mark data passed down the layers; 1 mark each layer adds a header (and trailer at link layer) to the data from the layer above; 1 mark headers removed in reverse order at the receiver; 1 mark router only uses link and internet layers / reads IP header; 1 mark payload above IP left unchanged/unread.

stem: A photographer in Nairobi uploads large image files to a print company's server.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of FTP.
parts.answer: To transfer files between a client and a server over a network.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of FTP.
parts.answer: Client can log in with a username and password (or anonymously); supports commands to list, upload, download, rename and delete files on the server; uses separate control and data connections; can transfer in text or binary mode.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why FTP should not be used to upload confidential files without additional security.
parts.answer: Standard FTP sends data, usernames and passwords as plain text, so they could be intercepted and read.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A university in Ghana distributes a large open-source operating-system image using BitTorrent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define each of these BitTorrent terms: (i) swarm (ii) seed (iii) tracker (iv) leech.
parts.answer: (i) Swarm: all the peers connected and sharing the same torrent/file. (ii) Seed: a peer that has the complete file and uploads pieces to others. (iii) Tracker: a server that keeps a list of the peers in the swarm and tells a new peer which peers to connect to. (iv) Leech: a peer that downloads much more than it uploads (has a poor share ratio), harming the swarm.
parts.working: 1 mark each. For leech also accept: a peer that is still downloading and does not yet have the complete file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why BitTorrent is described as a peer-to-peer protocol.
parts.answer: Each computer (peer) downloads pieces of the file from other peers and also uploads pieces it has to others; there is no single central server sending the whole file.
parts.working: 1 mark peers both download and upload / act as client and server; 1 mark no central server supplies the file.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An indie game studio in Lagos releases a free game update through BitTorrent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a new user downloads the file using BitTorrent.
parts.answer: The user obtains the torrent file (metadata including the tracker address and the hashes of each piece) and opens it in a BitTorrent client. The client contacts the tracker, which returns a list of peers in the swarm. The client connects to several peers and requests different pieces simultaneously. Each piece is checked against its hash and re-requested if corrupt. As soon as it has pieces, the client uploads them to other peers. When all pieces are received the file is reassembled, and the user may stay as a seed.
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 5: torrent file with metadata; contacts tracker; receives list of peers; downloads different pieces from several peers in parallel; pieces verified with hash; uploads pieces it has to others; reassembly / becomes a seed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 1.5 GiB video of a science lecture series is shared by BitTorrent with a piece size of 512 KiB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of pieces the file is split into.
parts.answer: 3072 pieces

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a client requests the rarest pieces in the swarm first.
parts.answer: If a rare piece is held by only one or two peers who then leave, nobody can complete the file; downloading and re-sharing rare pieces first spreads them so the swarm keeps every piece available.
parts.working: 1 mark rare pieces could be lost if their holders leave; 1 mark spreading them keeps the whole file available / speeds up overall distribution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why BitTorrent can deliver this file to 10 000 users faster than a single web server using HTTP.
parts.answer: With HTTP every user downloads from one server whose upload bandwidth is shared by all users; with BitTorrent every peer also uploads, so total upload capacity grows as more users join.
parts.working: 1 mark single server bandwidth is a bottleneck; 1 mark peers contribute upload bandwidth / load spread across many computers.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 6000-byte message is sent using TCP/IP. Each segment can carry at most 1460 bytes of message data, and each segment has 40 bytes of TCP and IP headers in total. Ignore link-layer headers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of segments needed to send the message.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of bytes transmitted, including headers.
parts.answer: 6200 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of transmitted bytes that are message data. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the last segment is less efficient than the others.
parts.answer: It carries only 160 bytes of data but still needs the full 40-byte header.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable protocol for each situation: (i) a browser requesting a web page; (ii) retrieving emails so they are kept on the server for access from several devices; (iii) downloading pieces of a large file from many other users at once; (iv) moving a backup file to a remote server using a dedicated file-transfer client.
parts.answer: (i) HTTP (ii) IMAP (iii) BitTorrent (iv) FTP
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A college in Jeddah runs an online examination portal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the transport layer makes sure that data arriving at the server is passed to the correct application.
parts.answer: Each segment's header holds a destination port number that identifies the application/service (e.g. web server or mail server); the receiving computer uses the port number to pass the data to that application.
parts.working: 1 mark port numbers in transport-layer header; 1 mark port identifies the application/process on the host.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how TCP makes sure all the data of an online exam submission arrives correctly, even if some packets are lost or arrive out of order.
parts.answer: Each segment has a sequence number; the receiver uses these to put segments back in the right order. The receiver sends acknowledgements for segments received. If the sender gets no acknowledgement before a timeout, it retransmits the segment. A checksum detects corrupted segments, which are discarded and resent.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sequence numbers; reordering at receiver; acknowledgements; timeout and retransmission; checksum for errors. Max 4.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bilal, whose email provider is based in Islamabad, sends an email to Fatima, whose email address is with a company based in London.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the email travels from Bilal's computer to Fatima's phone. Refer to the protocols used and to the role of DNS.
parts.answer: Bilal's mail client uses SMTP to send the email to his mail server (the Islamabad provider). The sending server uses DNS to look up the mail (MX) record for Fatima's domain and find the IP address of her mail server. It then uses SMTP to transfer the email to Fatima's mail server, where it is stored in her mailbox. Fatima's phone uses IMAP (or POP3) to retrieve the email from her mail server. Underneath, TCP and IP carry the data, split into packets routed across the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark each to max 6: SMTP client to sender's server; DNS lookup of recipient's domain (mail server record); server-to-server transfer with SMTP; stored on recipient's server/mailbox; retrieval by IMAP/POP3; reference to TCP/IP packets across the internet.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A tourism website promotes Hunza Valley.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens, in terms of HTTP, when a user clicks a link to a page on a web server.
parts.answer: The browser (client) sends an HTTP request (GET) with the address/resource of the page to the web server; the server processes the request and sends back an HTTP response containing a status code (e.g. 200 OK or 404 Not Found) and the HTML of the page; the browser renders the page and makes further requests for images, style sheets, etc.
parts.working: 1 mark HTTP request (GET) from client to server; 1 mark response with status code; 1 mark page content (HTML) returned and rendered / further requests.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the TCP/IP layer at which HTTP operates and the transport-layer protocol it normally uses.
parts.answer: Application layer; TCP.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the layer of the TCP/IP suite that is responsible for each task: (i) deciding the route a packet takes between networks; (ii) providing the email or web service that the user interacts with; (iii) converting frames into signals sent over the cable; (iv) numbering segments so they can be reassembled.
parts.answer: (i) Internet (ii) Application (iii) Link (iv) Transport
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A gaming company in Riyadh must deliver a 4 GiB update to 200 000 players on the same day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The company is deciding whether to distribute the 4 GiB update with HTTP from its own servers or with BitTorrent. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of BitTorrent for this company.
parts.answer: Advantages: the load is shared between peers, so the company needs far less server bandwidth and cost; download speed can increase as more users join; no single point of failure. Disadvantages: needs enough seeds – early in the release, or for unpopular files, downloads may be slow; users' upload bandwidth and data allowances are used, which customers may dislike; some networks block BitTorrent traffic; the company has less control/monitoring of who downloads; peers' IP addresses are visible to the swarm (privacy).
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per valid point, max 6, at least one advantage and one disadvantage, related to the scenario.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A packet travels from a laptop in Multan to a server in Frankfurt through 12 routers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two items found in an IP packet header and explain why each is needed.
parts.answer: Source IP address – so a reply/error message can be returned to the sender. Destination IP address – so routers can forward the packet towards the correct host. Time to live (hop limit) – so a packet that cannot be delivered is discarded instead of circulating forever. Header checksum – to detect errors in the header. Protocol field – identifies the transport protocol (e.g. TCP) to pass the data to.
parts.working: 2 marks per item (name + reason), any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the destination IP address stays the same for the whole journey but the link-layer (MAC) address changes at every router.
parts.answer: The IP address identifies the final destination host, so it is not changed; the MAC address is only used on each local link, so each router re-frames the packet with the MAC address of the next device (next hop).
parts.working: 1 mark IP is end-to-end/final destination; 1 mark MAC addresses are local to each link, replaced at each hop.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe circuit switching.
parts.answer: A dedicated communication path (circuit) is set up between the two ends before any data is sent; it is reserved for the whole communication and released at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark dedicated path set up before transmission; 1 mark reserved for the whole session and all data follows the same route.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe packet switching.
parts.answer: The data is split into packets, each with a header containing the destination address and sequence number. Packets are sent independently and may take different routes, decided by routers. They are reassembled in order at the destination.
parts.working: 1 mark split into packets with headers; 1 mark each packet routed independently / may take different routes; 1 mark reassembled using sequence numbers.

stem: A telephone company in Peshawar compares switching methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of circuit switching for a live telephone call.
parts.answer: Data arrives in order along a dedicated route; constant bandwidth and very little delay/jitter, so speech is not broken up; no reassembly needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of circuit switching.
parts.answer: The circuit's bandwidth is wasted when no data is being sent (e.g. silences); the circuit must be set up first, which takes time; if a link fails the connection is lost; no other user can use the reserved channel.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of a router in a packet-switched network.
parts.answer: A router receives a packet, reads the destination IP address in its header, looks it up in its routing table and forwards the packet to the next router (next hop) on the best available route; it can choose another route if a link is busy or has failed.
parts.working: 1 mark reads destination address; 1 mark uses routing table; 1 mark forwards to next hop / chooses route depending on traffic or failures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why packets from the same message may arrive out of order, and how the receiver deals with this.
parts.answer: Routers choose routes for each packet independently, so packets can take different paths with different lengths and congestion; the receiver uses the sequence numbers to reassemble them in the correct order, and asks for any missing packet to be resent.
parts.working: 1 mark different routes; 1 mark different delays/congestion; 1 mark reorder using sequence numbers (request missing packets).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each use, state whether circuit switching or packet switching is more suitable and justify your choice: (i) downloading a 200 MB software update; (ii) a traditional landline call between Karachi and Quetta.
parts.answer: (i) Packet switching – no need for a dedicated line; the network bandwidth is shared efficiently; lost or delayed packets can be resent and data reassembled; delay does not matter for a download. (ii) Circuit switching – a dedicated channel gives constant bandwidth and no delay or jitter, which real-time speech needs.
parts.working: 1 mark each choice; 1 mark each justification.

stem: A hospital in Peshawar sends a 2 000 000-byte scan to a specialist using a packet-switched network. Each packet carries at most 1480 bytes of data and a 20-byte header.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum number of packets needed to send the file.
parts.answer: 1352 packets

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of bytes sent, including headers.
parts.answer: 2 027 040 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: One router on the route fails during the transfer. Explain why the transfer can still complete with packet switching but a circuit-switched transfer would fail.
parts.answer: Routers send the remaining packets by another route and missing packets are retransmitted; in circuit switching the single dedicated path is broken and the circuit must be set up again.
parts.working: 1 mark rerouting of packets around the failure; 1 mark circuit uses one fixed path which is lost.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the time-to-live (TTL) field when the packet arrives at the destination, if it started at 64 and passed through 9 routers, each of which reduces the TTL by 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the TTL field in a packet-switched network.
parts.answer: It limits the number of hops a packet can make; when it reaches 0 the router discards the packet, so packets caught in a routing loop or that cannot be delivered do not circulate forever and waste bandwidth.
parts.working: 1 mark decremented at each router and discarded at 0; 1 mark stops packets circulating indefinitely / congestion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Another packet starts with TTL 8 and the route to its destination has 11 routers. State what happens to it.
parts.answer: It is discarded by the 8th router (TTL reaches 0) and never arrives; the sender may be notified with an error message.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three items of data that are found in the header of each packet in a packet-switched network.
parts.answer: Any three: source IP address; destination IP address; sequence number / packet number; total number of packets; packet length; time to live (hop count); protocol; checksum.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why packet switching uses network capacity more efficiently than circuit switching.
parts.answer: Links are shared – packets from many users are interleaved on the same links and no bandwidth is reserved while a user is silent or idle, so capacity is used whenever there is data to send.
parts.working: 1 mark links shared by many communications; 1 mark no capacity reserved/wasted during gaps.

stem: A circuit-switched call reserves a 64 kbps channel for its whole length of 10 minutes. The callers are speaking for only 40 % of the time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of data capacity, in megabytes, that is reserved for the call. 1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes.
parts.answer: 4.8 MB

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of reserved capacity, in megabytes, that is wasted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a packet-switched voice-over-IP call would avoid this waste, and describe one problem packet switching can cause for voice calls.
parts.answer: During silences VoIP sends few or no packets, so the shared links carry other users' packets instead. Problem: packets can be delayed by different amounts (jitter) or lost, causing gaps, echoes or out-of-sync speech; buffering adds delay.
parts.working: 1 mark no packets/bandwidth used in silence; 1 mark capacity shared with others; 1 mark problem: latency/jitter/lost packets with effect on speech.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A video-conference between doctors in Karachi and Kuala Lumpur uses the internet. Explain why packet switching on the internet can cause problems for real-time video, and describe one way the problem is reduced.
parts.answer: Packets take different routes and meet different congestion, so they arrive with variable delay (jitter), out of order, or are lost; real-time video cannot wait for retransmission, so the picture freezes or breaks up. Reduced by buffering packets at the receiver before playing, by giving video packets priority (quality of service), or by lowering resolution/compression when bandwidth drops.
parts.working: 1 mark variable delay/jitter; 1 mark lost or out-of-order packets; 1 mark effect on real-time video; 1 mark a valid method of reducing it.

stem: A farm in Punjab is choosing how its soil sensors will report to a central computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the three stages of a communication that uses circuit switching.
parts.answer: 1 Circuit establishment: a dedicated path through the switches/exchanges is set up between sender and receiver. 2 Data transfer: all data is sent along this path, in order, using the reserved bandwidth. 3 Circuit disconnection: when the communication ends the path is released so its links can be used by others.
parts.working: 1 mark each stage described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the set-up stage makes circuit switching unsuitable for sending many short messages, such as sensor readings every few seconds.
parts.answer: Setting up (and releasing) a circuit takes time and resources each time, which is large compared with the tiny amount of data sent.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a graph as used in artificial intelligence.
parts.answer: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) joined by edges (arcs). Edges can be directed (one way) or undirected, and can be weighted with a value such as distance, time or cost.
parts.working: 1 mark nodes/vertices representing objects or states; 1 mark edges/arcs representing connections/relationships; 1 mark edges may be weighted and/or directed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a graph can be used by a delivery robot in a hospital to plan its route.
parts.answer: Each room or corridor junction is a node, and each corridor is an edge weighted with its length or travel time; a shortest-path algorithm such as Dijkstra or A* searches the graph to find the fastest route between two rooms.
parts.working: 1 mark mapping locations to nodes and corridors to weighted edges; 1 mark algorithm finds the shortest/lowest-cost path.

The five-building network from the adjacency matrix below is used to test a shortest-path program. Rows/columns are K, L, M, N, O:

M: 2 3 0 9 8

O: 0 0 8 2 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a program that stores the graph in a 2D list Graph (0 = no edge), a function Dijkstra(Start) that returns a list of shortest distances and a list of previous nodes, and a function Route(Previous, Target) that returns the route as a string such as "K-M-L". The main program must output, for every node, its name, its shortest distance from K and its route. Give the test output. (Python shown; Java or VB.NET solutions are equally acceptable.)
parts.answer:
INF = 9999
Names = ["K", "L", "M", "N", "O"]
Graph = [[0, 6, 2, 0, 0],
         [6, 0, 3, 4, 0],
         [2, 3, 0, 9, 8],
         [0, 4, 9, 0, 2],
         [0, 0, 8, 2, 0]]

def Dijkstra(Start):
    Count = len(Graph)
    Distance = [INF] * Count
    Previous = [-1] * Count
    Visited = [False] * Count
    Distance[Start] = 0
    for Step in range(Count):
        Current = -1
        for Node in range(Count):
            if not Visited[Node] and (Current == -1 or Distance[Node] < Distance[Current]):
                Current = Node
        if Distance[Current] == INF:
            break
        Visited[Current] = True
        for Node in range(Count):
            Weight = Graph[Current][Node]
            if Weight > 0 and not Visited[Node]:
                if Distance[Current] + Weight < Distance[Node]:
                    Distance[Node] = Distance[Current] + Weight
                    Previous[Node] = Current
    return Distance, Previous

def Route(Previous, Target):
    Path = Names[Target]
    while Previous[Target] != -1:
        Target = Previous[Target]
        Path = Names[Target] + "-" + Path
    return Path

Distance, Previous = Dijkstra(0)
for Node in range(len(Names)):
    print(Names[Node], Distance[Node], Route(Previous, Node))

Test output:
K 0 K
L 5 K-M-L
M 2 K-M
N 9 K-M-L-N
O 10 K-M-O
parts.working: Graph stored as 2D list (1); distance list initialised to a large value and start set to 0 (1); previous and visited lists (1); outer loop runs once per node (1); select the unvisited node with the smallest distance (2); mark it visited (1); relax each neighbour with weight > 0, updating distance and previous (2); Route builds the path back from target using previous (1); main loop outputs every node (1); evidence of correct output (1).

parts.answer: A photograph has continuous tones and fine detail with no clear geometric shapes, so it cannot be described efficiently by a drawing list; a vector version would be huge or would lose the realistic detail.
parts.working: B1 photographs have many colour variations / not made of simple shapes. B1 vector would not represent the detail realistically / drawing list would be very large.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A news website shows thumbnail images on a widescreen layout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The width must be a multiple of 16 pixels and the height a multiple of 9 pixels, in the ratio 16 : 9 (width = 16k, height = 9k for a whole number k). The pixel data must not exceed 2 MiB and the colour depth is 24 bits. Calculate the largest resolution that can be used. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 size in bytes = 16k × 9k × 3 = 432k². M1 limit 2 × 1 048 576 = 2 097 152 bytes, so k² ≤ 4854.5. M1 k = 69 (k = 70 gives 2 116 800 bytes, too big). A1 1104 × 621.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many bytes of the 2 MiB limit are left unused at this resolution.
parts.answer: 40 400 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one other way, apart from reducing resolution, to fit a larger image inside the limit, and state a drawback.
parts.answer: Reduce the colour depth (e.g. to 16 bits) – drawback: fewer colours so possible banding. (Or compress the image – lossy compression loses some detail.)
parts.working: B1 valid method (reduce colour depth / compress). B1 matching drawback.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.answer: D6

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of bytes in 1 kibibyte (KiB) and in 1 kilobyte (kB).
parts.answer: 1 KiB = 1024 bytes; 1 kB = 1000 bytes

parts.label: b
