parts.answer: 5120 KiB

parts.label: c
parts.text: Put these units in order of size, smallest first: MiB, kB, GB, KiB, MB.
parts.answer: kB, KiB, MB, MiB, GB
parts.working: 2 marks for fully correct order; 1 mark if only one adjacent pair is swapped. kB (1000) < KiB (1024) < MB (10⁶) < MiB (1 048 576) < GB (10⁹).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A digital clock at a railway station shows the time 19:47. Each digit is stored in 4-bit Binary Coded Decimal (BCD). Write the 16 bits that store 1947.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four groups correct; 1 mark for three correct. 1 = 0001, 9 = 1001, 4 = 0100, 7 = 0111.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A display receives the BCD pattern 0101 1000 0011. State the denary number shown.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why BCD is used for the clock display rather than pure binary.
parts.answer: Each digit can be sent directly to its own display segment / no conversion from binary to separate digits is needed.
parts.working: B1 each 4-bit group maps to one displayed digit, so conversion is simple.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A web page sets a colour using the hexadecimal code #2E8B57, where the first two hex digits are the red value, the next two are green and the last two are blue. State the denary value of each component.
parts.answer: Red 46, green 139, blue 87

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of bits used to store one such colour code, and the number of different colours that can be represented.
parts.answer: 24 bits; 16 777 216 colours (2²⁴)
parts.working: B1 24 bits (6 hex digits × 4). B1 2²⁴ = 16 777 216.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why hexadecimal is used for colour codes instead of binary.
parts.answer: It is shorter and easier for people to read and write, with fewer errors, and converts directly to binary.
parts.working: B1 shorter / easier to read and remember / fewer copying errors.

stem: A student in Faisalabad uploads a 750 MiB video to a cloud drive over a connection that transfers data at a constant 40 Mbit/s (megabits per second). Ignore any extra data added by the network.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of the video file in bits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time, in seconds, to upload the file. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student must take care with the prefixes 'Mi' and 'M' in this calculation.
parts.answer: File sizes here use binary prefixes (1 MiB = 2²⁰ bytes) but transfer rates use decimal prefixes (1 Mbit = 10⁶ bits), so mixing them gives the wrong answer.
parts.working: B1 MiB is a power of 2 (1 048 576) while M in Mbit/s is a power of 10 (1 000 000).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the 12-bit binary number 1011 0110 1101 into hexadecimal.
parts.answer: B6D

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to part (a) into denary. Show your working.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the largest denary number that can be written with three hexadecimal digits, and the number of bits it needs.
parts.working: B1 FFF = 4095. B1 12 bits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Add the BCD numbers 0100 0111 and 0011 0101 using ordinary binary addition. State the 8-bit result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the result in part (a) is not a valid BCD answer.
parts.answer: The lower 4-bit group 1100 is 12 in denary, which is not a valid BCD digit (BCD digits go from 0000 to 1001).
parts.working: B1 lower nibble > 1001 / represents 12, not a single digit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A correction of 0110 is added to any 4-bit group that is greater than 1001. Apply the correction and state the final BCD result and its denary value.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why adding 0110 gives the correct answer.
parts.answer: A 4-bit group can hold 16 values but BCD uses only 10, so adding 6 skips the six unused codes and forces the carry into the next digit.
parts.working: B1 6 unused codes (1010–1111) are skipped / makes the group carry at 10 instead of 16.

stem: A wildlife photographer in the Deosai Plains stores raw images of 24 MiB each on a memory card labelled 64 GB. Ignore the space used by the file system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of complete images that can be stored on the card. Show your working.
parts.answer: 2543 images

parts.label: b
parts.text: The photographer had expected 64 × 1024 ÷ 24 ≈ 2730 images. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: The card size uses decimal GB (10⁹ bytes) but the image size uses binary MiB (2²⁰ bytes); 64 GB is only about 59.6 GiB, so fewer images fit.
parts.working: B1 card manufacturer uses GB = 10⁹ bytes. B1 the calculation treated it as 64 GiB / mixed binary and decimal prefixes.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The byte 1001 0011 is read by four different programs. State its value when it is read as: (i) an unsigned binary integer (ii) an 8-bit two's complement integer (iii) two BCD digits (iv) a hexadecimal number.
parts.answer: (i) 147 (ii) −109 (iii) 93 (iv) 93 hexadecimal (= 147 denary)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same bit pattern can have different meanings.
parts.answer: A bit pattern has no meaning on its own; the program decides how to interpret it from the data type it expects.
parts.working: B1 meaning depends on how the program/data type interprets the bits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why files are compressed before they are sent over the internet.
parts.answer: Any two of: less time to transmit; less bandwidth used; less storage needed on the server or device; lower data costs for the user.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: faster transfer; uses less bandwidth; uses less storage; cheaper data use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one lossless method of compressing a file.
parts.answer: Run-length encoding (RLE) (or dictionary-based encoding)
parts.working: B1 RLE / dictionary or Lempel-Ziv / Huffman coding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two methods of lossy compression that can be applied to a bitmap image.
parts.answer: Reduce the colour depth so each pixel uses fewer bits; reduce the resolution so there are fewer pixels; (or) group pixels of very similar colour and store them as one colour.
parts.working: For each method, 1 mark for naming it and 1 mark for how it reduces the size. Reduce colour depth – fewer bits per pixel. Reduce resolution – fewer pixels stored. Merge similar colours / blocks – fewer distinct values to store. Max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why lossless compression must be used for an executable program file.
parts.answer: Every bit of a program is an instruction or data value; if any were changed or lost, the program would not run correctly, so the original must be restored exactly.
parts.working: B1 the file must be identical after decompression. B1 a lost/changed bit would corrupt an instruction / the program would crash or behave wrongly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A school in Mardan sends a spreadsheet of exam marks to the board office. State whether lossy or lossless compression should be used and give a reason.
parts.answer: Lossless – every mark must be exactly correct; lossy compression could change or lose values.
parts.working: B1 lossless. B1 data must not be changed / all values must be exactly the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how perceptual coding is used to compress a sound file.
parts.answer: Sounds that the human ear cannot hear are removed: frequencies outside the range of human hearing are removed, and quieter sounds that are played at the same time as louder sounds (and so are masked) are removed; fewer bits are then stored.
parts.working: 1 mark each: removes sounds humans cannot hear; removes frequencies outside the hearing range; removes quiet sounds masked by louder ones; this data is lost permanently (lossy).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether perceptual coding is lossy or lossless.
parts.answer: Lossy
parts.working: B1 lossy.

stem:
A 1-bit black-and-white image of a barcode is compressed using run-length encoding (RLE). The encoding stores only the lengths of alternating runs, starting with a run of 0s. One row of 32 pixels is:
000000000000 1111 0000000000 111111
(12 zeros, then 4 ones, then 10 zeros, then 6 ones)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the run lengths for this row.
parts.working: B1 12 zeros, 4 ones, 10 zeros, 6 ones.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each run length is stored in one byte. Calculate the size of the uncompressed row and of the compressed row, in bytes.
parts.answer: Uncompressed 4 bytes; compressed 4 bytes
parts.working: M1 32 pixels × 1 bit = 32 bits = 4 bytes. A1 4 runs × 1 byte = 4 bytes (no saving).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why RLE gave no saving here even though the row has long runs, and describe a change that would make the method effective.
parts.answer: Each pixel only needs 1 bit, but each run length needs 8 bits, so a run must be longer than 8 pixels on average to save space. Storing run lengths in fewer bits (e.g. 4 bits) or using RLE on images with longer runs would save space.
parts.working: B1 a run length uses 8 bits compared with 1 bit per pixel. B1 use fewer bits per count / only effective for very long runs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A text compression program uses a version of RLE. A run of four or more identical characters is replaced by the flag character #, then the count (a single digit), then the character. All other characters are copied unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the compressed form of the string ABBBBBBCDDDDEF.
parts.answer: A#6BC#4DEF
parts.working: M1 run of six Bs written as #6B. A1 run of four Ds written as #4D; all other characters copied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each character, flag and count is stored in one byte. Calculate the number of bytes before and after compression.
parts.answer: 14 bytes before, 10 bytes after

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the method only encodes runs of four or more characters.
parts.answer: A coded run takes three bytes, so a run of three or fewer would not get smaller (it could even get larger).
parts.working: B1 encoded run costs 3 bytes so shorter runs give no saving.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the flag character # must not appear in the original text.
parts.answer: The decompression program would treat it as the start of a coded run and decode the text wrongly.
parts.working: B1 it would be mistaken for a flag / ambiguous decoding.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A song lasting 4 minutes is recorded in stereo at 44.1 kHz with a sampling resolution of 16 bits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of the uncompressed song in bits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The compressed song is streamed at 128 kbit/s (1 kbit = 1000 bits). Calculate the size of the compressed song in bits and the compression ratio, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether this compression is lossy or lossless and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Lossy – a ratio this large is achieved by removing sound data the listener is unlikely to notice (perceptual coding).
parts.working: B1 lossy with reason (data removed / perceptual coding / cannot get back original).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An 8 × 8 icon uses two colours, W (white) and K (black). The rows are:
Row 1: WWWWWWWW
Row 2: WWWKKWWW
Row 3: WWKKKKWW
Row 4: WKKKKKKW
Row 5: WKKKKKKW
Row 6: WWKKKKWW
Row 7: WWWKKWWW
Row 8: WWWWWWWW

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each row is compressed separately with RLE. A run is stored as a count byte followed by a colour byte. Calculate the total number of bytes in the compressed image.
parts.answer: 40 bytes
parts.working: M1 count runs per row: 1, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 1 = 20 runs. M1 20 × 2 bytes. A1 40 bytes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The uncompressed image uses one byte per pixel. Calculate the percentage reduction in size.
parts.working: M1 uncompressed = 64 bytes; (64 − 40) ÷ 64 × 100. A1 37.5%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Another 8 × 8 image is a chessboard pattern of alternating W and K pixels. Calculate its compressed size with the same method and explain the result.
parts.answer: 128 bytes – double the original 64 bytes, because every run has length 1 and each needs 2 bytes.
parts.working: B1 64 runs × 2 = 128 bytes. B1 no repeated pixels so every pixel needs a count as well → file gets bigger.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An image of a flag has 6 rows and 8 columns. Every row has the same pattern of colours:
R R G G B B R R
(R = red, G = green, B = blue).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The pixels are read row by row (left to right, top row first) as one continuous sequence, and RLE is applied to the whole sequence. Each run is stored as 2 bytes. Calculate the size of the compressed data.
parts.answer: 38 bytes (19 runs)
parts.working: M1 each row is R R G G B B R R; the R run at the end of one row joins the R run at the start of the next, giving R4. M1 runs: R2 G2 B2, then R4 G2 B2 five times, then a final R2 → 3 + 15 + 1 = 19 runs. A1 19 × 2 = 38 bytes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pixels are instead read column by column (top to bottom, left column first) as one continuous sequence. Calculate the size of the compressed data.
parts.answer: 8 bytes (4 runs)
parts.working: M1 columns 1–2 give 12 R, columns 3–4 give 12 G, columns 5–6 give 12 B, columns 7–8 give 12 R → 4 runs. A1 4 × 2 = 8 bytes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what this shows about the choice of scan order for RLE.
parts.answer: RLE works best when the scan order follows the direction in which colours repeat; choosing the order that gives the longest runs gives the best compression.
parts.working: B1 scan in the direction of the longest runs / pattern of the image affects the compression ratio.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each file, state whether lossy or lossless compression is most suitable and justify your choice: (i) the source code of a banking app (ii) background music for a mobile game (iii) a scanned signature used to authorise cheques.
parts.answer: (i) lossless – any change would alter the code; (ii) lossy – small loss is not noticed and a smaller file loads faster; (iii) lossless – exact detail is needed to compare signatures / prevent fraud.
parts.working: 1 mark per row with a correct choice and valid reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A user puts a folder of JPEG photographs into a ZIP file and finds the ZIP is almost the same size as the folder. Explain why.
parts.answer: JPEG files are already compressed, so they contain few repeated patterns for the lossless ZIP method to remove; little further reduction is possible.
parts.working: B1 JPEGs are already (lossy) compressed. B1 little redundancy/repetition left for ZIP to exploit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a vector graphic is usually compressed much less than a bitmap photograph of the same scene.
parts.answer: A vector graphic is already small because it stores only the objects and their properties, so there is little to gain.
parts.working: B1 vector file is already small / stores instructions not pixels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write +93 as an 8-bit two's complement integer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write −93 as an 8-bit two's complement integer. Show your method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the 8-bit two's complement integer 11100101 into denary.

parts.text: State the denary value of the 8-bit two's complement integer 01111111 and explain why it is the largest positive value.

parts.working: B1 127. B1 MSB 0 for positive and all remaining 7 bits are set.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the range of values that can be stored in 8 bits as (i) an unsigned binary integer (ii) a two's complement integer.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of values that can be stored in a 16-bit two's complement integer.
parts.working: B1 −2¹⁵ to 2¹⁵ − 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Add the 8-bit binary integers 10110101 and 01101110. Show your working, including the carries, and state the 8-bit result.
parts.answer: 10110101 + 01101110 = 1 00100011; the 8-bit result is 00100011 (with a carry out of 1)
parts.working: M1 correct column addition with carries shown. A1 00100011 with a carry out of the most significant bit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The two numbers are treated as unsigned integers. Explain why the 8-bit result is not correct.
parts.answer: 181 + 110 = 291, which is greater than 255, the largest 8-bit unsigned value; the carry (worth 256) is lost, so the register holds 35 instead of 291 (overflow).
parts.working: B1 181 + 110 = 291 > 255. B1 carry out lost / result needs 9 bits, so 8-bit result 35 is wrong (overflow).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The same two numbers are now treated as 8-bit two's complement integers. State the denary value of each number and of the 8-bit result, and explain why the result is now correct.
parts.answer: 10110101 = −75, 01101110 = +110, result 00100011 = +35; −75 + 110 = 35, so it is correct: the carry out is ignored and adding numbers of opposite signs cannot overflow.
parts.working: B1 −75, 110 and 35. B1 carry out ignored in two's complement / numbers have different signs so no overflow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write −37 and −52 as 8-bit two's complement integers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use two's complement addition to calculate −37 − 52 (that is, −37 + (−52)). Show your working, give the 8-bit result in binary and in denary, and state what happens to the carry out of the most significant bit.
parts.answer: 11011011 + 11001100 = 1 10100111; result 10100111 = −89; the carry out is discarded (there is no overflow because the result is in range and has the same sign as the inputs).
parts.working: M1 11011011 + 11001100 with carry out of the MSB. A1 10100111 = −128 + 39 = −89. B1 carry out ignored / no overflow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each addition of 8-bit two's complement integers, state whether overflow occurs. (i) 01100100 + 00110010 (ii) 11001110 + 11100010 (iii) 10011100 + 10101011
parts.answer: (i) overflow (ii) no overflow (iii) overflow

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a processor can detect overflow by looking only at the sign bits.
parts.answer: If both numbers have the same sign bit and the result has a different sign bit, overflow has occurred; adding numbers of different signs can never overflow.
parts.working: B1 two inputs with the same sign. B1 result sign differs → overflow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two's complement negative of 11010110 (that is, the 8-bit pattern for minus this number). Give the binary result and both denary values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Apply the same method to 10000000. State the result and explain why it happens.
parts.answer: The result is 10000000 again. −128 has no positive partner in 8 bits because the largest positive value is +127.
parts.working: B1 result unchanged (10000000). B1 +128 cannot be represented / range is −128 to +127.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Subtract 01110111 from 11001010, treating both as unsigned 8-bit integers. Show your working using borrows, or by adding the two's complement.
parts.working: M1 method shown (borrows, or 11001010 + 10001001 ignoring the carry out). A1 01010011. A1 check: 202 − 119 = 83.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the carry out of the most significant bit is ignored when subtraction is done by adding a two's complement.
parts.answer: The register holds only 8 bits; the carry represents 256, which is the amount added by forming the complement, so ignoring it gives the correct difference.
parts.working: B1 the carry corresponds to the 2⁸ added in the complement / result must fit in 8 bits.

stem: A freezer sensor in a vaccine store in Gilgit sends temperatures as 10-bit two's complement integers. Each integer is the temperature in quarter-degrees, so the stored integer equals the temperature in °C multiplied by 4.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sensor sends 1111011010. Calculate the temperature in °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the 10-bit code that the sensor would send for −20.75 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When the 8-bit two's complement integer X is added to 01101010, the 8-bit result is 00110011 and there is no overflow. Find X in binary and in denary. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the addition 01101010 + X and explain what happens to the carry out of the most significant bit.
parts.answer: 01101010 + 11001001 = (1)00110011; the carry out is discarded, leaving 00110011.
parts.working: B1 correct working giving 1 00110011. B1 carry out of the MSB is ignored – it does not indicate overflow when the signs differ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two 16-bit values are stored in hexadecimal as 7A3C and 1F90. Add them and give the result in hexadecimal.
parts.answer: 99CC

parts.text: The values are 16-bit two's complement integers. State the denary values of the two inputs and of the result, and explain what has gone wrong.

parts.text: Explain why the same adder circuit can be used for unsigned and two's complement addition.

parts.working: B1 bit-level addition is the same; only meaning/overflow detection differs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a sound must be sampled before it can be stored on a computer.
parts.answer: Sound is an analogue wave that changes continuously; a computer can only store discrete digital (binary) values, so the amplitude is measured at regular intervals.
parts.working: B1 sound is analogue / continuous. B1 computer stores digital/binary values, so measurements are taken at set time intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the property of the sound wave that is measured at each sample.
parts.answer: Its amplitude
parts.working: B1 amplitude (height of the wave).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the hardware component that converts the microphone signal into digital data.
parts.answer: Analogue-to-digital converter (ADC)
parts.working: B1 ADC.

stem: A messaging app in Rawalpindi records a 30-second mono voice note with a sampling rate of 8 kHz and a sampling resolution of 8 bits. Ignore any header data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of the voice note in bytes.
parts.answer: 240 000 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to KiB, giving the exact value.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of different amplitude values that can be stored with a sampling resolution of 12 bits.

parts.text: Explain how reducing the sampling resolution from 16 bits to 8 bits affects the quality of a recording.

A sound wave is sampled six times at equal intervals using a sampling resolution of 3 bits (levels 0 to 7). The measured heights of the wave are:

parts.label: a

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A telephone network samples voices at 8 kHz but music CDs are sampled at 44.1 kHz. Explain why a lower sampling rate is acceptable for telephone calls.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A heart-sound monitor in a cardiology clinic stores mono digital recordings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The amplitude must be divided into at least 1000 different levels. State the smallest sampling resolution that can be used and justify your answer.
parts.answer: 10 bits, because 2⁹ = 512 is fewer than 1000 but 2¹⁰ = 1024 is enough.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using this resolution, calculate the size in bytes of a 2-minute mono recording sampled at 16 kHz.
parts.answer: 2 400 000 bytes

author: HomiLabs

stem: An Urdu-language podcast episode lasts 45 minutes. It is recorded in stereo at 44.1 kHz with a sampling resolution of 16 bits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of the uncompressed recording in MiB, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The episode must be no larger than 100 MiB. Calculate the minimum compression ratio needed, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The producer suggests recording in mono at 22.05 kHz, keeping 16 bits, with no compression. Calculate the new size and state whether it meets the limit.
parts.answer: 113.55 MiB – still too large

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one further change that would meet the limit without compression, and state its drawback.
parts.answer: Reduce the sampling resolution to 8 bits (≈ 56.78 MiB) – drawback: more quantisation noise / lower quality.
parts.working: B1 valid change with drawback.

stem:
Sound-editing software stores mono samples as 8-bit two's complement integers (range −128 to +127). Four consecutive samples near the end of a recording are:
120, −80, 96, −64

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fade-out multiplies the four samples by 1, 0.75, 0.5 and 0.25 respectively. State the new sample values.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Instead, the original samples are all doubled to make the sound louder. Explain what happens to the first sample and describe the effect on the sound.
parts.answer: 120 × 2 = 240 cannot be stored in 8-bit two's complement (maximum 127), so it is clipped to 127; the top of the wave is flattened, causing distortion.
parts.working: B1 240 > 127 so value is limited/clipped to 127. B1 the wave shape is changed → distortion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how sound-editing software removes the first 2 seconds of a recording sampled at 22 050 Hz, and state the number of samples removed for a mono recording.
parts.answer: The first 44 100 samples are deleted from the file (and the file header updated).
parts.working: B1 delete the samples for the first 2 s. B1 2 × 22 050 = 44 100 samples.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A microphone produces a signal between −1.0 V and +1.0 V (a range of 2.0 V). The ADC divides this range into equal levels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of one quantisation step, in volts, when a 4-bit resolution is used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the largest possible quantisation error, in volts, when each sample is rounded to the nearest level, for (i) 4-bit (ii) 8-bit resolution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why increasing the sampling resolution by 1 bit halves the largest quantisation error.
parts.answer: Each extra bit doubles the number of levels over the same voltage range, so each step (and half-step) is halved.
parts.working: B1 doubles number of levels → step size halved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term character set.
parts.answer: The list of characters that a computer can represent, with the unique binary code used for each one.
parts.working: B1 all the characters recognised by the computer and their binary codes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why two computers that exchange text files must use the same character set.
parts.answer: Text is stored as binary codes; if the receiving computer uses a different set, the same codes would be shown as different characters and the text would be garbled.
parts.working: B1 each character is stored as a code. B1 different set → codes interpreted as wrong characters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ASCII code for 'a' is 97 and the codes for 'a' to 'z' are consecutive. State the denary ASCII code for 'r' and write it as an 8-bit binary number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ASCII code for 'R' is 82. Write it as an 8-bit binary number and state the place value of the only bit that is different in the codes for 'r' and 'R'.
parts.answer: 01010010; the bit with place value 32 (1 in 'r', 0 in 'R')
parts.working: B1 01010010. B1 bit worth 32 (bit 5) / codes differ by 32.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the result of 01110010 AND 11011111 and explain what this operation does to the code of any lower-case letter.
parts.answer: 01010010 ('R'); the mask clears the 32 bit, so every lower-case letter becomes the matching upper-case letter.
parts.working: B1 01010010 with explanation (clears the bit worth 32 → upper case).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of characters that can be represented in standard 7-bit ASCII and in 8-bit extended ASCII.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ASCII cannot be used to store a text written in Urdu.
parts.answer: ASCII only has codes for English letters, digits and some symbols, and has too few codes; it has no codes for Urdu letters, which need a larger character set such as Unicode.
parts.working: B1 ASCII only covers English/Latin characters. B1 no codes for Urdu script / not enough codes available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of using Unicode instead of ASCII.
parts.answer: Any two of: represents characters from almost all languages; allows symbols and emoji; one standard used worldwide so text displays the same everywhere; its first 128 codes match ASCII, so it is compatible.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using Unicode.
parts.answer: Characters may need more than one byte, so files take more storage / more bandwidth.
parts.working: B1 more bits/bytes per character → larger files.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ASCII code for the character '0' is 48. Write the four 8-bit ASCII codes used to store the text "2026".
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three. '2' = 50, '0' = 48, '6' = 54.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The number 2026 can also be stored as a 16-bit unsigned integer. Write this 16-bit value and explain why a program would store a year as an integer rather than as text.
parts.answer: 0000 0111 1110 1010; an integer uses less storage (2 bytes instead of 4) and can be used directly in arithmetic and comparisons.
parts.working: B1 0000011111101010. B1 less storage. B1 calculations possible without conversion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A message is sent as these ASCII codes, written in hexadecimal: 53 49 4E 44 48. Decode the message. (The ASCII code for 'A' is 41 in hexadecimal.)
parts.answer: SINDH
parts.working: M1 converting codes using A = 41₁₆ (S = 53, I = 49, N = 4E, D = 44, H = 48). A1 SINDH.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word KHI as ASCII codes in hexadecimal.

check: ''.join(['ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'[c - 0x41] for c in [0x53, 0x49, 0x4E, 0x44, 0x48]]) == 'SINDH' and [0x41 + 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'.index(c) for c in 'KHI'] == [0x4B, 0x48, 0x49]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function ToUpper(Ch : CHAR) RETURNS CHAR. If Ch is a lower-case letter, the function returns the matching upper-case letter; any other character is returned unchanged. Use the functions ASC() and CHR() and do not use any built-in case-conversion function.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION ToUpper(Ch : CHAR) RETURNS CHAR
   IF Ch >= 'a' AND Ch <= 'z' THEN
      RETURN CHR(ASC(Ch) - 32)
   ELSE
      RETURN Ch
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: function header and ENDFUNCTION; test for lower-case range 'a' to 'z' (or ASC 97–122); CHR(ASC(Ch) − 32); returns Ch unchanged otherwise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value returned by ToUpper('q') and by ToUpper('7').
parts.answer: 'Q' and '7'
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A program sorts words by comparing their character codes. Explain why "apple" is placed after "Zebra".
parts.answer: Strings are compared character by character using their codes; 'a' has code 97, which is greater than the code for 'Z' (90), so "apple" comes after "Zebra".
parts.working: B1 comparison uses character codes, first character first. B1 lower-case codes (97+) are greater than upper-case (65–90).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same program puts the text "10" before "9". Explain why.
parts.answer: The strings are compared character by character, not as numbers; the first character '1' (code 49) is less than '9' (code 57).
parts.working: B1 compared as text, first characters first. B1 '1' < '9' in ASCII.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the program could sort words alphabetically regardless of case.
parts.answer: Convert both strings to the same case (e.g. upper case) before comparing them.
parts.working: B1 convert to a single case before comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Urdu letter ب (beh) has the Unicode code point U+0628, written in hexadecimal. Convert this code point into denary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the 8-bit ASCII code for 'A' and the Unicode code point for 'A' have the same value.
parts.answer: The first 128 Unicode code points were made identical to ASCII so that existing ASCII text is valid Unicode.
parts.working: B1 Unicode includes ASCII as its first 128 codes / for compatibility.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the minimum number of bits needed to write the code point of ب as an unsigned binary integer.
parts.answer: 11 bits

stem: A bilingual SMS app stores text in Unicode. In UTF-8, each English (ASCII) character uses 1 byte and each Urdu character uses 2 bytes. In UTF-16, each of these characters uses 2 bytes. A message has 120 English characters and 80 Urdu characters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the storage needed for the message in (i) UTF-8 (ii) UTF-16.
parts.answer: (i) 280 bytes (ii) 400 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many more bytes ASCII would need than UTF-8 if the message contained only the 120 English characters.
parts.answer: 0 – both use 1 byte per English character (120 bytes)
parts.working: B1 none / same size.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second message contains 300 Urdu characters and no English characters. State which encoding gives the smaller file and explain why the advantage of UTF-8 depends on the language of the text.
parts.answer: Both need 600 bytes, so neither is smaller; UTF-8 saves space only for characters it can store in 1 byte (mainly English/ASCII), so its advantage disappears for scripts that need 2 or more bytes.
parts.working: B1 equal at 600 bytes. B1 UTF-8 saving comes from 1-byte ASCII characters only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function ToNumber(Digits : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER which converts a string of digit characters such as "4725" into the integer it represents. Do not use STR_TO_NUM; use ASC() and the fact that the codes for '0' to '9' are consecutive. If any character is not a digit, the function returns −1.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION ToNumber(Digits : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Value, Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   Value ← 0
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Digits)
      Ch ← MID(Digits, Index, 1)
      IF Ch < '0' OR Ch > '9' THEN
         RETURN -1
      ENDIF
      Value ← Value * 10 + ASC(Ch) - ASC('0')
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Value
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: initialise Value to 0; loop through every character (LENGTH); extract one character with MID; test for non-digit and RETURN −1; Value ← Value × 10 + (ASC(Ch) − 48); return Value after the loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Trace your function for the input "307" by giving the value of Value after each character.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The emoji 😀 has the Unicode code point U+1F600 (hexadecimal). Convert this to denary and state the minimum number of bits needed to store it as an unsigned binary integer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an encoding that always uses exactly 16 bits per character cannot represent this emoji in a single 16-bit unit.
parts.answer: 16 bits give only 65 536 values (0 to 65 535), but the code point is larger than that.
parts.working: B1 maximum 16-bit value is 65 535 < 128 512.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of different values that a 32-bit code can represent, and give one reason why fixed 32-bit character codes are rarely used for storing text.
parts.answer: 4 294 967 296; it would make every character, including plain English letters, use 4 bytes, wasting storage.
parts.working: B1 2³² = 4 294 967 296. B1 wasteful / files four times larger than ASCII for English text.

stem: A teacher in Quetta shows students a simple letter-shifting cipher that works on ASCII codes. The ASCII code of 'A' is 65 and the codes of 'A' to 'Z' are consecutive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function Shift(Ch : CHAR, N : INTEGER) RETURNS CHAR. Ch is always an upper-case letter and 0 ≤ N ≤ 25. The function moves Ch forward N places in the alphabet, wrapping round from 'Z' to 'A'. Use ASC(), CHR() and MOD.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Shift(Ch : CHAR, N : INTEGER) RETURNS CHAR
   DECLARE Pos : INTEGER
   Pos ← ASC(Ch) - ASC('A')
   Pos ← (Pos + N) MOD 26
   RETURN CHR(Pos + ASC('A'))
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: convert to position 0–25 by subtracting ASC('A') (65); add N; MOD 26 for the wrap-around; convert back with CHR(… + 65) and RETURN.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the result of applying Shift with N = 3 to each letter of QUETTA and of ZOX.
parts.answer: TXHWWD and CRA
parts.working: B1 TXHWWD. B1 CRA (Z wraps to C).

check: ''.join(['ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'[('ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'.index(c)+3) % 26] for c in 'QUETTA']) == 'TXHWWD' and ''.join(['ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'[('ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'.index(c)+3) % 26] for c in 'ZOX']) == 'CRA'

stem: A firmware team in Islamabad stores device settings in text files. Lines that begin with '#' are comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure CleanCopy(InFile : STRING, OutFile : STRING). The procedure copies every line of InFile into OutFile except lines that are empty and lines whose first character is '#'. OutFile must contain only the copied lines.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE CleanCopy(InFile : STRING, OutFile : STRING)
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   OPENFILE InFile FOR READ
   OPENFILE OutFile FOR WRITE
   WHILE NOT EOF(InFile)
      READFILE InFile, Line
      IF LENGTH(Line) > 0 THEN
         IF LEFT(Line, 1) <> '#' THEN
            WRITEFILE OutFile, Line
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE InFile
   CLOSEFILE OutFile
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: open InFile for READ and OutFile for WRITE; loop until EOF(InFile); READFILE into a variable; test for an empty line (LENGTH = 0 or = ""); test first character with LEFT(Line, 1) or MID(Line, 1, 1) – the empty test must come first or be separate so LEFT is not applied to an empty string; WRITEFILE only when both tests pass and close both files.

stem:
A shop in Gujranwala records each sale in the text file Sales.txt. Each line has an 8-character date in the form YYYYMMDD, then a comma, then the amount in rupees, for example:
20261003,1250.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function TotalForMonth(Month : STRING) RETURNS REAL. Month is six characters in the form YYYYMM, for example "202610". The function returns the total of the amounts for that month. You may assume the file exists.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION TotalForMonth(Month : STRING) RETURNS REAL
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   DECLARE Total : REAL
   Total ← 0
   OPENFILE "Sales.txt" FOR READ
   WHILE NOT EOF("Sales.txt")
      READFILE "Sales.txt", Line
      IF LEFT(Line, 6) = Month THEN
         Total ← Total + STR_TO_NUM(RIGHT(Line, LENGTH(Line) - 9))
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "Sales.txt"
   RETURN Total
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: initialise Total to 0; open file for READ and close it; loop until EOF reading each line; compare LEFT(Line, 6) with Month; extract the amount with RIGHT(Line, LENGTH(Line) − 9) or MID(Line, 10, …); convert with STR_TO_NUM, add to Total and RETURN Total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value returned by TotalForMonth("202610") if the file contains the lines 20261003,1250.5 and 20261117,800 and 20261029,349.5

stem: Two teachers at a college in Sargodha each keep a class list in a text file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure MergeFiles(). Lists A.txt and B.txt each contain student names in alphabetical order, one per line, and each file contains at least one name. The procedure writes every name from both files into All.txt so that All.txt is also in alphabetical order. You must not use arrays: read the files one line at a time.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE MergeFiles()
   DECLARE NameA, NameB : STRING
   DECLARE MoreA, MoreB : BOOLEAN
   OPENFILE "A.txt" FOR READ
   OPENFILE "B.txt" FOR READ
   OPENFILE "All.txt" FOR WRITE
   READFILE "A.txt", NameA
   READFILE "B.txt", NameB
   MoreA ← TRUE
   MoreB ← TRUE
   WHILE MoreA AND MoreB
      IF NameA < NameB THEN
         WRITEFILE "All.txt", NameA
         IF EOF("A.txt") THEN
            MoreA ← FALSE
         ELSE
            READFILE "A.txt", NameA
         ENDIF
      ELSE
         WRITEFILE "All.txt", NameB
         IF EOF("B.txt") THEN
            MoreB ← FALSE
         ELSE
            READFILE "B.txt", NameB
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   WHILE MoreA
      WRITEFILE "All.txt", NameA
      IF EOF("A.txt") THEN
         MoreA ← FALSE
      ELSE
         READFILE "A.txt", NameA
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   WHILE MoreB
      WRITEFILE "All.txt", NameB
      IF EOF("B.txt") THEN
         MoreB ← FALSE
      ELSE
         READFILE "B.txt", NameB
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   CLOSEFILE "A.txt"
   CLOSEFILE "B.txt"
   CLOSEFILE "All.txt"
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 8: open both input files for READ and All.txt for WRITE; read the first name from each file before the loop; loop while both files still have a current name; compare the two current names; write the smaller name; read the next name only from the file just used; detect the end of a file correctly so the last name is not lost or written twice; copy the remaining names from the other file; close all three files.

stem:
A linear queue at a photocopy shop in Bahawalpur is stored in the array Queue[1:6] OF INTEGER. FrontPointer starts at 1 and RearPointer starts at 0. Enqueue adds 1 to RearPointer and stores the item there. Dequeue returns Queue[FrontPointer] and adds 1 to FrontPointer. These operations are carried out in order:
Enqueue(14), Enqueue(9), Enqueue(22), Dequeue(), Enqueue(31), Enqueue(5), Dequeue(), Enqueue(17)

stem: A restaurant in Peshawar holds kitchen orders in a circular queue using the global array Orders[0:7] OF STRING, the global integers HeadPointer and TailPointer, and the global integer NumItems. TailPointer holds the index of the last item added. When the queue is empty, NumItems is 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function Enqueue(NewItem : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN. The function adds NewItem to the rear of the queue and returns TRUE, or returns FALSE if the queue is full.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Enqueue(NewItem : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   IF NumItems = 8 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   TailPointer ← TailPointer + 1
   IF TailPointer > 7 THEN
      TailPointer ← 0
   ENDIF
   Orders[TailPointer] ← NewItem
   NumItems ← NumItems + 1
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: check NumItems = 8 (full); return FALSE when full; increment TailPointer; wrap TailPointer to 0 after 7 (or use MOD 8); store NewItem at Orders[TailPointer]; increment NumItems and return TRUE.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The queue holds 3 items with HeadPointer = 6 and TailPointer = 0. State the indexes of the three items, from front to rear.

stem: A linked list of integers is stored in the global arrays Data[0:49] OF INTEGER and Pointer[0:49] OF INTEGER. The global integers StartPointer and FreePointer hold the index of the first node of the list and of the free list. The null pointer is −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function DeleteItem(Target : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN, which removes the first node whose data equals Target, adds that node to the front of the free list, and returns TRUE. If Target is not in the list, it returns FALSE.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION DeleteItem(Target : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Current, Previous : INTEGER
   Current ← StartPointer
   Previous ← -1
   WHILE Current <> -1 AND Data[Current] <> Target
      Previous ← Current
      Current ← Pointer[Current]
   ENDWHILE
   IF Current = -1 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   IF Previous = -1 THEN
      StartPointer ← Pointer[Current]
   ELSE
      Pointer[Previous] ← Pointer[Current]
   ENDIF
   Pointer[Current] ← FreePointer
   FreePointer ← Current
   RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: start at StartPointer with Previous set to null; loop while not null and data not found; move Previous and Current along; return FALSE if end reached; if first node, update StartPointer; otherwise Pointer[Previous] ← Pointer[Current]; link deleted node to old FreePointer; FreePointer ← Current and return TRUE.

PROCEDURE ReverseList()
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Temp : STRING

      Temp ← Items[Index]
      Items[Index] ← Items[Count - Index + 1]
      Items[Count - Index + 1] ← Temp

FUNCTION PeakHour() RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Day, Hour, Best : INTEGER

FUNCTION RemoveDuplicates() RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Last, Index : INTEGER
   IF Size = 0 THEN
      RETURN 0
   ENDIF
   Last ← 1
   FOR Index ← 2 TO Size

         Last ← Last + 1
         Codes[Last] ← Codes[Index]

   NEXT Index

parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure SortByTime(), which uses a bubble sort to put the records in Runners into ascending order of Time. Whole records must be swapped, not only the times.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE SortByTime()
   DECLARE Last, Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Temp : Runner
   DECLARE Swapped : BOOLEAN
   Last ← 40
   REPEAT
      Swapped ← FALSE
      FOR Index ← 1 TO Last - 1
         IF Runners[Index].Time > Runners[Index + 1].Time THEN
            Temp ← Runners[Index]
            Runners[Index] ← Runners[Index + 1]
            Runners[Index + 1] ← Temp
            Swapped ← TRUE
         ENDIF
      NEXT Index
      Last ← Last - 1
   UNTIL NOT Swapped OR Last = 1
ENDPROCEDURE

stem: A national scholarship form accepts dates of birth as strings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function IsValidDate(D : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN. D should be in the form DD/MM/YYYY. The function returns TRUE only if: D has 10 characters, the 3rd and 6th characters are '/', the month is 1 to 12, and the day is from 1 to the number of days in that month. February has 29 days in a leap year (a year divisible by 4 but not by 100, or divisible by 400). You may assume the day, month and year parts contain only digits.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION IsValidDate(D : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN
   DECLARE Day, Month, Year, MaxDay : INTEGER
   IF LENGTH(D) <> 10 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   IF MID(D, 3, 1) <> '/' OR MID(D, 6, 1) <> '/' THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   Day ← STR_TO_NUM(LEFT(D, 2))
   Month ← STR_TO_NUM(MID(D, 4, 2))
   Year ← STR_TO_NUM(RIGHT(D, 4))
   IF Month < 1 OR Month > 12 THEN
      RETURN FALSE
   ENDIF
   CASE OF Month
      4, 6, 9, 11 : MaxDay ← 30
      2 : IF (Year MOD 4 = 0 AND Year MOD 100 <> 0) OR Year MOD 400 = 0 THEN
             MaxDay ← 29
          ELSE
             MaxDay ← 28
          ENDIF
      OTHERWISE : MaxDay ← 31
   ENDCASE
   RETURN Day >= 1 AND Day <= MaxDay
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: length check; check both '/' positions with MID; extract day, month, year with LEFT/MID/RIGHT and STR_TO_NUM; month range check; 30-day months; February with correct leap-year rule; 31 days otherwise; final day range check returning a BOOLEAN.

parts.working: B1 no limit on n / any length → need recursion. B1 brackets can be nested to any depth and each ( must match a ).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert each infix expression into Reverse Polish notation (RPN). (i) (p + q) / r (ii) p − q * r + s (iii) p * (q + r * s)
parts.answer: (i) p q + r / (ii) p q r * − s + (iii) p q r s * + *
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the RPN expression 8 3 − 4 2 + * using a stack. Show the contents of the stack after each symbol is processed.
parts.working: M1 5 after −. M1 6 after + with 5 still below. A1 30.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the expression in infix form.
parts.working: B1 brackets needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the RPN expression a b − c / d e * + when a = 20, b = 8, c = 4, d = 3 and e = 5. Show the stack after each operator.
parts.working: M1 after −: 12; after /: 3. M1 after *: 3 15. A1 after +: 18.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the expression in infix form, using brackets only where needed.
parts.answer: (a − b) / c + d * e
parts.working: B1 brackets only round a − b.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why RPN does not need brackets.
parts.answer: The order of the operators in the expression gives the order of evaluation, so precedence never has to be worked out.
parts.working: B1 order of evaluation is fixed by position / no ambiguity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function EvaluateRPN(Expr : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER. Expr contains only single-digit operands and the operators + − * with no spaces, for example "34+2*". Use the procedure Push(Value : INTEGER) and the function Pop() RETURNS INTEGER of an existing stack.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION EvaluateRPN(Expr : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Index, Left, Right : INTEGER
   DECLARE Ch : CHAR
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Expr)
      Ch ← MID(Expr, Index, 1)
      IF Ch >= '0' AND Ch <= '9' THEN
         CALL Push(ASC(Ch) - ASC('0'))
      ELSE
         Right ← Pop()
         Left ← Pop()
         CASE OF Ch
            '+' : CALL Push(Left + Right)
            '-' : CALL Push(Left - Right)
            '*' : CALL Push(Left * Right)
         ENDCASE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Pop()
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: loop through each character; digit test; push the digit's numeric value; pop two operands for an operator; second value popped is the LEFT operand (correct order for −); push the result and return the final Pop().

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value returned for "34+2*" and for "92-3*".
parts.answer: 14 and 21

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each sequence, state whether it is a valid RPN expression. If valid, give its value; if not, explain what goes wrong on the stack. (i) 3 4 + * (ii) 3 4 5 + * (iii) 3 4 5 + * 2
parts.answer: (i) invalid – after + only one value is on the stack, so * cannot pop two (ii) valid, 27 (iii) invalid – two values are left on the stack at the end
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason/value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a rule, based on counting operands and operators, that every valid RPN expression with only binary operators obeys.
parts.answer: There is exactly one more operand than operators (and at every point, operands read so far exceed operators read so far).
parts.working: B1 operands = operators + 1 (accept running-count condition).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The operator ^ (power) is right-associative, so a ^ b ^ c means a ^ (b ^ c). Convert a ^ b ^ c and (a + b) ^ 2 * c into RPN.
parts.answer: a b c ^ ^ and a b + 2 ^ c *
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate a b c ^ ^ when a = 2, b = 3, c = 2, and evaluate your second RPN expression when a = 1, b = 2, c = 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student writes a b ^ c ^ for a ^ b ^ c. Evaluate the student's expression for a = 2, b = 3, c = 2 and explain the error.
parts.answer: 64; the student has treated ^ as left-associative, calculating (2³)² instead of 2^(3²).
parts.working: B1 64. B1 wrong associativity / evaluated left to right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An expression in RPN is x y + z w − * v /. Describe the binary expression tree for this expression by stating the root and the children of each operator node.
parts.answer: Root /: left child *, right child v. * has left child + and right child −. + has children x (left) and y (right). − has children z (left) and w (right).
parts.working: B1 root / with children * and v. B1 * with children + and −. B1 leaves of + and − correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the expression in infix form and in prefix (Polish) notation.
parts.answer: Infix: (x + y) * (z − w) / v; prefix: / * + x y − z w v
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the expression when x = 6, y = 4, z = 9, w = 3, v = 5, and state the maximum number of values on the stack during the RPN evaluation.
parts.answer: 12; maximum 3 values
parts.working: B1 10 × 6 ÷ 5 = 12. B1 3 (after z w pushed with 10 below).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a running process moves to the blocked state when it requests data from a disk.
parts.answer: The process cannot continue until the data arrives, which is slow; blocking it lets the processor run another (ready) process instead of waiting.
parts.working: B1 must wait for the I/O operation to finish. B1 processor given to another process / processor time not wasted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a process moves from blocked to ready, and not directly to running, when its data arrives.
parts.answer: Another process is using the processor; the unblocked process must wait in the ready queue until the scheduler chooses it.
parts.working: B1 processor is busy with another process. B1 the scheduler decides which ready process runs next.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a process control block (PCB).
parts.answer: A data structure kept by the operating system for each process, holding the information needed to manage it.
parts.working: B1 OS data structure / record holding details of one process.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three items of data stored in a PCB.
parts.answer: Any three of: process ID; process state; program counter value; register contents; priority; memory allocated / page table pointer; open files; accounting information such as CPU time used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why interrupts are given priorities.
parts.answer: Some events are more urgent than others (e.g. power failure versus a key press); priorities make sure the most urgent interrupt is handled first.
parts.working: B1 interrupts differ in urgency. B1 higher priority serviced first / can interrupt lower-priority ISRs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An interrupt service routine (ISR) for a printer is running when a higher-priority interrupt from a hardware timer arrives. Describe what happens.
parts.answer: The printer ISR is suspended: its register contents are saved (on the stack); the timer ISR is run; when it finishes, the printer ISR's registers are restored and it continues from where it stopped.
parts.working: 1 mark each: current ISR suspended / state saved; higher-priority ISR executed; original ISR restored and resumed.

stem:
Four processes arrive at the ready queue as shown.
Process | Arrival time (ms) | Burst time (ms)
P1 | 0 | 6
P2 | 1 | 3
P3 | 2 | 8
P4 | 4 | 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using first come first served (FCFS), calculate the waiting time of each process and the average waiting time.
parts.answer: P1 0, P2 5, P3 7, P4 13; average 6.25 ms
parts.working: M1 order P1 0–6, P2 6–9, P3 9–17, P4 17–19. M1 waiting = start − arrival. A1 average 25 ÷ 4 = 6.25 ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using non-pre-emptive shortest job first (SJF), give the order in which the processes run and calculate the average waiting time.
parts.answer: P1, P4, P2, P3; average 4.5 ms
parts.working: M1 P1 runs first (only process at time 0). M1 at 6 ms: P4 (2) then P2 (3) then P3 (8). A1 waits 0, 7, 9, 2 → 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5 ms.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Round robin scheduling is used with a time quantum of 3 ms. A process that arrives at the same moment as another process's time slice ends joins the ready queue first.
Process | Arrival time (ms) | Burst time (ms)
A | 0 | 5
B | 1 | 4
C | 3 | 2
D | 5 | 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the order in which the processes use the processor, with the start and end time of each time slice.
parts.working: M1 A runs first and is pre-empted at 3; C (arriving at 3) joins the queue before A. M1 D (arriving at 5) joins before B is re-queued at 6. A1 complete correct sequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the finishing time of each process and calculate the average turnaround time (finish − arrival).
parts.answer: A 10, B 14, C 8, D 13; average turnaround 9 ms
parts.working: M1 finishing times. M1 turnaround A 10, B 13, C 5, D 8. A1 36 ÷ 4 = 9 ms.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a single-core processor can appear to run several programs at the same time.
parts.answer: The scheduler gives each process a short time slice in turn and switches between them so quickly that the user sees them all progressing together.
parts.working: B1 processes take turns / time slicing. B1 switching is fast so it looks simultaneous.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens during a context switch.
parts.answer: The state of the running process (register values, program counter) is saved in its PCB, and the saved state of the next process is loaded so it continues where it stopped.
parts.working: B1 save current process's registers/PC into its PCB. B1 load the next process's saved state.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each time slice is 20 ms and each context switch takes 1 ms. Calculate the percentage of processor time spent on context switching, correct to 1 decimal place.

stem:
Four processes all arrive at time 0.
Process | Burst time (ms) | Priority
P1 | 4 | 3
P2 | 2 | 1
P3 | 6 | 4
P4 | 3 | 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Non-pre-emptive priority scheduling is used; a lower number means a higher priority. Give the order in which the processes run and calculate the average waiting time.
parts.answer: P2, P4, P1, P3; average waiting time 4 ms
parts.working: M1 order by priority. M1 waits P2 0, P4 2, P1 5, P3 9. A1 16 ÷ 4 = 4 ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by starvation in priority scheduling, and describe how ageing prevents it.
parts.answer: Starvation: a low-priority process never runs because higher-priority processes keep arriving. Ageing: the priority of a waiting process is gradually raised the longer it waits, so eventually it becomes high enough to run.
parts.working: B1 definition of starvation. B1 priority increased with waiting time. B1 so every process eventually gets the processor.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three jobs arrive at time 0 in the order J1 (burst 5 ms), J2 (burst 3 ms), J3 (burst 7 ms). Ignore context-switch time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using round robin with a quantum of 2 ms, give the finishing time of each job and calculate the average waiting time.
parts.answer: J1 12, J2 9, J3 15; average waiting time 7 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using round robin with a quantum of 10 ms, calculate the average waiting time, correct to 2 decimal places, and explain why the result is the same as FCFS.
parts.answer: 4.33 ms; every job finishes within its first time slice, so they simply run in arrival order.
parts.working: B1 (0 + 5 + 8) ÷ 3 = 4.33. B1 quantum larger than every burst → behaves like FCFS.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an operating system for a phone would still use a small quantum, even though it gives a larger average waiting time here.
parts.answer: Interactive processes need a quick response; a small quantum means every process gets the processor soon after it becomes ready, so the user interface stays responsive, although more context switches occur.
parts.working: B1 better response time for interactive tasks. B1 no long job can hold the processor; trade-off with switching overhead.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the four stages of compilation in the order in which they take place.
parts.answer: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, code generation, optimisation
parts.working: 2 marks all four in order; 1 mark all four named in the wrong order, or three in order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is output by the lexical analysis stage.
parts.answer: A string of tokens (and an updated symbol table)
parts.working: B1 tokens / token stream.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the keyword table and the symbol table used by a compiler.
parts.answer: The keyword table is fixed and holds the reserved words and operators of the language with their tokens; the symbol table is built during compilation and holds the identifiers and constants used in this program.
parts.working: B1 keyword table: predefined, reserved words/operators. B1 symbol table: created from the source program, identifiers/literals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one item stored for an identifier in the symbol table that is added after lexical analysis.
parts.answer: Its data type / its memory address / its scope
parts.working: B1 any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each error, state whether it is detected during lexical analysis, during syntax analysis, or not detected by the compiler. (i) the character £ appears in an identifier (ii) an IF statement has no ENDIF (iii) a variable is used but never declared (iv) a division by a variable that holds 0 at run time
parts.answer: (i) lexical analysis (ii) syntax analysis (iii) syntax (semantic) analysis (iv) not detected by the compiler – a run-time error
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to comments and extra spaces during lexical analysis, and explain why.
parts.answer: They are removed, because they are only for human readers and are not needed to produce the object code.
parts.working: B1 removed/ignored. B1 not needed for translation / reduces what later stages process.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A comment is removed during compilation. Explain why the programmer should still write comments.
parts.answer: Comments remain in the source code and help programmers understand and maintain it.
parts.working: B1 aid to maintenance / readability of the source code.

Identifiers and constants are added to the symbol table and given tokens in order of first appearance, starting at 80. The statement is:

stem:
A compiler is about to generate code for:
Seconds ← 3 * 60 * 60
A ← (B + C) * D
E ← (B + C) / F

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rewrite the code so that it is optimised but gives exactly the same results.
parts.answer:
Seconds ← 10800
Temp ← B + C
A ← Temp * D
E ← Temp / F
parts.working: B1 constant folding: 3 * 60 * 60 replaced by 10800. B1 common sub-expression B + C calculated once. B1 used in both statements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit of code optimisation for the user of a program and one cost for the developer.
parts.answer: Benefit: the program runs faster / uses less memory. Cost: compilation takes longer.
parts.working: B1 faster execution or less memory. B1 longer compile time / more complex compiler.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the syntax analysis stage does with the tokens for the statement Total ← Price * Qty + Tax.
parts.answer: The tokens are checked against the grammar rules (e.g. in BNF) of the language; a parse tree is built showing the structure, with Price * Qty grouped below +; any error found is reported.
parts.working: 1 mark each: checks tokens against grammar rules; builds a parse tree / structure; reports syntax errors (also semantic checks such as types).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the parse tree for the right-hand side of the statement by stating the root and its children.
parts.answer: Root +: left child is * (with children Price and Qty), right child is Tax.
parts.working: B1 + at the root. B1 * subtree on the left with Price and Qty, Tax on the right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some compilers produce intermediate code (such as bytecode) instead of machine code. Explain what is meant by intermediate code.
parts.answer: Code that is between source code and machine code; it is not specific to one processor and is run by a virtual machine or translated further.
parts.working: B1 lower-level than source but not machine code for a specific processor. B1 run by a virtual machine / interpreter or compiled later.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two benefits of producing intermediate code.
parts.answer: Any two of: the same compiled code can run on different processors (portable); source code is not shared; quicker to translate than full compilation; optimisation can be done on the intermediate code.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write assembly code for X ← (A + B) − (C − D). Use only the instructions LDD <address> (load from address into ACC), ADD <address>, SUB <address> and STO <address>, and the location TEMP if needed.
parts.answer:
LDD C
SUB D
STO TEMP
LDD A
ADD B
SUB TEMP
STO X
parts.working: 1 mark each: C − D calculated first; stored in TEMP; A + B calculated; TEMP subtracted and result stored in X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An optimising compiler uses the fact that (A + B) − (C − D) = A + B − C + D. Write the optimised code and state the number of instructions saved.
parts.answer:
LDD A
ADD B
SUB C
ADD D
STO X – 2 instructions saved (and no TEMP needed)
parts.working: B1 correct 5-instruction code. B1 2 instructions saved.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Check both versions with A = 10, B = 4, C = 7, D = 2 by stating the value stored in X.

stem:
A compiler is optimising this code. Rate is not changed anywhere in the loop.
FOR I ← 1 TO 100
   Total ← Total + Price[I] * Rate
   Tax ← Rate * 0.17
   OUTPUT I
NEXT I

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each proposed optimisation, state whether it is valid and explain why. (i) Move the statement Tax ← Rate * 0.17 to before the loop. (ii) Delete OUTPUT I, because it does not change Total. (iii) Move the statement Total ← Total + Price[I] * Rate to after the loop.
parts.answer: (i) valid – Rate does not change in the loop, so Tax gets the same value; it is calculated once instead of 100 times. (ii) invalid – the output is part of the program's behaviour; the user would no longer see the numbers. (iii) invalid – the statement depends on I and must be repeated for every element; after the loop it would add only one price.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark for valid/invalid, 1 mark for the reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the symbol table entry for the identifier Rate is created and then added to during the stages of compiling a program that contains DECLARE Rate : REAL and later Rate ← Rate * 1.05.
parts.answer: Lexical analysis: Rate is found to be an identifier not in the keyword table and is added to the symbol table with its token. Syntax analysis: the declaration is processed so its data type REAL (and scope) is recorded; later uses are checked against it, e.g. 1.05 is compatible with REAL. Code generation: a memory address is allocated for Rate and recorded, and the token is replaced by this address in the object code.
parts.working: 1 mark each: added in lexical analysis as a new identifier with a token; data type/scope added from the declaration; type checking of the assignment uses the entry; address allocated during code generation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the literal 1.05 may also be placed in the symbol table.
parts.answer: Constants need storage and a token too, so the code generator can place the value in memory and refer to it.
parts.working: B1 constants also need a token / storage location.

stem:
A program for traffic cameras on the Lahore ring road contains this statement:
IF Speed>=120THEN Fine←Fine+500

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of tokens in the statement and list them.
parts.answer: 10 tokens: IF, Speed, >=, 120, THEN, Fine, ←, Fine, +, 500
parts.working: B1 10. B1 correct list.

parts.label: b
parts.text: There is no space between 120 and THEN. Explain how the lexical analyser can still separate them.
parts.answer: It reads characters while they can be part of the current token: digits continue a number, so the token 120 ends when the letter T is met; then THEN is read as a new token and matched in the keyword table.
parts.working: B1 a token ends when a character that cannot belong to it is met. B1 120 ends at T; THEN is then recognised as a keyword.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why >= must be recognised as one token rather than as > followed by =.
parts.answer: It is a single operator (greater than or equal to) with its own meaning; reading the longest possible match prevents it being taken as two operators, which would give a syntax error or the wrong meaning.
parts.working: B1 >= is one relational operator. B1 longest match rule / two tokens would be invalid.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define each term used in paging: (i) page (ii) page frame (iii) page table.
parts.answer: (i) a fixed-size block of a program's logical (virtual) memory (ii) a block of physical memory of the same fixed size that can hold one page (iii) a table that maps each page of a process to the frame that holds it (or shows it is not in memory)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two tasks carried out by the memory management part of an operating system.
parts.answer: Any two of: allocating memory to processes when they start; freeing memory when processes end; keeping track of which memory is free; protecting each process's memory from other processes; moving pages/segments between memory and disk (virtual memory).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why memory protection is needed when several programs run at the same time.
parts.answer: To stop one program reading or overwriting another program's (or the operating system's) memory, by accident or on purpose.
parts.working: B1 prevents processes accessing each other's memory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the pages that are not in RAM are kept when virtual memory is used.
parts.answer: On secondary storage (hard disk/SSD) in a swap file / page file

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a computer that relies heavily on virtual memory runs slowly.
parts.answer: Pages have to be transferred between secondary storage and RAM; secondary storage is much slower than RAM, so the processor waits for the transfers.
parts.working: B1 frequent page swaps between disk and RAM. B1 disk access is much slower than RAM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe segmentation as a method of memory management.
parts.answer: A program is divided into segments of different sizes, each a logical unit such as the code, the data or the stack; each segment is loaded into memory as one block, found using a segment table.
parts.working: B1 variable-size segments. B1 based on logical divisions of the program (code/data/stack/modules).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of segmentation compared with paging.
parts.answer: Advantage: segments match the program's logical structure, so sharing and protecting a whole module is easy. Disadvantage: variable sizes cause external fragmentation (gaps between segments) / harder to allocate.
parts.working: B1 advantage. B1 disadvantage.

stem: A computer uses paging with a page size of 4 KiB (4096 bytes). Addresses are given in denary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the page number and offset of logical address 13 000.
parts.answer: Page 3, offset 712
parts.working: M1 13 000 ÷ 4096 = 3 remainder 712. A1 page 3, offset 712.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The page table shows that page 3 is in frame 9. Calculate the physical address.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the offset does not change when the logical address is translated.
parts.answer: Pages and frames are the same size, so the position of a byte inside its page is the same as its position inside the frame.
parts.working: B1 page size = frame size.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A process has 3 page frames, all empty at the start. It requests pages in this order:
2, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 5, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the least recently used (LRU) algorithm to show which pages are in memory after each request, and count the page faults.
parts.working: M1 when 5 arrives, the least recently used page is 3, giving {1,2,5}. M1 when 4 arrives the LRU page is 1 → {2,4,5}. M1 when 3 arrives LRU is 2 → {3,4,5}; when 2 arrives LRU is 4 → {2,3,5}. A1 7 faults.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why LRU is often a better choice than first-in first-out (FIFO).
parts.answer: Pages used recently are likely to be used again soon, so removing the page unused for the longest time usually causes fewer faults; FIFO may remove a page that is used all the time just because it was loaded first.
parts.working: B1 recently used pages likely to be used again (locality). B1 FIFO can remove a heavily used page.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A computer uses 32-bit virtual addresses and a page size of 4 KiB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of bits used for the offset and for the page number.
parts.answer: Offset 12 bits; page number 20 bits
parts.working: B1 4096 = 2¹² so 12 bits. B1 32 − 12 = 20 bits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of entries in a full page table for one process and the size of the table in MiB if each entry is 4 bytes.
parts.answer: 1 048 576 entries; 4 MiB

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a page fault.
parts.answer: The process tries to access a page that is not currently in RAM.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the steps the operating system takes to deal with a page fault.
parts.answer: An interrupt is generated and the process is suspended (blocked); the OS finds the page on secondary storage; if no frame is free, a page is chosen for replacement (written back to disk if it has changed); the needed page is loaded into the frame; the page table is updated and the process is made ready to continue.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: interrupt/trap and process blocked; locate page on disk; choose victim page using the replacement algorithm (save if modified); load page into frame; update page table and restart the instruction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the hardware uses the page table to convert a virtual address into a physical address.
parts.answer: The virtual address is split into page number and offset; the page number is used as an index into the page table to find the frame number (checking the present bit); the frame number is combined with the unchanged offset to give the physical address.
parts.working: 1 mark each: split into page number and offset; look up the page number in the page table to get the frame; physical address = frame number with the offset (frame × page size + offset).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the present (valid) bit in each page table entry.
parts.answer: It shows whether the page is currently in RAM; if it is not set, a page fault is raised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The page size is 1 KiB. Find the page number and the offset, in hexadecimal, of the virtual address 1A7F (hexadecimal).
parts.answer: Page 6, offset 27F
parts.working: M1 1A7F = 0001 1010 0111 1111; the lowest 10 bits are the offset. A1 page = 000110 = 6, offset = 10 0111 1111 = 27F.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Page 6 is held in frame 0B (hexadecimal). Calculate the physical address in hexadecimal and in denary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why page sizes are always powers of 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A computer in a school laboratory with 4 GiB of RAM runs a web browser with many tabs, a video editor and an antivirus scan at the same time. The disk light is on almost constantly and the programs barely respond. Explain what is happening, and evaluate three possible ways of solving the problem.
parts.answer: Disk thrashing: the processes together need more pages than fit in RAM, so pages are swapped out and almost immediately needed again; the processor spends most of its time waiting for page transfers instead of executing instructions. Solutions: (1) add more RAM – most effective, more pages stay resident, but costs money; (2) close programs / reduce the number of running processes (fewer tabs) – free and immediate, but limits what the user can do; (3) put the page file on a faster SSD – page transfers faster, so less waiting, but it does not reduce the number of swaps and adds wear to the SSD; (4) OS can suspend low-priority processes (e.g. schedule the scan later). Conclusion weighs cost against effect.
parts.working: Explanation (max 3): thrashing named; working sets do not fit in RAM; pages swapped in and out continuously; CPU idle waiting for disk. Evaluation (max 5): for each of three solutions, how it helps (1) and a limitation/cost (1), plus a justified conclusion (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a stack can be implemented as a linked list using dynamically created nodes, explaining how Push and Pop change the pointers.
parts.answer: Each node holds a data item and a pointer to the node below it. A TopPointer points to the top node (null when empty). Push: create a new node, set its pointer to the current TopPointer, then set TopPointer to the new node. Pop: if TopPointer is null the stack is empty; otherwise take the data from the top node, set TopPointer to that node's pointer and release the node.
parts.working: 1 mark each: node = data + pointer; TopPointer (null when empty); Push links new node to old top and updates TopPointer; Pop moves TopPointer to the next node (check for empty).

parts.label: b

parts.answer: The stack grows and shrinks as needed, so there is no fixed maximum size and no unused reserved memory.
parts.working: B1 dynamic size / no overflow until memory runs out.

stem:
An emergency department in a hospital in Lahore keeps waiting patients in a priority queue. Level 1 is the most urgent. The queue is a linked list held in the global array List[0:29] OF Patient, where:
TYPE Patient
   DECLARE Name : STRING
   DECLARE Level : INTEGER
   DECLARE Next : INTEGER
ENDTYPE
The global integers StartPtr and FreePtr point to the first node of the queue and of the free list. The null pointer is −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the procedure AddPatient(Name : STRING, Level : INTEGER), which takes a node from the free list and inserts the patient so that the list stays in ascending order of Level. A new patient must be placed after any patients who already have the same Level. If there is no free node, output "Full".
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE AddPatient(Name : STRING, Level : INTEGER)
   DECLARE NewNode, Current, Previous : INTEGER
   IF FreePtr = -1 THEN
      OUTPUT "Full"
   ELSE
      NewNode ← FreePtr
      FreePtr ← List[FreePtr].Next
      List[NewNode].Name ← Name
      List[NewNode].Level ← Level
      Previous ← -1
      Current ← StartPtr
      WHILE Current <> -1 AND List[Current].Level <= Level
         Previous ← Current
         Current ← List[Current].Next
      ENDWHILE
      List[NewNode].Next ← Current
      IF Previous = -1 THEN
         StartPtr ← NewNode
      ELSE
         List[Previous].Next ← NewNode
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark each: check for empty free list and output Full; take node from FreePtr and update FreePtr; store Name and Level; traverse from StartPtr keeping Previous; loop condition uses <= so equal levels stay first; new node points to Current; insert at start updates StartPtr; otherwise Previous.Next ← NewNode.

stem: A courier company in Karachi stores 500 parcel codes in ascending order in the global array Codes[1:500] OF INTEGER.

FUNCTION FindCode(Target : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   Index ← 1
   WHILE Index <= 500 AND Codes[Index] < Target
      Index ← Index + 1
   ENDWHILE
   IF Index <= 500 THEN
      IF Codes[Index] = Target THEN
         RETURN Index
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
   RETURN -1
ENDFUNCTION

stem: The global array Data[1:1000] OF INTEGER holds Count values in ascending order, where Count is a global integer.
