parts.text: Write pseudocode for the function InsertPosition(NewValue : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER. It uses a binary search to return the index at which NewValue should be inserted to keep the array in order. If NewValue is equal to an existing value, return the index of that value. If NewValue is larger than all values, return Count + 1.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION InsertPosition(NewValue : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Low, High, Mid : INTEGER
   Low ← 1
   High ← Count
   WHILE Low <= High
      Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2
      IF Data[Mid] = NewValue THEN
         RETURN Mid
      ELSE
         IF Data[Mid] < NewValue THEN
            Low ← Mid + 1
         ELSE
            High ← Mid - 1
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN Low
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: Low and High initialised to 1 and Count; loop while Low <= High; calculate Mid; return Mid when equal; adjust Low or High correctly; return Low after the loop.

stem:
A warehouse robot moves along grid lines, only right or down. Paths(R, C) gives the number of different routes across a rectangle R squares down and C squares across:
FUNCTION Paths(R : INTEGER, C : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   IF R = 0 OR C = 0 THEN
      RETURN 1
   ELSE
      RETURN Paths(R - 1, C) + Paths(R, C - 1)
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the values of Paths(1, 3), Paths(2, 2) and Paths(3, 3). Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an iterative pseudocode function PathsIter(R : INTEGER, C : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER that gives the same results for 0 ≤ R ≤ 20 and 0 ≤ C ≤ 20, using a 2D array Table[0:20, 0:20] OF INTEGER.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION PathsIter(R : INTEGER, C : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Table : ARRAY[0:20, 0:20] OF INTEGER
   DECLARE I, J : INTEGER
   FOR I ← 0 TO R
      FOR J ← 0 TO C
         IF I = 0 OR J = 0 THEN
            Table[I, J] ← 1
         ELSE
            Table[I, J] ← Table[I - 1, J] + Table[I, J - 1]
         ENDIF
      NEXT J
   NEXT I
   RETURN Table[R, C]
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: nested loops over rows 0 to R and columns 0 to C (filled so the cells above and to the left are done first); edge cells (I = 0 or J = 0) set to 1; other cells = Table[I − 1, J] + Table[I, J − 1]; RETURN Table[R, C].

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why the iterative version is better for large R and C.
parts.answer: Each value is calculated only once ((R + 1) × (C + 1) steps), whereas the recursive version recalculates the same sub-results many times and the number of calls grows very quickly; it also avoids the overhead of a stack frame for every call, so there is no risk of stack overflow.
parts.working: B1 no repeated calculation / far fewer steps. B1 no call overhead / no stack frames / no stack overflow.

stem: A university in Karachi has three departments. Each keeps its own spreadsheet of the same 4 000 students: Admissions (names, CNIC, address), Accounts (names, fees paid) and Examinations (names, marks). The university wants to replace them with one relational database managed by a DBMS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this plan. Refer to the problems of the current system and to the features of the DBMS.
parts.answer:
Problems now: redundancy (names/addresses stored three times); inconsistency (a change of address made in one sheet only); hard to produce reports needing data from more than one sheet; no fine-grained security – anyone with the file sees everything; data dependence/format differs between departments.
DBMS benefits: data stored once in linked tables (STUDENT, PAYMENT, RESULT) with StudentID as the key; integrity through validation and referential integrity; access rights so Accounts cannot see marks and Examinations cannot see fees; data dictionary documents the structure; queries join tables for reports; central backups.
Drawbacks: cost of software and training; time to transfer and clean up conflicting data; single point of failure, so backups and security become critical.
Conclusion: benefits outweigh costs because of the size of the data and the need for accurate, shared records.
parts.working: Level marking. 5–6: problems and matching DBMS features clearly linked to this scenario, at least one drawback, justified conclusion. 3–4: several relevant points, some linking. 1–2: list of general points. Max 4 if no drawback/conclusion.

parts.text: Calculate the maximum number of comparisons a binary search of the index needs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the designer does not index every field in the table.
parts.answer: Each index uses extra storage, and every insert, update or delete must also update all the indexes, which slows these operations down.
parts.working: 1 mark extra storage; 1 mark slower updates/inserts.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A water utility in Islamabad stores:
CUSTOMER(CustomerID, Name, Address)
METER(MeterNo, InstallDate, CustomerID)
READING(MeterNo, ReadingDate, Units)
CustomerID in METER is declared UNIQUE as well as being a foreign key.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between CUSTOMER and METER and explain how the design shows it.
parts.answer: One-to-one: METER holds CustomerID as a foreign key, and because it is UNIQUE each customer can appear on only one meter (each meter belongs to one customer).
parts.working: 1 mark one-to-one; 1 mark unique foreign key means a customer cannot be linked to two meters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between METER and READING and the primary key of READING.
parts.answer: One-to-many; primary key (MeterNo, ReadingDate).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the DBMS should refuse to delete a meter that has readings, and describe one alternative the utility could use.
parts.answer: Deleting it would leave readings whose MeterNo refers to nothing (orphan records), breaking referential integrity. Alternatives: delete (or archive) the readings first; use a cascading delete; or keep the meter and mark it as inactive/removed.
parts.working: 1 mark orphan records; 1 mark referential integrity; 1 mark sensible alternative.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A school's exam board stores entries as:
ENTRY(CandidateNo, CNIC, Subject, Session, Grade)
A candidate has one candidate number and one CNIC, takes many subjects and may re-sit a subject in a later session.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two candidate keys of ENTRY. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: (CandidateNo, Subject, Session) and (CNIC, Subject, Session). A candidate can take one subject only once in a session, so each combination identifies one entry; CandidateNo and CNIC identify the same person, so either can be used.
parts.working: 1 mark each candidate key; 1 mark explanation including why Session is needed (re-sits).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student suggests (CandidateNo, Subject) as the primary key. Explain the problem this would cause.
parts.answer: A candidate who re-sits a subject would need a second row with the same CandidateNo and Subject; the DBMS would reject it as a duplicate key, so the re-sit result could not be stored.
parts.working: 1 mark re-sits produce a duplicate; 1 mark consequence (insert rejected / data lost).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether CNIC should be kept in ENTRY.
parts.answer: No – CNIC depends only on the candidate, not on the subject or session, so it is repeated in every entry (redundancy). It belongs in a CANDIDATE table keyed on CandidateNo.
parts.working: 1 mark redundancy/partial dependency; 1 mark move to CANDIDATE table.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A bakery in Lahore takes online orders. Each customer can place many orders. Each order is placed by exactly one customer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the E-R diagram for CUSTOMER and ORDER.
parts.answer: Two entity boxes, CUSTOMER and ORDER, joined by a line; one end (single line) at CUSTOMER and the many end (crow's foot) at ORDER.
parts.working: 1 mark two entities joined by a relationship line; 1 mark crow's foot at ORDER end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which table contains the foreign key, and name it.
parts.answer: ORDER contains CustomerID (the primary key of CUSTOMER).
parts.working: 1 mark ORDER; 1 mark CustomerID.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A cricket board is designing a database.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each pair of entities, state the type of relationship: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.
(i) TEAM and CAPTAIN (each team has one captain; a captain leads one team)
(ii) GROUND and MATCH
(iii) PLAYER and MATCH
(iv) TEAM and PLAYER (a player is registered with one team)
parts.answer:
(i) one-to-one
(ii) one-to-many (one ground hosts many matches)
(iii) many-to-many (a player plays in many matches; a match has many players)
(iv) one-to-many (one team has many players)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An E-R diagram for a clinic is described: DOCTOR is linked one-to-many to APPOINTMENT, and PATIENT is linked one-to-many to APPOINTMENT.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between DOCTOR and PATIENT that this design represents.
parts.answer: Many-to-many (a doctor sees many patients; a patient may see many doctors).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the foreign keys in APPOINTMENT.
parts.answer: DoctorID and PatientID
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two other attributes of APPOINTMENT.
parts.answer: Any two: AppointmentDate, AppointmentTime, RoomNo, Reason, Fee.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a software company in Bengaluru every employee is given exactly one parking space, and every parking space belongs to exactly one employee.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of relationship between EMPLOYEE and PARKINGSPACE.
parts.answer: One-to-one

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how this relationship can be implemented in a relational database.
parts.answer: Put the primary key of one table as a foreign key in the other, e.g. SpaceID in EMPLOYEE, and make that foreign key unique so no space is given to two employees.
parts.working: 1 mark foreign key in one of the tables; 1 mark unique so it stays one-to-one.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a designer might instead store the parking space number as an attribute of EMPLOYEE.
parts.answer: If the space has no other attributes worth storing, a separate table adds an unnecessary join; one table is simpler.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A music festival in Islamabad has several stages. Each band performs in one or more time slots. Each time slot is on one stage and is given to exactly one band. A stage has many time slots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the entities and describe the relationships in the E-R diagram.
parts.answer:
Entities BAND, SLOT, STAGE.
BAND one-to-many SLOT (crow's foot at SLOT).
STAGE one-to-many SLOT (crow's foot at SLOT).
parts.working: 1 mark three entities; 1 mark each relationship with correct cardinality (2); 1 mark crow's feet both at SLOT end.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a table design for SLOT, showing its primary key and foreign keys.
parts.answer: SLOT(SlotID, StageID, BandID, SlotDate, StartTime). Primary key SlotID; foreign keys StageID and BandID. Accept composite key (StageID, SlotDate, StartTime).
parts.working: 1 mark sensible primary key; 1 mark both foreign keys.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hotel group uses these tables:
HOTEL(HotelID, Name, City)
ROOM(HotelID, RoomNo, Type)
GUEST(GuestID, Name, Phone)
STAY(StayID, GuestID, HotelID, RoomNo, CheckIn, Nights)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the E-R diagram for these four tables. For each relationship state the entities and the type.
parts.answer: HOTEL one-to-many ROOM; ROOM one-to-many STAY; GUEST one-to-many STAY. (HOTEL and GUEST are therefore linked many-to-many through STAY.)
parts.working: 1 mark each of the three relationships; 1 mark correct direction of all crow's feet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ROOM needs a composite primary key.
parts.answer: Room numbers repeat across hotels (every hotel can have room 101), so RoomNo alone is not unique; HotelID + RoomNo is unique.
parts.working: 1 mark RoomNo repeats in different hotels; 1 mark combination is unique.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hardware wholesaler buys products from suppliers. Each product can be bought from several suppliers, and each supplier sells many products. The price depends on both the product and the supplier.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the relationship between PRODUCT and SUPPLIER cannot be implemented directly.
parts.answer: It is many-to-many. A foreign key field can hold only one value, so neither table can store a list of the other's keys without a repeating group.
parts.working: 1 mark many-to-many; 1 mark a field cannot hold several keys / repeating group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Design the link entity. Give its name, attributes, primary key and the new relationships.
parts.answer: SUPPLY(ProductID, SupplierID, Price). Primary key (ProductID, SupplierID). PRODUCT one-to-many SUPPLY; SUPPLIER one-to-many SUPPLY.
parts.working: 1 mark link table with both foreign keys; 1 mark composite primary key; 1 mark Price stored in the link table and two one-to-many relationships.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student draws this E-R design for a driving school: INSTRUCTOR one-to-many LESSON, LEARNER one-to-many LESSON. She writes the tables as:
INSTRUCTOR(InstructorID, Name, LessonID)
LEARNER(LearnerID, Name, Phone)
LESSON(LessonID, LessonDate, LearnerID)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the error in the table design and explain why it is wrong.
parts.answer: LessonID has been put in INSTRUCTOR (the 'one' side). An instructor gives many lessons, so this field would need many values; the foreign key must go on the 'many' side.
parts.working: 1 mark identifies LessonID in INSTRUCTOR; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite INSTRUCTOR and LESSON correctly.
parts.answer:
INSTRUCTOR(InstructorID, Name)
LESSON(LessonID, LessonDate, LearnerID, InstructorID)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A car-sharing club in Berlin wants a database. Members book cars. Each booking is for one member and one car, with a start and end time. Each car is kept at one parking station; a station holds many cars. When a car is returned damaged, a damage report is written; a booking can have several damage reports, each with a description and a repair cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the entities and describe the E-R diagram, including the type of every relationship.
parts.answer:
Entities: MEMBER, CAR, STATION, BOOKING, DAMAGEREPORT.
MEMBER one-to-many BOOKING; CAR one-to-many BOOKING; STATION one-to-many CAR; BOOKING one-to-many DAMAGEREPORT.
parts.working: 1 mark all five entities; 1 mark for each correct relationship (4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the table designs. Show primary keys and foreign keys.
parts.answer:
MEMBER(MemberID, Name, LicenceNo, Email)
STATION(StationID, Address)
CAR(CarID, RegNo, Model, StationID)
BOOKING(BookingID, MemberID, CarID, StartTime, EndTime)
DAMAGEREPORT(ReportID, BookingID, Description, RepairCost)
parts.working: 1 mark CAR with StationID; 1 mark BOOKING with MemberID and CarID; 1 mark DAMAGEREPORT with BookingID; 1 mark sensible primary keys throughout.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A university in Lahore timetables teaching sessions. A module (e.g. CS201) is taught by one or more lecturers, and a lecturer teaches several modules. Each teaching session is for one module, in one room, at one date and time, and is led by one lecturer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe an E-R design for this scenario. Name each entity and give each relationship and its type.
parts.answer:
Entities: MODULE, LECTURER, ROOM, SESSION, and link entity MODULELECTURER (TEACHES).
MODULE one-to-many MODULELECTURER; LECTURER one-to-many MODULELECTURER (resolving many-to-many).
MODULE one-to-many SESSION; ROOM one-to-many SESSION; LECTURER one-to-many SESSION.
parts.working: 1 mark many-to-many MODULE–LECTURER identified; 1 mark resolved by link entity; 1 mark SESSION linked to MODULE; 1 mark linked to ROOM; 1 mark linked to LECTURER.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a table design for SESSION and state a check that cannot be enforced by keys alone.
parts.answer: SESSION(SessionID, ModuleCode, LecturerID, RoomNo, SessionDate, StartTime). Check: the lecturer leading a session must be one who is listed as teaching that module (or: a room/lecturer is not booked twice at the same time – needs extra rules).
parts.working: 1 mark primary key; 1 mark three foreign keys; 1 mark valid extra rule.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An airline sells seats on flights. A passenger can make many bookings. Each booking is for one passenger on one flight and has a seat number. A flight is operated by one aircraft; an aircraft operates many flights. The seat number must be unique on each flight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why BOOKING is an entity rather than just a relationship between PASSENGER and FLIGHT.
parts.answer: It has its own attributes (seat number, booking date, fare class) and resolves the many-to-many between PASSENGER and FLIGHT, so it must be a table.
parts.working: 1 mark own attributes; 1 mark resolves many-to-many.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the E-R diagram and give the table designs with keys.
parts.answer:
AIRCRAFT one-to-many FLIGHT; FLIGHT one-to-many BOOKING; PASSENGER one-to-many BOOKING.
AIRCRAFT(AircraftID, Model, Seats)
FLIGHT(FlightID, FlightNo, FlightDate, AircraftID)
PASSENGER(PassengerID, Name, PassportNo)
BOOKING(BookingID, PassengerID, FlightID, SeatNo)
parts.working: 1 mark three relationships; 1 mark FLIGHT has AircraftID; 1 mark BOOKING has PassengerID and FlightID; 1 mark keys.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the design ensures a seat is not sold twice on the same flight.
parts.answer: Make (FlightID, SeatNo) a candidate key (unique) in BOOKING, so a second booking with the same seat on the same flight is rejected.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three tables are shown. The primary key of each is given after its name.
P: VET(VetID, VetName, Phone) – primary key VetID
Q: VISIT(PetID, VisitDate, PetName, Reason) – primary key (PetID, VisitDate)
R: PET(PetID, PetName, OwnerID, OwnerName) – primary key PetID

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each table state the highest normal form (1NF, 2NF or 3NF) and give a reason.
parts.answer:
P: 3NF – single key, every attribute depends only on VetID.
Q: 1NF – PetName depends on PetID only, part of the composite key (partial dependency).
R: 2NF – OwnerName depends on OwnerID, a non-key attribute (non-key/transitive dependency); single key, so no partial dependency.
parts.working: 1 mark each normal form, 1 mark each reason.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a partial dependency.
parts.answer: In a table with a composite primary key, a non-key attribute depends on only part of the key, not on the whole key.
parts.working: 1 mark composite key; 1 mark depends on part of it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give an example of a partial dependency in the table RESULT(StudentID, SubjectCode, StudentName, Mark), whose primary key is (StudentID, SubjectCode).
parts.answer: StudentName depends only on StudentID.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a table with a single-attribute primary key is always in 2NF, provided it is in 1NF.
parts.answer: A partial dependency needs a key with more than one part; a single-field key has no 'part', so no partial dependency is possible.

stem:
A vet clinic in Karachi keeps one record per owner:
OWNER(OwnerID, OwnerName, Phone, PetName1, Species1, PetName2, Species2, PetName3, Species3)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this design is not in first normal form.
parts.answer: It has a repeating group: the pet name and species are repeated across columns (PetName1…PetName3), so the number of pets is limited and many fields may be empty.
parts.working: 1 mark repeating group; 1 mark explanation from the table.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the data in 1NF using two tables.
parts.answer:
OWNER(OwnerID, OwnerName, Phone)
PET(PetID, PetName, Species, OwnerID)
parts.working: 1 mark each table with correct key; OwnerID foreign key in PET required for the second mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A delivery firm uses DRIVER(DriverID, DriverName, VanReg, VanCapacity), with primary key DriverID. Each driver uses one van; a van is used by one driver at a time but has its capacity stored in every row it appears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the dependency that stops this table being in 3NF.
parts.answer: VanCapacity depends on VanReg, which is not the primary key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe an update anomaly that this could cause.
parts.answer: If a van's capacity is recorded wrongly and is changed in one row but not in other rows for the same van (e.g. historical rows), the database holds two different capacities for one van.
parts.working: 1 mark change needed in more than one place; 1 mark leads to inconsistent data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a deletion anomaly that this design could cause.
parts.answer: If the only driver of a van leaves and their row is deleted, the van's registration and capacity are lost too.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A company stores staff as:
STAFF(StaffID, StaffName, DeptID, DeptName, DeptFloor)
The table is in 2NF.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the table is in 2NF but not in 3NF.
parts.answer: The primary key is a single attribute, so there is no partial dependency (2NF). DeptName and DeptFloor depend on DeptID, a non-key attribute (non-key dependency), so it is not 3NF.
parts.working: 1 mark reason for 2NF; 1 mark identifies the non-key dependency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Normalise the table to 3NF.
parts.answer:
STAFF(StaffID, StaffName, DeptID)
DEPARTMENT(DeptID, DeptName, DeptFloor)
parts.working: 1 mark each table; DeptID must remain in STAFF as a foreign key.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A training centre stores marks as:
SCORE(TraineeID, CourseCode, TraineeName, CourseTitle, Tutor, Score)
The primary key is (TraineeID, CourseCode). Each course has one tutor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify all the partial dependencies.
parts.answer: TraineeName depends only on TraineeID; CourseTitle and Tutor depend only on CourseCode.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Normalise the data to 2NF.
parts.answer:
TRAINEE(TraineeID, TraineeName)
COURSE(CourseCode, CourseTitle, Tutor)
SCORE(TraineeID, CourseCode, Score)
parts.working: 1 mark each table with keys.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether your tables are also in 3NF. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Yes – in each table all non-key attributes depend only on the whole primary key; there are no non-key dependencies.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A school in Abbottabad stores tutor groups like this:
CLASSLIST(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID, TutorName, TutorRoom)
S01 | Hamza | T2 | Mrs Khan | B12
S02 | Iqra | T1 | Mr Ali | A03
S03 | Javed | T2 | Mrs Khan | B12
S04 | Laiba | T3 | Ms Shah | C07

S06 | Noor | T1 | Mr Ali | A03

parts.text: Mrs Khan moves to room B15. State how many values must be changed in the table.
parts.working: B1: rows S01, S03, S05.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the non-key dependencies in the table.
parts.answer: TutorName and TutorRoom depend on TutorID (not on StudentID).
parts.working: 1 mark TutorID determines; 1 mark both attributes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Normalise the table to 3NF and state how many values must now be changed when Mrs Khan moves room.
parts.answer:
STUDENT(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID)
TUTOR(TutorID, TutorName, TutorRoom)
Only 1 value changes.
parts.working: 1 mark each table; 1 mark one value.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hotel stores bookings as:
BOOKING(BookingNo, GuestID, GuestName, GuestCountry, RoomNo, RoomType, NightlyRate, ArrivalDate)
BookingNo is the primary key. Each room has one type, and the nightly rate depends only on the room type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the dependencies that prevent the table being in 3NF.
parts.answer: GuestName and GuestCountry depend on GuestID; RoomType depends on RoomNo; NightlyRate depends on RoomType.
parts.working: 1 mark each dependency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Normalise the data to 3NF.
parts.answer:
BOOKING(BookingNo, GuestID, RoomNo, ArrivalDate)
GUEST(GuestID, GuestName, GuestCountry)
ROOM(RoomNo, RoomType)
ROOMTYPE(RoomType, NightlyRate)
parts.working: 1 mark each table with correct keys/foreign keys.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A restaurant-delivery app in Lahore prints this order slip:
Order 5512, 2026-09-14, Customer C88 Sana Iqbal, 14 Mall Road
Restaurant R3 Karahi House
Item K1 Chicken karahi × 1 @ Rs 1450
Item N2 Garlic naan × 4 @ Rs 90
Item D5 Mint raita × 2 @ Rs 120
Each item belongs to one restaurant and has one price. An order is from one restaurant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the data as one unnormalised table, showing the repeating group in brackets.
parts.answer: ORDER(OrderNo, OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, Address, RestaurantID, RestaurantName, (ItemCode, ItemName, Price, Quantity))
parts.working: 1 mark all non-repeating attributes; 1 mark repeating group correctly identified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Normalise the data to 3NF. Give each table, with primary keys and foreign keys.
parts.answer:
CUSTOMER(CustomerID, CustomerName, Address)
RESTAURANT(RestaurantID, RestaurantName)
ITEM(ItemCode, ItemName, Price, RestaurantID)
ORDER(OrderNo, OrderDate, CustomerID, RestaurantID)
ORDERLINE(OrderNo, ItemCode, Quantity)
parts.working: 1 mark ORDERLINE with composite key and Quantity; 1 mark ORDER with foreign keys; 1 mark CUSTOMER; 1 mark RESTAURANT; 1 mark ITEM with RestaurantID; 1 mark no derived/total fields and no repeated attributes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the order total and explain why it should not be stored in the ORDER table.
parts.answer: Rs 2050. It can be calculated from ORDERLINE quantities and ITEM prices, so storing it is redundant and it could become inconsistent if a line is changed.
parts.working: 1 mark 1450 + 360 + 240 = 2050; 1 mark derived data/inconsistency.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A college library records loans in this table. The primary key is (BookID, LoanDate).
BookID | LoanDate | Title | MemberID | MemberName | ReturnDate
B1 | 2026-01-05 | Clean Code | M4 | Rafay | 2026-01-19
B2 | 2026-01-05 | Dune | M7 | Zara | 2026-01-12
B1 | 2026-02-02 | Clean Code | M7 | Zara | 2026-02-16
B3 | 2026-02-02 | Dune | M4 | Rafay | 2026-02-20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, explain why Title must depend on BookID and not on the whole key.
parts.answer: B1 has the title 'Clean Code' on two different loan dates – the title is the same whatever the date, so it depends only on BookID (a partial dependency). (Two copies, B2 and B3, can share the title 'Dune', so Title does not identify the book.)
parts.working: 1 mark same BookID gives same Title on different dates; 1 mark names partial dependency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the other functional dependencies in the table.
parts.answer: MemberName depends on MemberID (a non-key dependency); MemberID and ReturnDate depend on the whole key (BookID, LoanDate).
parts.working: 1 mark MemberID → MemberName; 1 mark the full-key dependencies.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Normalise the table to 3NF.
parts.answer:
BOOK(BookID, Title)
MEMBER(MemberID, MemberName)
LOAN(BookID, LoanDate, MemberID, ReturnDate)
parts.working: 1 mark each table with keys.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student designs this table for a school chess tournament and claims it is in 3NF:
GAME(GameID, Round, WhiteID, WhiteName, BlackID, BlackName, Result, ArbiterID, ArbiterPhone)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's claim.
parts.answer: The claim is wrong. The key GameID is a single attribute, so the table is in 2NF, but WhiteName depends on WhiteID, BlackName on BlackID and ArbiterPhone on ArbiterID – all non-key dependencies – so it is not in 3NF. Players' names would be repeated in every game they play.
parts.working: 1 mark 2NF reason; 1 mark at least two non-key dependencies; 1 mark conclusion with consequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Produce a 3NF design.
parts.answer:
PLAYER(PlayerID, PlayerName)
ARBITER(ArbiterID, ArbiterPhone)
GAME(GameID, Round, WhiteID, BlackID, Result, ArbiterID) – WhiteID and BlackID are both foreign keys to PLAYER.
parts.working: 1 mark PLAYER single table used for both colours; 1 mark ARBITER; 1 mark GAME with all foreign keys.

stem:
A school bus service stores:
RIDER(StudentID, StudentName, StopID, StopName, RouteNo, DriverID, DriverName)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the chain of dependencies in RIDER.

parts.working: 1 mark StopID → StopName, RouteNo; 1 mark RouteNo → DriverID; 1 mark DriverID → DriverName.

parts.text: Normalise the table to 3NF.
parts.answer:
STUDENT(StudentID, StudentName, StopID)

ROUTE(RouteNo, DriverID)
DRIVER(DriverID, DriverName)

stem:

BikeID – always 6 characters, e.g. 'AMS042'

Electric – yes or no
FrameSize – a whole number of centimetres
BatteryLevel – a percentage such as 72.5
LastService – the date of the last service

parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A plant nursery in Murree wants a table PLANT with these fields: PlantID (exactly 5 characters, primary key), CommonName (up to 40 characters), Price (a decimal number), Indoor (true/false).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the SQL to create the table PLANT.
parts.answer:
CREATE TABLE PLANT(
 PlantID CHARACTER(5),
 CommonName VARCHAR(40),
 Price REAL,
 Indoor BOOLEAN,
 PRIMARY KEY (PlantID)
);
parts.working: 1 mark CREATE TABLE PLANT( … ); 1 mark PlantID CHARACTER(5); 1 mark other three fields with types; 1 mark PRIMARY KEY (PlantID).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A clinic database has the table DOCTOR(DoctorID, Name, Speciality).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an SQL statement to add a new field RoomNo, a whole number, to DOCTOR.
parts.answer: ALTER TABLE DOCTOR ADD RoomNo INTEGER;
parts.working: 1 mark ALTER TABLE DOCTOR; 1 mark ADD RoomNo INTEGER.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a data definition language (DDL) and a data manipulation language (DML).
parts.answer: DDL creates and changes the structure of the database (databases, tables, fields, keys). DML adds, changes, deletes and queries the data stored in the tables.
parts.working: 1 mark DDL = structure; 1 mark DML = data.

stem:
A food-testing laboratory stores samples and the tests done on them.
SAMPLE: SampleID (8 characters), Product (up to 50 characters), DateReceived (date)
TEST: TestID (integer), SampleID, TestName (up to 30 characters), Result (decimal number), Passed (true/false)
Each test is on one sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the SQL DDL to create both tables, including primary keys and the foreign key.
parts.answer:
CREATE TABLE SAMPLE(
 SampleID CHARACTER(8),
 Product VARCHAR(50),
 DateReceived DATE,
 PRIMARY KEY (SampleID)
);
CREATE TABLE TEST(
 TestID INTEGER,
 SampleID CHARACTER(8),
 TestName VARCHAR(30),
 Result REAL,
 Passed BOOLEAN,

);

stem:
A programmer writes this SQL to create a table for a football academy:
CREATE TABLE TRAINEE
 TraineeID CHARACTER(4),
 Name VARCHAR,
 Age INTEGER,

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three errors in the SQL and write the corrected statement.
parts.answer:
Any three of: no opening bracket after TRAINEE; no closing bracket before the semicolon; VARCHAR has no maximum length; PRIMARY KEY needs brackets round the field name.
CREATE TABLE TRAINEE(

);
parts.working: 1 mark each error (max 3); 1 mark fully correct statement.

stem:
A railway freight database was created without keys:
WAGON(WagonNo, Type, CapacityTonnes)
CONSIGNMENT(ConsignmentID, WagonNo, Goods, WeightTonnes)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write SQL statements to make WagonNo the primary key of WAGON and to make WagonNo in CONSIGNMENT a foreign key referencing WAGON.
parts.answer:
ALTER TABLE WAGON ADD PRIMARY KEY (WagonNo);
ALTER TABLE CONSIGNMENT ADD FOREIGN KEY (WagonNo) REFERENCES WAGON(WagonNo);
parts.working: 1 mark ALTER TABLE WAGON ADD PRIMARY KEY; 1 mark (WagonNo); 1 mark ALTER TABLE CONSIGNMENT ADD FOREIGN KEY (WagonNo); 1 mark REFERENCES WAGON(WagonNo).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the primary key of WAGON must be set before the foreign key in CONSIGNMENT.
parts.answer: A foreign key must refer to a primary (or unique) key in another table; until WagonNo is the primary key of WAGON there is nothing for the foreign key to reference, so the DBMS would reject it.
parts.working: 1 mark foreign key references a primary key; 1 mark would otherwise be rejected/integrity cannot be checked.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A sports club in Dubai records which members attend which classes:
ATTENDANCE(MemberID, ClassID, AttendDate)
MemberID is CHARACTER(5) and refers to MEMBER; ClassID is CHARACTER(3) and refers to CLASS. A member can attend the same class on many dates but only once per date.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the SQL to create the table ATTENDANCE with a suitable composite primary key and both foreign keys.
parts.answer:
CREATE TABLE ATTENDANCE(
 MemberID CHARACTER(5),
 ClassID CHARACTER(3),
 AttendDate DATE,
 PRIMARY KEY (MemberID, ClassID, AttendDate),
 FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES MEMBER(MemberID),
 FOREIGN KEY (ClassID) REFERENCES CLASS(ClassID)
);
parts.working: 1 mark fields with types; 1 mark composite key; 1 mark AttendDate included in key (justified by repeat attendance); 1 mark each foreign key (max 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why AttendDate must be part of the primary key.
parts.answer: Without it a member could attend a class only once, because (MemberID, ClassID) would be repeated on later dates.

stem: An NGO in Quetta runs mobile health camps. Each camp has an ID (integer), a village name (up to 40 characters) and a date. Each volunteer has an ID (6 characters), a name (up to 50 characters) and a phone number (up to 15 characters, may start with + or 0). Volunteers work at many camps and each camp has many volunteers; for each volunteer at each camp the number of hours worked (a decimal) is recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the SQL DDL to create the database HEALTHCAMPS and the three tables needed, with all primary and foreign keys.
parts.working: 1 mark CREATE DATABASE; 1 mark CAMP; 1 mark VOLUNTEER; 1 mark link table identified; 1 mark composite key; 1 mark each foreign key (2); 1 mark all data types sensible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Phone is not stored as an INTEGER.
parts.answer: Phone numbers can start with + or 0 (leading zeros would be lost as an integer) and are never used in calculations; a phone number may also be too long for an integer type.
parts.working: 1 mark leading 0/+ lost or not allowed; 1 mark no arithmetic needed / length.

stem: A company stores 25 000 customer records. Its Address field can be declared as CHARACTER(60) or VARCHAR(60). Assume CHARACTER(60) always uses 60 bytes, and VARCHAR(60) uses 1 byte per character stored plus 2 bytes to record the length. The average address is 22 characters long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the storage needed for the Address field of all records with each data type.
parts.answer:
CHARACTER(60): 1 500 000 bytes
VARCHAR(60): 600 000 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the saving, in bytes, from using VARCHAR(60).
parts.answer: 900 000 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why CHARACTER(n) is still the better choice for a field such as a 13-digit CNIC number stored as text.
parts.answer: Every value is exactly the same length, so no space is wasted by fixed length and no extra length bytes are needed; fixed-length fields are also quicker for the DBMS to locate.
parts.working: 1 mark values always the same length; 1 mark no overhead / faster access.

stem:
This DDL has been run:
CREATE TABLE AUTHOR(
 AuthorID CHARACTER(4),
 Name VARCHAR(40),
 PRIMARY KEY (AuthorID)
);
CREATE TABLE TITLE(
 ISBN CHARACTER(13),
 BookName VARCHAR(60),
 AuthorID CHARACTER(4),
 PRIMARY KEY (ISBN),
 FOREIGN KEY (AuthorID) REFERENCES AUTHOR(AuthorID)
);
AUTHOR contains one row: ('A001', 'Bapsi Sidhwa').

parts.label: a
parts.answer:
(i) Accepted – A001 exists in AUTHOR.
(ii) Rejected – A002 does not exist in AUTHOR (referential integrity).
(iii) Rejected – A001 is already used as a primary key (duplicate key).
(iv) Rejected – TITLE still has a book referring to A001; deleting it would leave an orphan record.
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the statements, in order, needed so that 'The Crow Eaters' can be stored with a new author A002, 'Bapsi Sidhwa (pen name)'.
parts.answer:
INSERT INTO AUTHOR VALUES ('A002', 'Bapsi Sidhwa (pen name)');
INSERT INTO TITLE VALUES ('9780000000024', 'The Crow Eaters', 'A002');
parts.working: 1 mark author inserted first; 1 mark then title.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An e-commerce company's DBMS makes a full backup of its 40 GB database every Sunday night and an incremental backup every other night (Monday to Saturday). Each incremental backup averages 1.5 GB. The database fails on Thursday morning, before that day's work starts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the backup storage used in one week with this scheme, and with a full backup every night instead.
parts.answer:
Full + incremental: 49 GB
Full every night: 280 GB

parts.label: b
parts.text: List, in order, the backups that must be restored after the failure on Thursday morning.
parts.answer: Sunday's full backup, then the incremental backups of Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday nights, in that order.
parts.working: 1 mark full backup first; 1 mark the three incrementals in date order.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss one disadvantage of the incremental scheme and one way the DBMS can reduce the data lost in a failure.
parts.answer: Restoring takes longer and needs every incremental backup in the chain – if one is damaged, later changes are lost. The DBMS can keep a transaction log/journal of every change since the last backup and replay it, so almost no work is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark disadvantage; 1 mark transaction log / more frequent backups / mirrored copy.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Data was imported from an old system into a courier database. The primary keys are CourierID and ParcelNo. CourierID in PARCEL is a foreign key to COURIER.
COURIER
CourierID | Name
C1 | Tariq
C2 | Mehwish
C2 | Yasir
(blank) | Saima

PARCEL
ParcelNo | CourierID | Destination
9001 | C1 | Gwadar
9002 | C4 | Turbat
9003 | C2 | Pasni
9001 | C1 | Ormara

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify every row that would be rejected by the DBMS if the keys had been enforced. For each one give the rule it breaks.
parts.answer:
COURIER: second C2 row (Yasir) – duplicate primary key; blank CourierID (Saima) – a primary key cannot be null/empty (entity integrity).
PARCEL: 9002 – C4 does not exist in COURIER (referential integrity); second 9001 (Ormara) – duplicate primary key.
Row 9003 (C2) is accepted because C2 exists, but C2 is ambiguous while the duplicate row is present.
parts.working: 1 mark each of the four rejected rows with rule; 1 mark naming entity integrity vs referential integrity correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a primary key value must never be null.
parts.answer: A null value cannot identify a record, and two nulls cannot be told apart, so the row could never be found or referenced reliably.

stem:
A blood bank in Peshawar keeps:
DONOR: DonorID (exactly 7 characters), Name (up to 60 characters), BloodGroup (up to 3 characters, e.g. 'AB+'), Eligible (true/false)
DONATION: DonationNo (integer), DonorID, DonationDate, DonationTime, VolumeML (integer)
A donor can give blood many times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the SQL DDL to create both tables with all keys.
parts.answer:
CREATE TABLE DONOR(
 DonorID CHARACTER(7),
 Name VARCHAR(60),
 BloodGroup VARCHAR(3),
 Eligible BOOLEAN,
 PRIMARY KEY (DonorID)
);
CREATE TABLE DONATION(
 DonationNo INTEGER,
 DonorID CHARACTER(7),
 DonationDate DATE,
 DonationTime TIME,
 VolumeML INTEGER,
 PRIMARY KEY (DonationNo),
 FOREIGN KEY (DonorID) REFERENCES DONOR(DonorID)
);
parts.working: 1 mark DONOR fields/types; 1 mark DONOR key; 1 mark DONATION fields incl. DATE and TIME; 1 mark DONATION key; 1 mark FOREIGN KEY; 1 mark REFERENCES DONOR(DonorID).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The blood bank now wants to store each donor's phone number. Write the SQL to do this.
parts.answer: ALTER TABLE DONOR ADD Phone VARCHAR(15);
parts.working: 1 mark ALTER TABLE DONOR ADD; 1 mark Phone with a text type.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an SQL query to output the name of each eligible donor with blood group 'O-' together with the total volume they have donated.
parts.answer:
SELECT DONOR.Name, SUM(DONATION.VolumeML)
FROM DONOR INNER JOIN DONATION ON DONOR.DonorID = DONATION.DonorID
WHERE DONOR.BloodGroup = 'O-' AND DONOR.Eligible = TRUE
GROUP BY DONOR.Name;
parts.working: 1 mark SELECT Name, SUM(VolumeML); 1 mark join on DonorID; 1 mark WHERE both conditions; 1 mark GROUP BY.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode to declare a record type TVehicle for this data.

stem:
TYPE TDirection = (North, East, South, West)
DECLARE Heading : TDirection

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what kind of user-defined data type TDirection is, and whether it is composite or non-composite.
parts.answer: Enumerated; non-composite.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Heading has the value South. State the value of each expression.
(i) Heading = East
(ii) Heading = South
parts.answer: (i) FALSE (ii) TRUE
parts.working: 1 mark each – Heading holds one value, so it equals East only if it is East and equals South only if it is South.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
TYPE TIntPtr = ^INTEGER
A procedure is written to swap two integers using pointers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the pseudocode procedure Swap(P1 : TIntPtr, P2 : TIntPtr) so that it swaps the values that P1 and P2 point to.
parts.answer:
PROCEDURE Swap(P1 : TIntPtr, P2 : TIntPtr)
 DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
 Temp ← P1^
 P1^ ← P2^
 P2^ ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE
parts.working: 1 mark local Temp declared; 1 mark Temp ← P1^ and P1^ ← P2^; 1 mark P2^ ← Temp (dereferencing used throughout).

parts.label: b
parts.text: X has the value 8 and Y has the value 3. State the values of X and Y after the call Swap(@X, @Y).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Swap(X, Y) with INTEGER parameters passed by value would not swap the original variables.
parts.answer: Passing by value gives the procedure copies of X and Y; the copies are swapped but the originals are unchanged. Passing addresses (pointers) lets the procedure change the original memory locations.
parts.working: 1 mark copies; 1 mark pointers give access to the originals.

stem:
An NGO matches volunteers to jobs.
TYPE TSkill = (Driving, FirstAid, Urdu, Pashto, Computing)
TYPE TSkillSet = SET OF TSkill
DEFINE Needed (Driving, FirstAid, Pashto) : TSkillSet
DEFINE Hina (Driving, Urdu, Pashto, Computing) : TSkillSet

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Give the result of each operation.
(i) Needed INTERSECTION Hina
(ii) Needed DIFFERENCE Hina
(iii) Needed UNION Hina
parts.answer:
(i) (Driving, Pashto)
(ii) (FirstAid)
(iii) (Driving, FirstAid, Urdu, Pashto, Computing)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the NGO could use one of these operations to decide whether a volunteer has every skill a job needs.
parts.answer: Find Needed DIFFERENCE Volunteer; if the result is the empty set, the volunteer has all the needed skills (Hina does not, because FirstAid is left).
parts.working: 1 mark uses DIFFERENCE (or INTERSECTION = Needed); 1 mark test for empty set / equality.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value of the expression Urdu IN Needed.
parts.answer: FALSE

author: HomiLabs

stem:
TYPE TStatus = (Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Returned)
TYPE TOrder
 DECLARE OrderID : STRING
 DECLARE Value : REAL
 DECLARE Status : TStatus
ENDTYPE
DECLARE Orders : ARRAY[1:300] OF TOrder
DECLARE NumOrders : INTEGER   // number of elements in use

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a pseudocode function CountStatus(S : TStatus) RETURNS INTEGER that returns how many orders in use have status S.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION CountStatus(S : TStatus) RETURNS INTEGER
 DECLARE Count, i : INTEGER
 Count ← 0
 FOR i ← 1 TO NumOrders
  IF Orders[i].Status = S THEN
   Count ← Count + 1
  ENDIF
 NEXT i
 RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark header and RETURN; 1 mark count initialised; 1 mark loop 1 to NumOrders; 1 mark compare Orders[i].Status = S and increment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a pseudocode statement that outputs the total value of returned orders, using a function TotalValue(S : TStatus) RETURNS REAL that you may assume exists.
parts.answer: OUTPUT TotalValue(Returned)
parts.working: B1 – the enumerated value is used without quotes.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
TYPE TIntPtr = ^INTEGER
DECLARE A, B : INTEGER
DECLARE P, Q : TIntPtr
Memory addresses: A is at 5000, B at 5001, P at 5002, Q at 5003.
A ← 12
B ← 30
P ← @A
Q ← @B
P^ ← P^ + Q^
Q ← P
Q^ ← Q^ − 5
B ← P^ * 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the final values of A, B, P, Q and P^.
parts.working: 1 mark each. P^ ← P^ + Q^ makes A 42; Q then points to A, so Q^ ← Q^ − 5 makes A 37; B ← 37 × 2 = 74.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of @P.
parts.working: B1 – the address of the pointer variable itself.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why changing Q^ after the statement Q ← P changes A and not B.
parts.answer: After Q ← P, Q holds the same address as P (5000, the address of A), so dereferencing Q accesses A; B's address is no longer stored in Q.
parts.working: 1 mark Q now holds A's address; 1 mark dereference accesses that location.

author: HomiLabs

stem: An airline seat-planning program in Karachi needs to store, for each seat on an aircraft: the seat code (e.g. '14C'), the cabin (Economy, Premium or Business), the meals the passenger has asked for from a fixed list (Vegetarian, Halal, Diabetic, Child, Gluten-free – any combination), whether it is a window seat, and a link to the passenger's record held in dynamic memory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write pseudocode type declarations for this data. Use an enumerated type, a set type, a pointer type and a record type. Assume TPassenger is already declared.
parts.answer:
TYPE TCabin = (Economy, Premium, Business)
TYPE TMeal = (Vegetarian, Halal, Diabetic, Child, GlutenFree)
TYPE TMealSet = SET OF TMeal
TYPE TPassPtr = ^TPassenger
TYPE TSeat
 DECLARE SeatCode : STRING
 DECLARE Cabin : TCabin
 DECLARE Meals : TMealSet
 DECLARE Window : BOOLEAN
 DECLARE Passenger : TPassPtr
ENDTYPE
parts.working: 1 mark enumerated cabin; 1 mark enumerated meal; 1 mark set of meals; 1 mark pointer type; 1 mark record with all five fields; 1 mark fields use the new types.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Justify the choice of a set for the meals rather than an array of five Booleans.
parts.answer: A set holds any combination of distinct values with no duplicates and no order, which matches meal requests exactly; set operations (IN, UNION, DIFFERENCE) make it easy to test or combine requests, e.g. Halal IN Meals.
parts.working: 1 mark matches unordered/no-duplicate nature; 1 mark use of set operations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the passenger is linked by a pointer instead of copying the passenger record into every seat.
parts.answer: The passenger record is stored once in dynamic memory; the seat holds only its address, saving memory, and any change to the passenger record is seen through every pointer. An unoccupied seat can hold a null pointer.
parts.working: 1 mark avoids duplication/saves memory; 1 mark changes seen everywhere or null for empty seat.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

stem: In this question, floating-point numbers use a 10-bit mantissa followed by a 6-bit exponent, both in two's complement form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show how the denary number +13.5 is represented as a normalised floating-point number in this format.
parts.answer: Mantissa 0110110000, exponent 000100
parts.working: M1 13.5 = 1101.1 in binary; M1 = 0.11011 × 2⁴; A1 mantissa 0110110000 and exponent 000100.
